item.title: Eric Clapton says selling these two legendary guitars was a “big, big mistake”: “They're very sacred things to me”
item.dc:content:
Eric Clapton says he made a “big, big mistake” selling two of the most important guitars of his career, even though he sold them for a cause close to his heart.

The 1964 Cherry Red Gibson ES-335 and “Blackie” — the legendary Stratocaster assembled with parts from a trio of 1956/’57 Strats — were among the guitars Clapton auctioned in 2004 to raise money for the Crossroads Centre, the addiction treatment facility he founded in Antigua. More than two decades later, he says he still struggles with letting them go.

Speaking to Guitar Center, Clapton explains why guitars hold such significance for him.

“If you're in a bad place and you pick up a guitar there's a strong chance you’ll get out of that,” he says. “They're very sacred things to me.”

That makes the loss of Blackie and the ES-335 particularly difficult. Together, the guitars brought $1,807,000 at the 2004 auction, which raised $7.44 million in total, with approximately $6.4 million going to Crossroads.

But Clapton says he had to keep reminding himself why he was willing to part with them.

“When the auction was going on, I had to constantly keep saying, ‘This is your purpose. You are an alcoholic, and if you don't stay sober, you won’t be able to help other alcoholics to achieve sobriety,’” he says. “So this is all for that purpose. Crossroads is for that purpose. So I’m disproportionately obsessed with the survival of that place.

“My primary purpose is to stay sober, and help other alcoholics to achieve sobriety. That’s above me being a musician or a husband or a father. It’s the number one thing.”

The comments come as Clapton’s latest Crossroads Guitar Festival has once again put the cause in the spotlight. The event supports the Antigua-based treatment center, which Clapton established in 1998 following his own struggles with addiction.

The guitars he sold for it could hardly have been more significant to his career.

The ES-335 was a 1964 cherry-red model Clapton had acquired during his Yardbirds days and subsequently used with Cream. It featured during the band’s final run of performances in 1968, including their November show at London’s Royal Albert Hall. An Epiphone reissue of the guitar is reportedly due in 2027.

Blackie, meanwhile, became the defining Stratocaster of Clapton’s career. Inspired by his admiration for Jimi Hendrix and Steve Winwood, Clapton moved away from the Gibson Les Pauls he had favored and began playing Fender Stratocasters around 1970.

His first major Strat was a sunburst model known as “Brownie.” Blackie came together after Clapton bought six 1950s Strats from Sho-Bud in Nashville. He gave three to George Harrison, Pete Townshend and Winwood, then took the remaining three apart and assembled what he considered the best components into a single instrument.

“They were so out of fashion you could pick up a perfectly genuine Strat for two hundred or three hundred dollars,” Clapton said in the 2004 book The Stratocaster Chronicles. “So I bought all of them.”

Ahead of the auction that same year, Clapton described Blackie to Christie’s as an unusually personal instrument.

“It is such a personal thing,” he said. “I almost made this guitar myself – from different components, and I’ve never done that before or since.”

Blackie went on to become Clapton’s main guitar for years, appearing on recordings including “Cocaine,” “I Shot the Sheriff” and “Lay Down Sally.” Its history even includes a brief cameo from Todd Rundgren, who borrowed it onstage after breaking a string.

Clapton may never get either guitar back. But his latest comments make clear that, more than 20 years after the auction, he still feels the weight of what he gave up — even if he remains convinced of why he did it.

item.title: Fans want Keanu Reeves to induct Peter Hook into the Rock Hall after “Love Will Tear Us Apart” tribute
item.dc:content:
It’s with good reason that Joy Division’s 1980 hit “Love Will Tear Us Apart” consistently scores highly in various rankings of the world’s greatest basslines. Now, actor and bass player Keanu Reeves has his own small chapter in the song’s immortal legacy.

Released a month after singer Ian Curtis’ suicide, the song quickly became a defining track of the post-punk sound, with NME even crowning it the greatest single ever in 2002, despite the fact that it never appeared on a studio album.

The song has been named as Reeves’ all-time favorite, and it’s a fine example of his love of highly melodic basslines. Asked to pick one desert-island song by Stephen Colbert in 2022, he chose it with little hesitation.

Fast forward to September 21, 2026, and after introducing Peter Hook & the Light onstage at a show at the Warfield in San Francisco, the English bass icon dedicated the song to the 62-year-old Canadian.

For those uninitiated, Reeves enjoyed mild success with his alt-rock power trio, Dogstar, in the early 1990s, before his acting gigs took over his life. The band reunited in 2020 and have since released two albums, in 2023 and 2026.

Dogstar’s early days were fueled by a $300 bass he bought in a Guitar Center parking lot, but Reeves recently took possession of an innovatively wired Fender Custom Shop. It shows that his ear for tone runs deep.

The actor, who is currently on tour with Dogstar, was fortunate enough to have an off day on September 21, ahead of a San Francisco show of his own the following night. That afforded him the chance to introduce one of his heroes to the stage at the Warfield.

A post shared by @thequakesanfrancisco

A photo posted by

“The one, the only Peter Hook and the Light, playing the music we all love from then, today and tomorrow,” he beamed. He then embraced Hook before retreating to a private box, where he was seen revelling in the band’s 29-song set, which concluded with that enduring Joy Division song.

Before his tour, Hook — who plays in the band alongside his bassist son, Jack Bates — sat down to discuss his legacy with Guitar Player. He’s set to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame this fall in recognition of his work in Joy Division and New Order, following Soundgarden, Bad Company, and Warren Zevon getting the nod last year.

A post shared by @musicpocketmagazine

A photo posted by

Yet, when asked how he came up with so many memorable basslines over his career, he admitted that the secret is lost on him.

Comments on an Instagram post from Hook that showed “a couple of bass players hanging out in San Francisco” have suggested Reeves should be the one to induct Hook into the Hall of Fame in November. After Jim Carrey inducted Soundgarden and David Letterman did the same for the late Warren Zevon last year, it isn’t out of the question.

A post shared by Peter Hook & The Light (@peterhook_thelight)

A photo posted by

item.title: Todd Rundgren says only one Beatle “survived” the breakup: “All the other guys had some sort of issues”
item.dc:content:
When the Beatles broke up in 1970, each member faced the daunting task of establishing a career outside the biggest band in the world. John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr all found varying degrees of post-Beatles success, but the transition wasn’t always easy.

Harrison, who had spent his Beatles years struggling to break through the Lennon-McCartney stronghold, came out of the gates quickest, with 1970’s All Things Must Pass a reputation-reaffirming smash. McCartney initially floundered away from the band, while Lennon and Starr also went on to enjoy solo success.

But according to Todd Rundgren, only one of the four truly managed to leave the Beatles behind.

“Ringo was maybe the only one who survived the Beatles,” he tells Vulture in a new interview. “All the other guys had some sort of issues they had to deal with. Paul McCartney, even today, is so afraid that people forget who he is that he’ll show up at a mall opening.”

While McCartney initially floundered away from the band, even questioning whether there was some truth to the ‘Paul is dead’ rumors after all, Lennon and Starr also went on to enjoy solo success. With this year’s Long Long Road his 22nd solo album, it’s hard to argue that Starr’s output over the last 56 years has been anything but tireless.

As a member of the Ringo Starr All-Star Band, Rundgren saw the drummer’s operation up close, and he felt the shadow of his former glories never hung over him.

“Ringo finally got over being a Beatle and became Ringo,” he notes. “[But] there was a time early on during the All-Starr tours where he was afraid that, if he stopped anywhere in public, he’d be mobbed to death. So he would ignore everybody.”

That had changed, Rundgren adds, by the latter years of his All-Star Band tenure, which stretched from the early 1990s to 2017. Even the first shows he played, in 1992, were some 22 years after the band’s breakup, so Rundgren concedes that Starr’s wounds and worries didn’t heal overnight.

“After the Beatles were done, he recorded some stuff but didn’t go out on tour,” the guitarist says. “He was too stage shy. Cut to 10 years later, and Ringo decides that as part of his rehabilitation he’s going to start playing again. He got into real big trouble because when he stopped playing, he didn’t know what to do with himself.

“He started hanging around with [American singer-songwriter] Harry Nilsson and getting into all sorts of mischief, and he realized that he was probably going to die unless he got into rehab. Part of the rehab was to start the All-Starr Band.”

Countless tours and eight All-Star live albums later, it’s clear the rehabilitation worked for the drummer. Rundgren has been in the news recently for a much less complimentary assessment of Taylor Swift’s songwriting, which he called “the apotheosis of mediocrity” in a recent interview.

Still, it’s not the only time Rundgren and the Beatles have crossed paths. He saved one recording session after Harrison stepped away. He’s also worked with Meat Loaf, David Bowie, and, much to his disdain, nearly jammed with Hendrix, but never quite got that feather in his cap.
item.description: The guitarist looks back on the Fab Four’s post-Beatles struggles and the rehabilitation that helped one member move beyond the shadow of the band

item.title: Rival Son’s Scott Holiday on the hit-and-run accident that inspired his new solo album
item.dc:content:
A not-so-funny but impactful thing happened to Rival Sons’ Scott Holiday on the way to making his first solo album, the just-released Topology.

The album was already well underway last October 17, when the guitarist spent an evening hanging out with friends at a bar about a block away from his house in Huntington Beach, California.

“Not getting obliterated or going too big or anything. Just hanging out and having a social night,” Holiday explains.

Shortly after midnight, he hopped on his electric bike to head home and began pulling out of the parking lot.

“The only thing I remember is a flash, and then I have a wake-up from paramedics,” Holiday tells Guitar Player via Zoom. “I have a little blank spot there, which is just no fun.”

Holiday was the victim of a hit-and-run, and the driver was never found. The guitarist broke six ribs — some in multiple spots, requiring titanium plates to fix — and “had a couple pretty good knocks on the head.”

A feared year of healing turned into about 30 days. “You can’t move, you can’t breathe, you can’t clear your throat, coughing is out of the question, a sneeze is an emergency on planet Earth,” he says. “You’re kinda in this still state, just trapped.”

But in that still state, a vision for the nine-track Topology — a “psychedelic, exploratory, maybe even poppier sounding record” released under the moniker Hol1D4y — began to coalesce.

“I’m just kind of in this delirious state, having to get real meditative and deep,” Holiday recalls. “And in that state I spent a lot of time thinking about a lot of things, and Topology was always percolating in the back of my head — ‘How am I going to get back? I’m in the middle of this and I’m inspired and I need to get healed, ’cause I got to get back to it.’

“I had already decided that I was going to sing on the album. I wondered, ‘If I’m going to use my voice and raise it up, is there something I care about enough to sing songs about it?’

“And there were a lot of things that were on my mind that I would want to share with people — things I talk about with my friends and my family and my wife, things that we get intellectual about and that resonate with me deeply.

“So I began to approach the album, song by song, in that state.”

Rival Sons spent 2025 on the road supporting its 2023 album Lightbringer. During the summer, Holiday began working on new music, writing some of it around drum tracks he solicited from bandmate Mike Miley.

“There was no idea for a solo record at all,” Holiday says. “I thought I was just writing for the next Rival Sons record.”

But Holiday began noticing that some of those things were not like the others.

“There were some songs that just felt like a different thing,” he explains.

When bassist Dave Beste asked for demos without the bass guitar parts on them, Holiday had a revelation.

“The second I went to remove the bass I decided, ‘I can’t take the bass off, ’cause I like the bass. I actually like what I’m playing.’ So I began to realize these tracks were a little more personal to me. I think they presented themselves to me as a solo project.

“And I just immediately ran with it … with a vote of confidence from the rest of the band, ’cause they all loved the material.”

Even then, Holiday thought he’d be making an instrumental album.

“But then I had a few of these tracks, like ‘Autonomatic,’ ‘Holotropic,’ that didn’t feel exactly like instrumentals,” he recalls. “I really felt like they were asking for a story, asking for a more traditional form.”

Rather than bring in guest vocalists “like we see a lot of guitar players do,” Holiday decided to step up to the mic himself. “I felt a close connection to these tunes,” he says, “and I didn’t want to take that closeness away by having somebody else sing them.

“And then I started thinking about what I wanted to sing about.”

Topology’s lyrics are undeniably — and unapologetically — cerebral and high-minded, as evidenced even by the titles mentioned as well as tracks such as “Panoptic,” “Equanimity” and “Metacognition.” Holiday even commissioned philosopher Dylan Trigg to write an explanatory essay for the back cover.

The album is, in a nutshell, “about connection,” Holiday explains. “It’s about aligning ourselves, waking up and optimizing ourselves in this material world.

“I know it sounds airy-fairy and far-out,” he says with a laugh, “but this is something that’s resonated with me for a long, long, long time.

“So that’s where I went. After the accident, I got into such a physically vulnerable state that it affected my mental vulnerability in a way I actually welcomed. It shook some stuff loose, literally and in an analogous way, that I was able to go, ‘Oh, man, I feel close to that mental, sensitive part of myself’ … and I wanted to hang onto that coming into the record and singing and using my voice, ’cause it’s different than the guitar, it’s different than bass. It’s different than drums.”

While Holiday brought in Jesse Nason to perform with an arsenal of vintage keyboards — including Moog, Oberheim and Prophet synthesizers — Topology is very much a guitar player’s showpiece.

That’s particularly true on “Crism,” a nearly 12-minute instrumental that cascades through mood and tempo changes, as well as some of Holiday’s most biting and soaring guitar solos. And surprisingly it was composed to a single drum track that Miley provided.

“We had just lost Jack DeJohnette, so we were all listening to a bunch of those wonderful records from the early ’70s, totally inspired,” says Holiday, who also cites John Coltrane, early Miles Davis and 1970s-era King Crimson as influential sources. “And I had just told the guys that for the solo record I wanted to do something like that.”

Miley’s drum track captured that vibe perfectly.

“It was different from anything he had ever sent me,” Holiday says. “I was completely blown away. I just told him, ‘It’s a masterpiece!’ I told him, ‘I’m not gonna edit it.’ Jesse came over and we plugged in and played all the way through the song five times, full takes, and I took sections from each of them and made the song.”

Holiday kept the gear for Topology “pretty simple … the cream of the crop of my goodies,” including a 1961 Gibson ES-345, a 1964 “Platypus” Firebird and a 1966 ES-330. Custom Kauer and Banker models were used for overdubs, while the acoustic guitars were a Martin OM42 and Guild F412. All of the bass parts were recorded with a Supro Huntington.

For amplifiers Holiday used some Universal Audio models but primarily stuck to a pair of small Supros — an Amulet and a 1600 Supreme. He “didn’t want to go too bananas” with effects, using Fjord Fuzz Odin octave fuzz and Fjaer reverb pedals as well as an Electro-Harmonix POG octave generator on the track “Veridream.”

But the “star of the show,” Holiday says, was a prototype from effects-maker Jeorge Tripps.

“This pedal is able to make eight presets, and I used them all and it sounds like eight different pedals,” Holiday explains. “So this is the star of the show, and I love that I made a record with a pedal that’s unavailable to the world — and may never be, who knows?”

Holiday knows that between him singing and the different playing approaches, Topology presents him in a manner that might surprise Rival Sons fans. And he’s looking forward to them hearing it.

“I didn’t overthink at all when I made this music,” he continues. “This was more like, ‘This is natural. This is what I should do. This is where the color goes, this is where the texture goes, this is how long the songs need to be.’

“It was like releasing a valve, but, ‘Oh, wow, I didn’t even know that valve needed to be released, but there it is,’ and things moved a lot easier.”

As for the Hol1D4y moniker, it reflects Holiday’s interest in numerology and sacred geometry.

“I really loved this idea of using a 1 and 4. In numerology the 1 and 4 become a 5. In numerology, 5 represents: adventure, freedom, curiosity and dynamic change. In sacred geometry the number 5 represents the bridge between the physical and spiritual realms.

“So it has great significance with the things I’m talking about and felt about this project.”

Now Holiday is preparing to make Hol1D4y a live endeavor. He’s assembled a five-member band and has built three special rigs for himself and the two others who will play guitar. He’s also worked with Banker’s Matt Hughes to create a custom double-neck guitar and bass.

“Sometimes I’ll be playing bass on a verse and then I’m playing guitar on the chorus, or vice versa,” Holiday says. “I move it all around. Basically I’m gonna be super selfish and just want to play and have fun.”

Rival Sons returns to the road in late October for U.S. dates through November, followed by studio work on a new album in early 2027. Holiday hopes to launch Hol1D4y live in February or March.

“But we are going to tour this, one way or another. I promise you that. Where there’s a will, there’s a way.”
item.description: The Rival Sons guitarist goes solo with Topology, a cerebral, exploratory record that finds him singing, embracing prog and fusion, and pushing his guitar playing into new territory
item.dc:creator: Gary Graff

“I’m just kind of in this delirious state, having to get real meditative and deep,” Holiday recalls. “And in that state I spent a lot of time thinking about a lot of things, and Topology was always percolating in the back of my head — ‘How am I going to get back? I’m in the middle of this and I’m inspired and I need to get healed, ’cause I got to get back to it.’

“I had already decided that I was going to sing on the album. I wondered, ‘If I’m going to use my voice and raise it up, is there something I care about enough to sing songs about it?’

“And there were a lot of things that were on my mind that I would want to share with people — things I talk about with my friends and my family and my wife, things that we get intellectual about and that resonate with me deeply.

“So I began to approach the album, song by song, in that state.”

Rival Sons spent 2025 on the road supporting its 2023 album Lightbringer. During the summer, Holiday began working on new music, writing some of it around drum tracks he solicited from bandmate Mike Miley.

“There was no idea for a solo record at all,” Holiday says. “I thought I was just writing for the next Rival Sons record.”

But Holiday began noticing that some of those things were not like the others.

“There were some songs that just felt like a different thing,” he explains.

When bassist Dave Beste asked for demos without the bass guitar parts on them, Holiday had a revelation.

“The second I went to remove the bass I decided, ‘I can’t take the bass off, ’cause I like the bass. I actually like what I’m playing.’ So I began to realize these tracks were a little more personal to me. I think they presented themselves to me as a solo project.

“And I just immediately ran with it … with a vote of confidence from the rest of the band, ’cause they all loved the material.”

Even then, Holiday thought he’d be making an instrumental album.

“But then I had a few of these tracks, like ‘Autonomatic,’ ‘Holotropic,’ that didn’t feel exactly like instrumentals,” he recalls. “I really felt like they were asking for a story, asking for a more traditional form.”

Rather than bring in guest vocalists “like we see a lot of guitar players do,” Holiday decided to step up to the mic himself. “I felt a close connection to these tunes,” he says, “and I didn’t want to take that closeness away by having somebody else sing them.

“And then I started thinking about what I wanted to sing about.”

Topology’s lyrics are undeniably — and unapologetically — cerebral and high-minded, as evidenced even by the titles mentioned as well as tracks such as “Panoptic,” “Equanimity” and “Metacognition.” Holiday even commissioned philosopher Dylan Trigg to write an explanatory essay for the back cover.

The album is, in a nutshell, “about connection,” Holiday explains. “It’s about aligning ourselves, waking up and optimizing ourselves in this material world.

“I know it sounds airy-fairy and far-out,” he says with a laugh, “but this is something that’s resonated with me for a long, long, long time.

“So that’s where I went. After the accident, I got into such a physically vulnerable state that it affected my mental vulnerability in a way I actually welcomed. It shook some stuff loose, literally and in an analogous way, that I was able to go, ‘Oh, man, I feel close to that mental, sensitive part of myself’ … and I wanted to hang onto that coming into the record and singing and using my voice, ’cause it’s different than the guitar, it’s different than bass. It’s different than drums.”

While Holiday brought in Jesse Nason to perform with an arsenal of vintage keyboards — including Moog, Oberheim and Prophet synthesizers — Topology is very much a guitar player’s showpiece.

That’s particularly true on “Crism,” a nearly 12-minute instrumental that cascades through mood and tempo changes, as well as some of Holiday’s most biting and soaring guitar solos. And surprisingly it was composed to a single drum track that Miley provided.

“We had just lost Jack DeJohnette, so we were all listening to a bunch of those wonderful records from the early ’70s, totally inspired,” says Holiday, who also cites John Coltrane, early Miles Davis and 1970s-era King Crimson as influential sources. “And I had just told the guys that for the solo record I wanted to do something like that.”

Miley’s drum track captured that vibe perfectly.

“It was different from anything he had ever sent me,” Holiday says. “I was completely blown away. I just told him, ‘It’s a masterpiece!’ I told him, ‘I’m not gonna edit it.’ Jesse came over and we plugged in and played all the way through the song five times, full takes, and I took sections from each of them and made the song.”

Holiday kept the gear for Topology “pretty simple … the cream of the crop of my goodies,” including a 1961 Gibson ES-345, a 1964 “Platypus” Firebird and a 1966 ES-330. Custom Kauer and Banker models were used for overdubs, while the acoustic guitars were a Martin OM42 and Guild F412. All of the bass parts were recorded with a Supro Huntington.

For amplifiers Holiday used some Universal Audio models but primarily stuck to a pair of small Supros — an Amulet and a 1600 Supreme. He “didn’t want to go too bananas” with effects, using Fjord Fuzz Odin octave fuzz and Fjaer reverb pedals as well as an Electro-Harmonix POG octave generator on the track “Veridream.”

But the “star of the show,” Holiday says, was a prototype from effects-maker Jeorge Tripps.

“This pedal is able to make eight presets, and I used them all and it sounds like eight different pedals,” Holiday explains. “So this is the star of the show, and I love that I made a record with a pedal that’s unavailable to the world — and may never be, who knows?”

Holiday knows that between him singing and the different playing approaches, Topology presents him in a manner that might surprise Rival Sons fans. And he’s looking forward to them hearing it.

“I didn’t overthink at all when I made this music,” he continues. “This was more like, ‘This is natural. This is what I should do. This is where the color goes, this is where the texture goes, this is how long the songs need to be.’

“It was like releasing a valve, but, ‘Oh, wow, I didn’t even know that valve needed to be released, but there it is,’ and things moved a lot easier.”

As for the Hol1D4y moniker, it reflects Holiday’s interest in numerology and sacred geometry.

“I really loved this idea of using a 1 and 4. In numerology the 1 and 4 become a 5. In numerology, 5 represents: adventure, freedom, curiosity and dynamic change. In sacred geometry the number 5 represents the bridge between the physical and spiritual realms.

“So it has great significance with the things I’m talking about and felt about this project.”

Now Holiday is preparing to make Hol1D4y a live endeavor. He’s assembled a five-member band and has built three special rigs for himself and the two others who will play guitar. He’s also worked with Banker’s Matt Hughes to create a custom double-neck guitar and bass.

“Sometimes I’ll be playing bass on a verse and then I’m playing guitar on the chorus, or vice versa,” Holiday says. “I move it all around. Basically I’m gonna be super selfish and just want to play and have fun.”

Rival Sons returns to the road in late October for U.S. dates through November, followed by studio work on a new album in early 2027. Holiday hopes to launch Hol1D4y live in February or March.

“But we are going to tour this, one way or another. I promise you that. Where there’s a will, there’s a way.”

item.title: Eric Clapton doesn’t like this classic Cream track, even though it’s key to his legend: “I think there’s something wrong with it”
item.dc:content:
Did Eric Clapton ever really know what kind of group Cream was? He formed the band with bass guitarist Jack Bruce and drummer Ginger Baker in 1966, after seeing his hero Buddy Guy perform with a trio in London. Convinced his future lay in a blues-rock trio, he quit John Mayall’s Bluesbreakers to make a fresh start.

What he failed to consider was that Bruce and Baker both had strong jazz backgrounds. For them, Cream was nothing less than a jazz-rock fusion outfit, one of the first in an era that would include artists like the Free Spirits (featuring guitarist Larry Coryell), Miles Davis, Frank Zappa, and Clapton's old pal Jeff Beck, to name a few.

“I thought of Cream as sort of a jazz band,” Bruce once said, “only we never told Eric he was really Ornette Coleman! Kept quiet about that.”

Like a jazz band, Cream made spirited, virtuoso improvisation a key part of their approach in concert. Together, Eric Clapton, Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker introduced jamming to rock audiences, first in concert and later on albums like Wheels of Fire and Goodbye, and, following their breakup in 1968, on concert discs like Live Cream and Live Cream Volume II.

Some of the longest jams in their catalog include Wheels of Fire’s “Spoonful” (16:47) and “Toad” (16:16), Goodbye’s “I’m So Glad” (9:13), Live Cream’s “N.S.U.” (10:13) and “Sweet Wine” (15:15), and Live Cream Volume II’s “Steppin’ Out” (13:38).

And then there’s “Crossroads,” certainly the best known of the trio’s live jams. The song appeared on the second disc of 1968’s double-LP Wheels of Fire, along with other live recordings from Cream’s March 7–10 concerts at San Francisco’s Fillmore and Winterland venues that same year. Recorded at Winterland on March 10, 1968, “Crossroads” comes in at a tidy 4 minutes and 18 seconds, making it one of the shorter live cuts in Cream’s catalog.

For fans of Eric Clapton’s electric guitar soloing, there is perhaps no better example of his guitar prowess. Over six verses, Clapton plays some of the most lyrical and impassioned guitar in blues rock — not just guitar wankery but lines that build and develop into statements you can recall in an instant and even sing. No less a Clapton fan than Eddie Van Halen learned the “Crossroads” solos note for note. That's how important they are.

So wouldn’t it be great if there was actually a longer version of this celebrated recording?

If the late producer Tom Dowd is to be believed, there is. Over his long career as an engineer and producer, Dowd recorded Clapton in Cream, solo and in Derek and the Dominos, which is why he was chosen to reminisce about the guitarist and his recordings for Guitar Player’s July 1985 Eric Clapton issue. In doing so, he made an admission that was tantalizing to Clapton fans.

“On the Wheels of Fire album, in the live portion, a lot of things were ultimately brought down to shorter versions than were played onstage,” Dowd said. “We did two recordings in San Francisco in three days' time — one at Winterland and the other at the Fillmore.

"'Crossroads' onstage, for instance, was never under seven to 10 minutes long. So the solos between the vocals were edited. But there was no overdubbing whatsoever on any of the live albums.”

Definitive as it may sound, Dowd’s declaration has a few problems. For one thing, nearly 60 years on, no “unedited” recordings of the Winterland "Crossroads" have surfaced. In addition, other live cuts of "Crossroads” from the group's autumn 1968 farewell tour are arranged like the Wheels of Fire track, right down to Bruce's "Eric Clapton" acknowledgement at the song's end. The group’s L.A. Forum and San Diego Sports Arena performances in October 1968 both clock in at around four minutes and change, while Cream’s November 26, 1968 presentation at the Royal Albert Hall runs the same length as the Wheels of Fire version.

If anything gives support to Dowd’s memory of the recording, it’s the moment at 2:44 where Clapton seemingly gets ahead of the beat and the players lose the “one” for a couple of measures. Did the group make a masterful save and recover before going completely off the rails? Or is this a less-than-ideal edit made to trim the song down to a more reasonable length?

Eric Clapton seems to think it was the former. The guitarist, who was interviewed by Dan Forte in that same issue as Dowd, couldn’t say if the producer was right, but he acknowledged that the group often came close to completely losing it when jamming.

GUITAR PLAYER "Cream's live version of 'Crossroads' is often cited as one of the best live cuts and live guitar solos ever recorded. Was that edited from a longer jam?"

ERIC CLAPTON "I can't remember. I haven't heard that in so long — and I really don't like it, actually. I think there's something wrong with it. I wouldn't be at all surprised if we weren't lost at that point in the song, because that used to happen a lot. I'd forget where the 1 was, and I'd be playing the 1 on the 4, or the 1 on the 2 — that used to happen a lot. Somehow or another, it would make this crazy new hybrid thing, which I never liked, because it's not what it was supposed to be.

"What I'm saying is, if I hear the solo and think, God, I'm on the 2 and I should be on the 1, then I can never really enjoy it. And I think that's what happened with 'Crossroads.' It is interesting, and everyone can pat themselves on the back that we all got out of it at the same time. But it rankles me a little bit."

What’s curious is that even Clapton isn’t sure if the song was edited down — and he performed it.

But perhaps there are aspects to this we don’t know. Let’s say Dowd was right and “Crossroads” was originally much longer. Imagine Cream, out on their farewell tour in autumn 1968, decided to perform the song in its abbreviated Wheels of Fire format for one reason or another — maybe they preferred it, or figured it would let them wrap up the show faster and get out of each other’s hair. By the time of this interview, even Clapton could be excused if he'd forgotten such minor details.

Instead, what he recalled was his reaction — it rankled him. All guitarists would be blessed to feel so rankled. But then Clapton never did fully enjoy his role in Cream, where he was something of the odd man out. As Jack Bruce explained in a 2012 interview with Guitarist, Clapton thought Cream would be a blues trio and give him a chance to be like his idol, Buddy Guy. Meanwhile, Bruce and Baker were jazzheads hellbent on infusing the group’s blues-rock with freeform improvisation.

The results speak for themselves. As for "Crossroads," at any length it serves up some of the greatest guitar playing in rock and roll history.

item.title: Rick Nielsen on the origin of his Hamer five-neck guitar: “I wanted a 12-string and a fretless, and...”
item.dc:content:
As Rick Nielsen’s guitars, cars and memorabilia head to the Julien’s auction block in October, it’s a good time to recall some of the vintage and one-of-a-kind guitars the Cheap Trick guitarist has owned over the years. Several are among the offerings in the October 24 Rick Nielsen Collection auction.

One of the most conspicuous is the stage-played 2004 Hamer “Five Neck” Korina, which will be offered for sale publicly for the first time ever in the landmark auction.

The unusual electric is among three five-necked models Nielsen had built to his custom specs. The original orange-finished example was made in 1981. He explained its origins to Guitar Aficionado magazine.

“How did I come up with such a backbreaking idea for an instrument? Well, back at shows in the late ’70s and early ’80s, I used to stack up as many as five guitars for my guitar solo. I'd play one for a little bit, then throw it away and play the one hanging underneath it.”

This eventually led to the birth of the five-necked guitar. Nielsen originally envisioned it as a six-necked model “that spun like a roulette wheel, so that I could play one neck and then rotate to the next,” he explained. “But then I decided to go with something more conservative — five necks in a row!”

He admitted that the monster of a guitar was a chore to build, due not only to its size and wiring but because of his specifications for each of the guitars. “I wanted a 12-string and a fretless, and one that sounded like a Stratocaster and one that sounded like a Junior,” he said. “But Hamer, never to be daunted, managed to put all the ideas together and made it work.”

It was left to Hamer’s Frank Untermeyer to bring Nielsen’s creation to life.

“Rick's out of his mind, but in a wonderful way,” Untermeyer told Guitar Aficionado. “By 1981, we had already done some pretty wacky stuff for him and Cheap Trick, like the checkerboard Standard, an electric mandocello, and a 12-string bass, so we were used to the fact that they set all standards for going to the limit.

“For this guitar, we cut apart five double-cutaway Hamer Special bodies and laminated them together, and then sanded in between the necks to get that sort of swoopy look. As I recall, routing the wires through this thing was also a huge pain in the ass.”

Hamer subsequently built two more five-neck guitars for Nielsen, including the 2004 Korina model now headed to auction.

The auction guitar has had a substantial stage career of its own. Nielsen used it at the 2004 Another State of Mind benefit show at Chicago’s Metro and continued playing it through at least 2013, when Cheap Trick performed its Budokan 35th Anniversary concert at the CBGB’s John Varvatos venue in New York. The guitar also appears in an episode of Gibson Guitars’ The Collection series featuring Nielsen.

Routing the wires through this thing was also a huge pain in the ass.”

— Frank Untermeyer

As the guitarist and songwriter behind Cheap Trick, Nielsen helped create some of the band’s most enduring songs, including “Surrender” and “Dream Police,” while his distinctive guitar work and larger-than-life stage presence helped propel the group from Rockford, Illinois, to international stardom.

Nielsen grew up around his parents’ music store and started out as a drummer before the Beatles and Rolling Stones helped turn his attention toward the guitar. He bought his first Les Paul — a 1955 Goldtop — for $65 and still owns it. Over the decades, his collection expanded to include rare and unusual instruments ranging from two 1958 Gibson Explorers to a 1963 Guild Merle Travis, one of only three ever made.

“I couldn’t sing or dance, but I was big into songwriting, and I tried to put everything I had into that,” Nielsen said. “I never wanted to be like anybody else — I just wanted to be me. I knew I was never going to be a virtuoso, so I ended up being a ‘medium-oso.’”

Now, after more than five decades of collecting, Nielsen is parting with a portion of that archive.

“I started out with one guitar, and over the years the collection just kept growing. It seemed like a good time to sell some of it — you can’t take it with you. When it’s all over, hopefully I’ll still have one guitar.”

More Rick Nielsen guitars headed to auction

The five-neck Hamer is far from the only notable guitar in The Rick Nielsen Collection.

Among the other highlights is a stage-played 1975 Hamer Standard, which Nielsen used on Don Kirshner’s Rock Concert on November 10, 1977, and during Cheap Trick’s April 28, 1978 performance at Japan’s Budokan. It carries an estimate of $200,000 to $300,000.

Also offered is a sunburst 1963 Fender Stratocaster with a mint-green pickguard, chrome tremolo bridge and output jack plate, and white pickup covers and knobs. Its estimate is $40,000 to $60,000.

A 1984 Gibson Les Paul XPL is another unusual entry. The model combines the Les Paul body shape with the Explorer headstock, part of Gibson’s mid-1980s experiments with pairing the Explorer headstock with other body designs. Nielsen’s sunburst example comes with its original rectangular Gibson hardshell case and carries an estimate of $15,000 to $20,000.

The October 24 Rick Nielsen Collection auction will also include cars, stage-worn clothing, awards and other personal memorabilia. The sale will benefit St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital and will be held live at the Musicians Hall of Fame & Museum at the Historic Nashville Municipal Auditorium.

Visit Julien’s Auctions to view the collection.

“I started out with one guitar, and over the years the collection just kept growing. It seemed like a good time to sell some of it — you can’t take it with you. When it’s all over, hopefully I’ll still have one guitar.”

More Rick Nielsen guitars headed to auction

The five-neck Hamer is far from the only notable guitar in The Rick Nielsen Collection.

Among the other highlights is a stage-played 1975 Hamer Standard, which Nielsen used on Don Kirshner’s Rock Concert on November 10, 1977, and during Cheap Trick’s April 28, 1978 performance at Japan’s Budokan. It carries an estimate of $200,000 to $300,000.

Also offered is a sunburst 1963 Fender Stratocaster with a mint-green pickguard, chrome tremolo bridge and output jack plate, and white pickup covers and knobs. Its estimate is $40,000 to $60,000.

A 1984 Gibson Les Paul XPL is another unusual entry. The model combines the Les Paul body shape with the Explorer headstock, part of Gibson’s mid-1980s experiments with pairing the Explorer headstock with other body designs. Nielsen’s sunburst example comes with its original rectangular Gibson hardshell case and carries an estimate of $15,000 to $20,000.

The October 24 Rick Nielsen Collection auction will also include cars, stage-worn clothing, awards and other personal memorabilia. The sale will benefit St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital and will be held live at the Musicians Hall of Fame & Museum at the Historic Nashville Municipal Auditorium.

Visit Julien’s Auctions to view the collection.

item.title: Ultravox’s Midge Ure on Phil Lynott, Kate Bush, the Sex Pistols and Robert Fripp: “He brought these 40 Japanese students along”
item.dc:content:
Midge Ure is most famous for his time in Ultravox, the British new wave act whose biggest hit was 1981’s “Vienna.” But outside of the group, Ure has quite a star-studded resume that includes stints in Thin Lizzy and Rich Kids, a short-lived band formed with Sex Pistols bass guitarist Glen Matlock.

In fact, the Glaswegian guitarist was himself asked to join the Sex Pistols in 1975, when manager Malcolm McLaren was forming the punk rockers. Ure had just exited a local music store in Glasgow when he found himself in the presence of McLaren and Clash manager Bernie Rhodes.

“They were selling some slightly hot equipment from the back of the car,” he recalls. “They’d driven from London and stopped off at cities all the way up to Glasgow. Bernie Rhodes saw me coming out of the music shop and approached me and asked that I speak to his friend Malcolm McLaren who was around the corner. Malcolm told me about the New York Dolls, about his fashions with Vivienne Westwood, all of which meant nothing.

“And then about 20 minutes into the conversation, he says, ‘I’m putting a band together. Would you join?’ And I said, ‘Well, no, because you haven’t asked me what I do. You don’t know if I’m a guitarist or a drummer or a singer or a musician at all. I just happen to be coming out of a music shop.’”

Ure was sporting short hair at the time, when everyone else was wearing their hair long.

“I must have looked the part rather than sounded the part,” he reasons. “It seemed that was what he was looking for. He was looking for a band that he could dress up in Vivienne’s clothes to sell some bondage trousers. I have to say, he chose the right guys. I would have been the wrong guy.”

Thin Lizzy

However, Ure proved to be the right choice for Thin Lizzy. He was quickly hired for his brief stint with the Irish rockers after Gary Moore had quit the band in the middle of an American trek in 1979 to support their album Black Rose: A Rock Legend.

“It was my first ever time in America, and I didn’t get to see much of it, as I was in a hotel room with Scott Gorham, working out harmony guitar parts,” Ure recalls. “I spent most of the night just rerunning those things because I was petrified of getting it wrong because every song had a harmony guitar part, every tune. And then I had to walk out in front of 30,000 people and hope and pray that I wasn’t going to make any massive blunders. And I probably did. But they were very gracious and very forgiving.”

Ure was working late in the studio when the offer to join Thin Lizzy came via a phone call from the group’s bass-playing frontman, Phil Lynott. Ure and Lynott’s friendship dated back several years to Glasgow, when Lynott was fronting a three-piece Thin Lizzy.

“I’d seen him play a tiny club just after Philip had set up Thin Lizzy after singing with Skid Row with a young 16-year-old Gary Moore,” says Ure. “I absolutely fell in love with Phil’s voice and his songwriting. I had bumped into him in Glasgow when I was playing in a band and he was wandering around the streets of Glasgow about to play at a university that night and I took him back to my mum’s house and she gave him egg and chips and fed him.

“And he remembered this years later when I moved to London. We bumped into each other again coming out of an underground in London and he said, ‘You’re that kid. I know exactly who you are.’ We just hung out together and became friends. Philip was a great guy, but I wouldn’t trust him with my girlfriend or my wife.”

Lynott may have also been thinking of Ure at that moment, as Ure had co-written the Black Rose track “Get Out of Here.”

By the time Ure returned home from the studio, a plane ticket, several cassettes of music and a list of songs he needed to learn were waiting for him, together with a directive that first thing next morning a driver would take him to London’s Heathrow airport so he could board the Concorde and fly to New York City.

“I was supposed to learn all the songs on the plane, which I couldn’t do,” he explains, “then get a connecting flight down to New Orleans, and meet up with the band there.”

Ure also brought along his main electric guitar at the time, a Yamaha SG-2000 that he first bought in 1976. But a few dates into the Thin Lizzy tour, he was told that the guitar needed to go.

“They decided it wasn’t cool enough and so, they swapped it out for a Les Paul Junior,” he says. “It was a really old Les Paul Junior, which might have been similar to the one that Gary was using. And I had two Marshall stacks, which were deafening. I’d never heard anything so loud in my life!”

Kate Bush

In 1982, Kate Bush was assembling a band to accompany her for a live performance at the Prince’s Trust Rock Gala concert. Ure was one of the musicians invited by Bush to join her backing band. During rehearsals for the show, Ure witnessed first-hand how much of a taskmaster the “Running Up That Hill” singer really was.

“She was an absolute perfectionist,” he remembers of Bush. “She would in a wonderfully kind of way, basically tell you, you weren’t doing a very good job, ‘Let’s run that again, let’s just make sure we get that part in.’ In the band was also Phil Collins on drums, Pete Townshend on guitar and Mick Karn from Japan and she didn’t hold back with those guys either. She would say, ‘No, no, it’s not quite right, let’s just do that one more time.’ She knew what she wanted.”

Robert Fripp

When Ure invited King Crimson guitarist Robert Fripp to contribute his six-string atmospherics to several tracks on Ure’s 1996 solo album Breathe, it came with a caveat.

“When I asked him if he would do some of his Frippertronics and soundscapes and stuff on one of my albums, he was more than happy to do it, but asked, ‘Can I bring my Japanese students with me?’” explains Ure. “I said, ‘Yeah.’ So, he brought these 40 Japanese students along, who all had cameras, and were taking photographs of everything that Robert said and did.

“And so, Robert sat in the big room with me, while they [students] were in the control room. And he said, ‘This is Midge, this is his record. Midge does this, Midge does that.’ And they’re all taking photographs.

“And then he says, ‘I’m going to play this over a B minor, and this is,’ you know, whatever. And then he starts layering up these wonderful Frippertronics with his electronics. And it was amazing to watch him doing it in real time while he was teaching these 40 Japanese guitar students. It was quite incredible.”

Ure continued to run into Fripp, usually backstage at various ’80s festivals, where Fripp’s wife, Toyah Willcox, and Ure have been regulars on the retro festival circuit. “Robert is such a placid, lovely guy,” he says. “He is there walking around with his guitar strapped around his neck, doing scales — just playing scales, talking to you, chatting away. He still practices six hours a day! I’ve never practiced in my life. That’s why I’m not as good as him.”

item.title: Keanu Reeves on his bass guitar origins: “I was 22, went to Guitar Center and ended up buying a bass in the parking lot”
item.dc:content:
Keanu Reeves is back on the road with Dogstar, and ahead of the band’s upcoming tour, the actor and bass guitarist took time to talk about his history with the instrument, his influences and the gear he’s using onstage.

In a new video with No Treble and The Bass Nerds, Reeves walks through his current rig, which includes a Fender American Ultra Precision Bass and a Gallien-Krueger 2001RB Legacy head driving four 4x12 cabs.

But the conversation quickly goes beyond gear, with Reeves recalling the unlikely circumstances of his first bass purchase and the players who shaped his approach to the instrument.

“I started playing when I was 22, went to Guitar Center in Hollywood and I ended up buying a bass in the parking lot,” Reeves says. “It was a white Ibanez, four-string, with a rosewood neck for 300 bucks.”

From there, he moved on to Fender Precision Basses, although he also spent some time playing a Music Man.

“I played a MusicMan too for a little bit,” he says. “But in the progression I did a P Bass, but never did a Jazz.

“Now I like PJs,” he adds, referring to Precision basses fitted with both Precision Bass and Jazz Bass pickups, such as the Ultra and Ultra II models.

Reeves also demonstrates what Dogstar calls “Reeves’ riff,” the bass figure that became the foundation of “All in Now,” the title track and first single from the band’s new album.

His musical influences go back to some of the defining bass sounds of punk and alternative rock. Reeves cites the Ramones, Pixies bass guitarist Kim Deal and Joy Division/New Order bass guitarist Peter Hook among his favorites. At one point in the video, he plays Hook’s instantly recognizable bass line from Joy Division’s “Disorder.”

“I guess when I wanted to learn how to play when I was 22, it was the Ramones, a little punk rock. There was also the bass line to [Lou Reed’s] ‘Walk on the Wild Side.’ There was Kim Deal,” he says, attempting to play Deal’s bass line from the Pixies’ “Gigantic.”

That emphasis on the bass as a melodic instrument, rather than simply a rhythmic foundation, seems to have been central to Reeves from the beginning.

“Having the melody from the bass — I guess my ear always went to that... So yeah, I was drawn to that stuff.”

Dogstar’s All In Now Tour launches September 29 at the Fonda Theatre in Los Angeles.
item.description: With Dogstar back on the road behind its new album All In Now, the bass guitarist recalls the $300 Ibanez that started it all and players that shaped his style

item.title: Todd Rundgren takes aim at Taylor Swift: “There’s an argument to be made that she ruined music”
item.dc:content:
Todd Rundgren has never been shy about taking aim at pop music, but his latest target is one of the biggest stars in the world. In a recent career-spanning interview, the singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and producer argued that Taylor Swift represents everything he considers mediocre about contemporary music.

“There’s an argument to be made that she ruined music,” Rundgren told Vulture. “It’s an understandable phenomenon. It’s just that, to me, Taylor Swift is the apotheosis of mediocrity.”

Rundgren’s comments came while discussing his work on Meat Loaf’s 1977 debut, Bat Out of Hell. The album famously drew on the theatrical excesses of Bruce Springsteen, and Rundgren was asked which contemporary artist he might lampoon if he were making a similar record in 2026.

“Taylor Swift, of course,” he replied.

He then offered a theory for why female artists have become so dominant in mainstream music, arguing that the industry’s audience shifted after young men began spending more money on video games than records during the 1990s.

“So you got Lady Gaga, Taylor Swift, P!nk, and many artists of that ilk,” Rundgren said.

He was considerably more complimentary toward Gaga, whom he described as “a real musician” and noted is a classically trained piano player. Swift, by contrast, came in for a much harsher assessment.

“Taylor Swift doesn’t do anything particularly great except grow hair,” he said. “She’s not a great singer. She’s not a great songwriter. She’s not a great dancer.”

Rundgren did acknowledge Swift’s enormous influence, particularly among women who have grown up with her music.

“She’s a role model for what was a very young generation of women, and now for those women’s daughters as well, because it’s mothers and daughters going to Taylor Swift shows,” he said.

Rundgren has a long history of speaking candidly about his experiences with fellow musicians. He has criticized XTC frontman Andy Partridge over his attitude during the making of Skylarking, the 1986 album Rundgren produced, and he has also taken issue with George Harrison receiving a production credit on Badfinger’s “Day After Day” after Rundgren took over production of the band’s Straight Up album.

His view on Swift stands in contrast to the praise she has received from several prominent figures in the rock world. Exodus and Slayer guitarist Gary Holt said in 2024, “I love Taylor Swift. Why all the hate? She’s an extraordinarily hard worker.” Rush guitarist Alex Lifeson has likewise praised Swift’s talent and the way she treats her touring crew, while acknowledging that he isn’t particularly familiar with her music.

item.title: Robin Trower on still making music at 81. “I’m thankful for my blessings every day. You try to make the most of it”
item.dc:content:
A great many descriptors have been used for Robin Trower and his playing since he emerged as part of Procol Harum back in 1967.

Slack has never been one of them.

With his signature Stratocaster and endless vocabulary of solos, the London-born guitarist, songwriter and bandleader has released more than three dozen studio albums as a principal artist — including the short-lived BLT trio with Jack Bruce and drummer Bill Lordan — plus session work for Bruce and Bryan Ferry. During the past decade alone, he’s delivered eight albums, including collaborations with Maxi Priest and blues singer Sari Schorr — a remarkable output by any measure but all the more remarkable when you consider that Trower turned 81 in March and is still producing at a volume that’s leaving those half his age, and younger, in the dust.

The latest entry in the Trower travelogue is Shine, a 10-track set that came out September 25 that was produced by Trower, who also played bass as well as guitar, joined by drummer Chris Taggard, with Richard Watts, mostly, on vocals, as well as Jeff Hayes. Mining a familiar but hardly worn array of rock, blues, soul and some funk, it’s an album Trower had spoken about finishing around the time its predecessor, 2025’s Come and Find Me, came out. As he spoke to Guitar Player from Florida at the outset of his latest U.S. tour, it doesn’t sound like he’ll be taking his foot off the pedal — wah-wah or otherwise — any time soon.

Shine is an album you were talking about when Come and Find Me came out just 16 months ago. Do you feel like those, and maybe all of the albums you’ve been releasing in pretty rapid succession, are of some kind of a piece you’re creating?

I think the point behind it all, really, is I’m coming up with a lot of material, so in a way I’m always working on a couple of albums at the time. Then when the time comes for me to put an album out, I have to choose from a certain amount of songs, a group of songs that I think work together. But there’s always extra songs that will go toward the next album.

That has to be a reassuring way to work, making music more than making albums.

That’s right, yeah. Each song is treated as an individual, and I then try to put together a bunch of songs that I feel do hang together — hopefully from a lot of choices that are around.

I think I’ve concentrated more on working, just making sure I play the guitar every day, and that’s where ideas come —  when I’m sort of doodling about.”

— Robin Trower

So how large of a universe did you draw Shine from?

I think I had about six other songs that didn’t make it on this album; they just didn’t quite fit in this group. So they’ll go forward, and I’m working on a lot of new material since then, of course.

What accounts for your level of recent productivity? There aren’t many, maybe any, peers of your age that compare.

There’s no doubt about it; I have hit a bit of a purple patch the last few years. I think I’ve concentrated more on working, just making sure I play the guitar every day, and that’s where ideas come — when I’m sort of doodling about. An idea will present itself, and as long as I think I can keep working I can come up with new material.

Do you have a process you follow at this point?

Every song I write starts off with a guitar idea, basically; that is the formula. I get a guitar idea that I think could be turned into a song. I’ll work on it for an hour, and if it’s gonna be good it’ll be pretty much together by the end of the hour.

I know when a line, a guitar line, is gonna be good because it rings a bell in my body. I just know that’s what I’m looking for. Then I start to think about the top line, what the vocal line will be, and once I’ve got that nailed down I’m also working on lead guitar ideas, and melodies as well. Then I start to work on the lyrics. That is the longest part of the process; that can take me two or three days, to finish the lyrics.

There are probably some songwriters out there who will read that and think two or three days is not a long time.

[chuckles] Yeah, that’s lovely. I mean, I have taken longer than that, but not always. The ultimate sort of goal of a lyric is that it enhances the atmosphere of the song itself and fits right into the mood of it. But if you can’t reach that kind of goal, then at least have a lyric that doesn’t detract from it.

Shine and your other recent albums, certainly Come and Find Me, seem to be digging a little deeper, lyrically. There are songs about politics, mortality. Is that part of being a man of a certain age and having more experiences to draw from?

I think my whole approach has always been and always will be that the best is yet to come as far as my work is concerned.”

— Robin Trower

I think that’s true. I think what’s happening in the world has impacted the lyrics the last few years, there’s no doubt about it. The world is unfortunately in a much darker place at the moment. I think that gets into it. Obviously you’re going to express your worries, fears, whatever.

On “Live Your Time” on Shine, however, you strike a more optimistic tone even in that environment.

I think that’s more or less saying, “Well, we can worry ourselves to death and worry about those things we can’t really change,” and I think that lyric is just sort of pointing out that you’ve got to love yourself and live your time. That’s it — make the very most of it. Obviously we have to be concerned, but not to the detriment of our own lives. And eventually we have a moment for us to make a difference.

“The Race,” meanwhile, sounds pretty defiant — again, a kind of statement from a man of a certain age.

I really believe that. You’re always looking forward — and happy about it. If you had asked me in the ’70s, there’s no way I thought I’d still be doing it at 81. But I’m thankful for my blessings every day, so that’s it. You try to make the most of it.

What do you find you can do now, through the benefit of knowledge and experience, that you couldn’t have 40 or 50 or more years ago?

That’s a good point, because I think I try and be more organized and not quite so gung-ho as I was when I was starting out. I think now I’m more interested, for instance, in lead guitar being more melodic, having actual melodies. Obviously I still want to make it passionate and soulful, but I think that would be the difference between then and now, more melody.

Has the litmus of what works changed for you much over the years? Is it easier or harder to reach that bar you aspire toward?

I think both. Experience is a big, big help, because you bypass all the sort of clutter to get to the point, and the point is always further down the road, unfortunately. So you’re always chasing what you’re after, but that’s all part of the fun of the fair, isn’t it? When you give up is when you don’t feel like you’re growing or coming up with something fresh. The most important thing is to come up with something fresh to you, something you haven’t created before. A lot of the ingredients are very similar to what you did before, but it has that little something about it that piques your interest.

What did that in particular on Shine?

Well, “Love By Any Other Name” is maybe one of the best songs I’ve ever written. I’m fascinated by that track. It’s deep, for a start; it’s a deep piece of music. It’s also got a fabulous vocal on it by Richard. I think that combination gives it a potency which...it’s fascinating.

Any different gear on this album?

It’s all basically the same stuff I always use — my signature model Strat, Marshall amps and all the pedals from Fulltone. They keep giving me pedals since the early ’90s, and I’ve always used them since then.

As Paul McCartney once asked Elvis Presley, how are you coming along on the bass, then?

The reason I play bass is because when I’m writing I usually have in the back of my mind what the bass and drums should be doing. I’m not saying I’m a great bass player or anything, but I think the parts are key, coming up with the right part that suits the vocal, suits the guitar parts. I think that’s why I like to do the bass myself.

You released anniversary editions of some of your albums recently, like Bridge of Sighs, For Earth Below, the first Live! album. Do those at all impact on new writing and recording you do?

No, I don’t think so. I’m not one for looking back; most of those albums I haven’t heard since I made them. So, no. You just keep moving forward. You don’t want to get hung up on what was successful earlier; it might impact on what you’re trying to create, or can create.

What keeps the older songs fresh for you in concert?

I think that’s the great thing about being a three-piece — every song is a challenge every night. That’s all there is to it; you’ve got to work hard to pull them off, basically. I think that’s what keeps it on its toes. That keeps it alive.

Is a next album in motion, or even finished?

No. I’m working on something at the moment; I have a lot of spare material, but I haven’t got it pinned down to what it’s gonna be yet. I’m gonna be doing a little more recording, I think, in November, and then take some time off and come back to it in the new year.

item.content:encoded:
A great many descriptors have been used for Robin Trower and his playing since he emerged as part of Procol Harum back in 1967.

Slack has never been one of them.

With his signature Stratocaster and endless vocabulary of solos, the London-born guitarist, songwriter and bandleader has released more than three dozen studio albums as a principal artist — including the short-lived BLT trio with Jack Bruce and drummer Bill Lordan — plus session work for Bruce and Bryan Ferry. During the past decade alone, he’s delivered eight albums, including collaborations with Maxi Priest and blues singer Sari Schorr — a remarkable output by any measure but all the more remarkable when you consider that Trower turned 81 in March and is still producing at a volume that’s leaving those half his age, and younger, in the dust.

The latest entry in the Trower travelogue is Shine, a 10-track set that came out September 25 that was produced by Trower, who also played bass as well as guitar, joined by drummer Chris Taggard, with Richard Watts, mostly, on vocals, as well as Jeff Hayes. Mining a familiar but hardly worn array of rock, blues, soul and some funk, it’s an album Trower had spoken about finishing around the time its predecessor, 2025’s Come and Find Me, came out. As he spoke to Guitar Player from Florida at the outset of his latest U.S. tour, it doesn’t sound like he’ll be taking his foot off the pedal — wah-wah or otherwise — any time soon.

I think the point behind it all, really, is I’m coming up with a lot of material, so in a way I’m always working on a couple of albums at the time. Then when the time comes for me to put an album out, I have to choose from a certain amount of songs, a group of songs that I think work together. But there’s always extra songs that will go toward the next album.

That has to be a reassuring way to work, making music more than making albums.

That’s right, yeah. Each song is treated as an individual, and I then try to put together a bunch of songs that I feel do hang together — hopefully from a lot of choices that are around.

I think I’ve concentrated more on working, just making sure I play the guitar every day, and that’s where ideas come —  when I’m sort of doodling about.”

— Robin Trower

item.title: “I won’t watch the films.” Paul McCartney’s ex has no interest in the new Fab Four biopics
item.dc:content:
Jane Asher has spent decades declining to revisit her relationship with Paul McCartney, even though their time together helped inspire some of the Beatles’ most enduring songs. Now, as that relationship is set to be dramatized on the big screen, she has no intention of watching.

Asher, who dated the Beatle bass guitarist for five years and became engaged to him in 1967, is being portrayed by Lucy Boynton in Sam Mendes’ upcoming four-part Beatles film series. The actor says the filmmakers did reach out to her, but she gave them the same response she has given to inquiries about her relationship with McCartney for years.

“They approached me about it, of course, but I said my usual,” Asher told The Telegraph.

Asher and McCartney met in 1963, when she interviewed the Beatles at London’s Royal Albert Hall. Their relationship quickly became serious, with McCartney eventually moving into the Asher family home. The years they spent together coincided with one of the Beatles’ most creatively fertile periods, and Asher has been connected to several McCartney compositions from the era.

People would offer me money to talk about it, all sorts of things. But I won’t discuss it. It was so long ago.”

— Jane Asher

The years they spent together coincided with one of the Beatles’ most creatively fertile periods, and Asher was a direct influence on several of McCartney’s songs. “And I Love Her” (from 1964’s A Hard Day’s Night),“I’m Looking Through You” (from 1965’s Rubber Soul) and “For No One” (from 1966’s Revolver) have all been associated with their relationship.

Their engagement ended in 1968, with Asher making the announcement during a BBC television appearance. McCartney married Linda McCartney the following year.

Asher, now 80, has made clear that she considers the relationship a closed chapter. She said she has turned down offers of money to talk about McCartney and has no interest in reopening the subject for the new films.

“People would offer me money to talk about it, all sorts of things,” she said. “But I won’t discuss it. It was so long ago.”

That extends to Boynton’s portrayal of her. Asked about the casting, Asher acknowledged that her onscreen counterpart is “beautiful,” but said she won’t see the finished films.

“Well, of course, Lucy is beautiful. But I won’t watch the films, otherwise everyone will ask me what I thought.”

Mendes’ The Beatles – A Four-Film Cinematic Event will tell the band’s story four times, with each movie centered on a different Beatle. Paul Mescal plays McCartney, with Harris Dickinson as John Lennon, Joseph Quinn as George Harrison and Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr.

The ensemble also includes Saoirse Ronan as Linda McCartney, Anna Sawai as Yoko Ono, Aimee Lou Wood as Pattie Boyd and Mia McKenna-Bruce as Maureen Starkey.

The project has the participation of Apple Corps and the surviving Beatles, giving Mendes access to the group’s music rights as well as their approval for the films. The four movies are scheduled to open in theaters simultaneously in April 2028.

Asher isn’t the only Beatles partner whose connection to the project has attracted attention. Boyd said earlier this year that she had not been contacted by the production about her portrayal, adding, “I could have really told them great stories.”

item.title: In a brand-new interview, Ritchie Blackmore says Deep Purple reunion was like coming back from war
item.dc:content:
Ritchie Blackmore has compared his surprise return to the Deep Purple stage to coming home from war.

The legendary guitarist reunited with his former bandmates for a performance of “Smoke on the Water” at Jones Beach Theater in Wantagh, New York, on August 12, 33 years after his departure from the band. And while the appearance lasted only a few minutes, Blackmore says the experience carried considerably more weight.

“I felt like I was one of the soldiers that had come back from the Western Front, and everybody thought I was dead,” Blackmore recalls. “And there I was — I was alive.”

Blackmore revisited the reunion in a new, 13-part interview series with Now Spinning magazine editor-in-chief Phil Aston, explaining that the idea came to him early one morning after he learned Deep Purple would be performing at Jones Beach, which he described as a “magnificent place.”

The electric-guitar legend had been thinking about contacting his former bandmates when the opportunity presented itself. The communication ultimately went through his wife and Blackmore’s Night co-leader, Candice Night, as Blackmore had only recently learned how to use modern phones and generally keeps his distance from technology.

“Now Candice sent the e-mail and Ian [Gillan] said, ‘Yes, of course. Welcome aboard. All the band is up for it. Come onstage for ‘Smoke’.’ I just wanted to do one song, and I thought that would be the song. It’s big over here [in the U.S.] — bigger here than it was in Europe.”

The appearance was publicized just enough to let fans know what was coming, and Blackmore says ticket sales subsequently increased.

The stakes became apparent once he actually stepped onstage. Blackmore says everyone around him was “incredibly nice” — almost to the point of “overkill” — and although he didn’t participate in a soundcheck, his roadie handled it and reported that everything sounded good.

Then came “Smoke on the Water.”

Blackmore admits that revisiting one of Deep Purple’s defining songs after more than three decades was “tricky.” Still, the response from the crowd was overwhelming.

“And I played my three or four minutes of ‘Smoke on the Water’, which seemed to go down like I just invented the cure for cancer,” he says. “The people went nuts, and half of them were sitting in water. For some reason, the venue kind of gets covered in water at certain points ’cause it is right on the water. So they’re now all sitting in the water, the front three or four rows.”

The performance also earned praise from Deep Purple’s current guitarist, Simon McBride, who described the night as “magical.” McBride acknowledged that Blackmore’s playing may not have been at the same level it was when “Smoke on the Water” appeared on 1972’s Machine Head, while adding that he would be more than happy to have the same level of ability when he reaches Blackmore’s age.

For Blackmore, though, the night was less about proving what he could still do onstage than reconnecting with people he had once shared the stage with.

“I felt very good about it because it was like playing with old friends,” he says. “Everybody was super nice and super efficient.”

That made the performance all the more meaningful — and all the more nerve-racking.

“And thank goodness it went off without a hitch, but it could have quite easily have fallen apart, and that would’ve been embarrassing,” Blackmore says.

In the end, he says the reception made him feel like a celebrity for the few minutes he was onstage, despite having little interest in celebrity himself.

“I just play the guitar — sometimes well, sometimes not so well,” he says. “But it was well worth doing.”

Blackmore says the idea had come to him almost spontaneously, and the possibility that it might be his final opportunity to share a stage with his former bandmates gave the reunion an added poignancy.

“It was a good idea that I had, and it came to me very early one morning when I was in bed. I just thought, ‘Why not?’ ’Cause we never know when we’re going to meet again, which is like a sad note in a way.”

The first part of the interview series is below.
item.description: The legendary guitarist reflects on his surprise return to the stage with his former bandmates after 33 years and the overwhelming response to “Smoke on the Water”

item.title: Brian May on Freddie Mercury and the mega-hit that changed Queen’s relationship with their audience
item.dc:content:
Sometimes a song becomes something bigger than a hit. It strikes a nerve with its audience and becomes an anthem that unites listeners with its message.

Brian May had no idea Queen were on the verge of recording such a momentous tune as the group set out to make News of the World, their sixth album, in 1977. Frontman Freddie Mercury had been working on a song designed to encourage audience participation. But when he first presented it to May, bass guitarist John Deacon and drummer Roger Taylor at a rehearsal, they didn’t get it.

Part of the problem was its lyrics, in which Mercury moved from complaints about having paid his dues to telling his audience his climb to the top had been “no bed of roses.”

Worst of all was the title: “We Are the Champions.”

“Our initial sense of it was that it was something very big-headed,” May told Guitar Player. “We all looked at Fred and said, ‘Really?’

“But he had a very clear view of it. It was aimed at an audience that wanted to feel a togetherness and a power and an optimism. He knew people would sing it.”

More than a gifted vocalist, Mercury was a performer who knew how to unite an audience. Which was only appropriate, considering that Queen had decided to bring them into the show with News of the World,

The genesis of this approach came after Queen’s 1977 show at Bingley Hall in Stafford, England, where the audience sang along loudly and enthusiastically to every song.

“We did an encore and then went off,” May explained in a BBC interview that year, “and instead of just keeping clapping, they sang ‘You'll Never Walk Alone‘ to us, and we were just completely knocked out and taken aback.”

As they began to work on News of the World, the band was inspired to write tracks that would harness that collective energy. May brought along “We Will Rock You,” sensing its stomp-clap rhythm and simple vocal refrain would be good way to bring the audience together. Mercury, meanwhile, envisioned “We Are the Champions” as a theme that would unify fans in a moment of collective celebration.

“This was the first album where we contemplated audience participation. Up until that point, we were sort of tentative.”

— Brian May

“This was the first album where we contemplated audience participation,” May told Guitar Player. “Up until that point, we were sort of tentative. We didn't expect the audience to sing along because they didn't in those days. It was a big transition for us to realize that the audience was part of the show, and we decided to encourage that.”

As he explained, this shift in audience behavior was evident more in England and Europe than in America.

“This phenomenon started in Europe way before in the states,” he said. “And I used to prefer that people didn't sing, to be honest. I liked them to hear all the delicate nuances of what we were doing. I found it kind of annoying, as if it was getting in the way of Freddie’s vocals. It's funny to look back on that.”

Regarding “We Are the Champions,” May recalls that it was recorded in what was a typical fashion for Queen at the time.

“Normally, [Mercury] would put down the piano part with Roger and John live, and when it was good enough — after three or four takes — that would be what we used. And that's pretty much what happened with ‘Champions.’”

Working that way allowed May to think about his guitar parts while the others were recording their parts. But sometimes his best ideas came later, as they did for “We Are the Champions.” Roughly two weeks after initially completing his part, he added two new guitar tracks of bell-like chimes using his Red Special electric guitar.

Panned in stereo on the song’s second verse, they ping-pong from speaker to speaker during the lines “It’s been no bed of roses, no pleasure cruise,” adding a bit of decoration as the arrangement builds to a new high ahead of the chorus.

“I remember listening to it in the car the day it was to be mixed and thinking that my guitar wasn't good enough. I told them to give me one more go.”

— Brian May

“I remember listening to it in the car the day it was to be mixed and thinking that my guitar wasn't good enough,” he explained. “I told them to give me one more go and planned that little piece in stereo that happens in verse two, which I really like, it's that sort of bell effect between two guitars. So I know I did some extra work on this one in the light of having lived with it for a couple of weeks.”

May also added some guitar lines — “the lead guitar responses to Freddie’s vocal, particularly at the end,” he said. But when listening to them in the final mix, he felt they were too obtrusive.

“We were very wary of that, because we liked order in our music,” he said. “But the guitar in that case was kind of competing with Freddie’s vocal.”

However, Mercury felt it was exactly what the song needed: a contest of wills. He told May, “No. The guitar is fighting with the vocal here, and that’s the way it should be.”

“That song doesn’t have a solo as such,” May said, “and I don’t think it’s ever needed one.”
