item.title: Bay City Rollers guitarist Neil Henderson dies at 73: “His memory will live on”
item.dc:content:
Neil Henderson, the Scottish guitarist who played with the Bay City Rollers during the band’s formative years, has died at 73.

Henderson’s death was announced by Middle of the Road, another Scottish pop group he later joined. In a statement on Facebook, the band remembered him as its “original lead guitarist, songwriter and friend,” adding that he had been ill for some time and had been working to recover from a stroke suffered several years ago. The group offered its condolences to Henderson’s daughters, Heather and Shona, along with his family and friends.

Henderson joined the Bay City Rollers in 1970, when the group was still establishing itself in Scotland. He played on the band’s 1971 single “Keep On Dancing,” which reached number nine on the U.K. singles chart and gave the Rollers their first Top 10 hit.

He left the group the following year, reportedly after disagreements over its musical direction. His departure came well before the Bay City Rollers’ international breakthrough in the mid-1970s, when the band became one of the era’s biggest pop acts with songs including “Saturday Night” and “Money Honey.”

Henderson subsequently joined Middle of the Road, which was enjoying considerable success in Europe at the time. The group established itself as the leaders of Europop in the years before ABBA’s rise, selling more than five million records, including the international hits “Chirpy Chirpy Cheep Cheep,” “Tweedle Dee, Tweedle Dum” and “Soley Soley.” As a guitarist and songwriter for the group, Henderson contributed to songs such as “Rockin’ Soul” and “Everybody Loves a Winner.”

Henderson’s death also prompted a tribute from Stuart “Woody” Wood, the guitarist who played with the Bay City Rollers during their period of greatest commercial success. Wood said he had never met Henderson personally but noted that the band’s late bass guitarist Alan Longmuir had spoken highly of him.

“Just heard the very sad news about Neil Henderson, one of the original Bay City Rollers,” Wood wrote. “Though I never met him personally Alan spoke very highly of him. Sincere condolences to all his family and friends.”

Middle of the Road concluded its tribute by remembering Henderson’s lasting connection to the musicians he had worked alongside: “His memory will live on with all who had the pleasure of sharing the stage with him as will his music.”

item.title: Rita Coolidge says Eric Clapton owes her a writing credit for one of the most celebrated songs in rock
item.dc:content:
More than half a century since the release of “Layla,” one of the most iconic tracks in Eric Clapton’s canon, Rita Coolidge is still waiting to be credit for writing the outro’s piano lines.

Clapton's own signature is, of course, all over the eponymous 1970 track from Derek & the Dominos' Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs, an album with an intriguing backstory of its own. The album is a uniquely personal entry in Clapton's catalog, written and recorded while the guitarist was in the throes of longing for Pattie Harrison, the wife of his famous Beatle pal George.

While the song's signature electric guitar riff was penned by the then largely unknown Duane Allman, who guested on the record, the tune was Clapton's entirely — up to the piano coda that concludes the song's final minutes. That final icing on the cake was written by Dominos drummer Jim Gordon and singer Coolidge.

Coolidge was hardly anonymous at the time. Like Clapton and the rest of his band, she had served in Delaney and Bonnie Bramlett's band, ground zero for Derek & the Dominos. Since then, Coolidge had gone on to record with artists that included Joe Cocker, Leon Russell — who wrote Cocker's hit "Delta Lady" for her — Stephen Stills and Clapton himself on his self-titled debut solo album.

As the singer explained in a TikTok post, she was in Miami's Criteria studio — the same facility where Layla was recorded — having her photo taken to promote her 1971 debut solo album, when she heard the song being played.

“I’m like, ‘Wait a minute, I recognize this music and know this music,'" she said. “They’re like, ‘You don’t know it, it’s a brand-new Eric Clapton record,’ and I said, ‘It’s my music!’ They took pictures of the veins popping out in my neck. I was so upset.”

@professor.of.rock2

♬ original sound - Professor of Rock

Coolidge said that, after hearing the song, she rushed to Tower Records, where, to her dismay, she found her name absent in the credits.

“I started trying to get in touch with Eric through Robert Stigwood, who was his manager at the time, and was just a mogul,” she recalled. “I got him finally on the phone, and I said, ‘I’m one of the writers, that’s my music.’ He said, ‘Yeah, what are you gonna do about it? You’re a girl. You don’t have the money to fight this. Let it go.’ And that was it.”

In her memoir, Delta Lady, Coolidge wrote that Clapton heard her play the song during their previous recording sessions together, long before he’d woven it into “Layla’s” tapestry.

“We played the song for Eric Clapton in England,” she wrote. “I remember sitting at the piano in Olympic Studios while Eric listened to me play it. Jim and I left a cassette of the demo, hoping, of course, that he might cover it.”

Although he hasn't publicly addressed Coolidge's claims, Clapton told Guitar Player in 1985 that he had coaxed the song away from Gordon for use as the coda to "Layla."

"Jim Gordon wrote that and had been secretly going back into the studio and recording his own album, without any of us knowing it," Clapton told assistant editor Dan Forte. "And they were all love songs composed on the piano. And we caught him playing this one day and said, 'Come on, man. Can we have that?'

"So he was happy to give us that part. And we made the two pieces into one song."

While Clapton did give Gordon a co-writing credit for the song, Coolidge's part in Derek and the Dominos' short-lived legacy remains overlooked.

item.title: Steve Howe recalls his strangest guest sessions, from Lou Reed to Ella Fitzgerald:
item.dc:content:
In addition to his own bands — Yes, Asia, GTR, the Syndicate, the In Crowd/Tomorrow — Steve Howe has served as a hired gun for a number of other artists, appearing on albums for the sometimes incongruous likes of Queen, Bee Gees, Frankie Goes to Hollywood, Dixie Dregs, Dream Theater, William Shatner and others.

One of his earliest, meanwhile, was on Lou Reed, the self-titled debut album by the iconoclastic New York rocker fresh out of the Velvet Underground. Both he and Yes keyboardist Rick Wakeman found themselves recruited for the album in January 1972 when Yes were woodshedding new ideas at Morgan Studios in London during a break between legs of its world tour supporting its then-current album Fragile. Reed was in another studio at Morgan working on his album.

“We were in two separate buildings, but they were right across the road,” Howe recalls. “So, for Rick and I, it was about the simplest session we ever did. We just walked across the road, into another building.

“Lou was great. He played us two songs, demos; they were very simplistic — voice, maybe a keyboard and a guitar. He said, ‘They’re the two songs we’re doing.’ I think he gave us chord charts, or we made chord charts, ’cause I don’t read music so notation’s no use to me at all. As long as I’ve got a chord chart I can navigate my way through pretty much anything.

“I remember the studio had the old-fashioned kind of booths, separation booths, and the drummer, Clem Cattini, was in the corner. Basically we spent the afternoon doing those songs.”

Howe says he was not particularly a Reed fan at the time, however. “I wasn’t really big on American bands from that era,” he explains. “We liked the Byrds pretty much exclusively. Country Joe & the Fish, Janis Joplin, Lou Reed, blah, blah … it’s sort of like they were too American for us. We were into this other sort of prog/psychedelic music at the time.”

It was very smart ’cause he got us in there and he got us to contribute, which is better than telling us, ‘Here’s what you’re gonna play.’”

— Steve Howe

Which of the Lou Reed album’s 10 tracks Howe appeared on remains a matter of guesswork all these years later, as any published credits for the project have always been general. (Caleb Quaye and Paul Keogh also played on the album.) The moody, atmospheric album-closer “Ocean” — first attempted with the Velvet Underground for 1970’s Loaded — is a likely candidate, with Wakeman’s cascading piano and carefully deployed guitar licks throughout, along with the loping “Lisa Says.”

“It was very smart ’cause he got us in there and he got us to contribute, which is better than telling us, ‘Here’s what you’re gonna play,’” Howe remembers. “All I know in music is to contribute — not copying, not simulating or repeating, but actually contributing. I’m sure it was good for us.

“I think all guest appearances, I almost never turn them down. They always surprise you, and I like surprise — like when I stood in for Stone the Crows [at the Great Western Festival, summer of 1972]; I didn’t know I was gonna do that. Even with Queen [for the title track for Innuendo, 1991], I didn’t know I was going to do that until about two hours before.

“They also wanted spontaneous playing, because they didn’t have a part for me. I could’ve gone in and said, ‘Okay, what do you want me to play?’, but they said, ‘Just play anything. Do what you do.’ So they understood me quite thoroughly, that I wasn’t going to come in and play a ditty, a tune on top of it. They really wanted me to improvise.”

An “almost” on Howe’s guesting resume, meanwhile, came early when he was booled into London’s Olympic Sound Studios during May of 1969 at a session for Ella Fitzgerald’s album Ella, which came out later that year.

“I was in very early years … and was known as a bit of a jazzer, even though I couldn’t play jazz. I went there on a bus — the number. 13 from Holloway to Putney — with my 175,” he says, referring to the Gibson ES-175 electric guitar that has been mainstay throughout his career. “And when I get there, who do I pass in the corridor? Ella Fitzgerald. So I’m like, ‘Wow, Ella … Where’s she going? I just got here.’

“They told me, ‘Okay, well, set your amp up and we’ll do something,’ and lo and behold in the control room there were people like Mick Jagger standing there. I don’t know what they were doing there. I think Ron Wood was there. I think the drummer was one of the most famous drummers in the world; I can’t remember if it was Mick Fleetwood or Charlie Watts. I thought, ‘This is good,’ but I’ve forgotten who it was — obviously you don’t forget Mick Jagger’s in the control room.

“I recorded something, but I don’t know what, or if it was used, and I doubt that anybody in the world knows what it is. But if anybody does, give me a call, please.”

Howe is currently recuperating from “an essential operation” that scuttled Yes’s plans to promote its latest album, Aurora, which came out in April. The group will be returning to the road next May for dates in the U.K. and also plans to tour in Japan and North America.
item.description: The Yes guitarist looks back on the unexpected recording dates that put him in studios with Reed, Queen and other unlikely collaborators

“They also wanted spontaneous playing, because they didn’t have a part for me. I could’ve gone in and said, ‘Okay, what do you want me to play?’, but they said, ‘Just play anything. Do what you do.’ So they understood me quite thoroughly, that I wasn’t going to come in and play a ditty, a tune on top of it. They really wanted me to improvise.”

An “almost” on Howe’s guesting resume, meanwhile, came early when he was booled into London’s Olympic Sound Studios during May of 1969 at a session for Ella Fitzgerald’s album Ella, which came out later that year.

“I was in very early years … and was known as a bit of a jazzer, even though I couldn’t play jazz. I went there on a bus — the number. 13 from Holloway to Putney — with my 175,” he says, referring to the Gibson ES-175 electric guitar that has been mainstay throughout his career. “And when I get there, who do I pass in the corridor? Ella Fitzgerald. So I’m like, ‘Wow, Ella … Where’s she going? I just got here.’

“They told me, ‘Okay, well, set your amp up and we’ll do something,’ and lo and behold in the control room there were people like Mick Jagger standing there. I don’t know what they were doing there. I think Ron Wood was there. I think the drummer was one of the most famous drummers in the world; I can’t remember if it was Mick Fleetwood or Charlie Watts. I thought, ‘This is good,’ but I’ve forgotten who it was — obviously you don’t forget Mick Jagger’s in the control room.

“I recorded something, but I don’t know what, or if it was used, and I doubt that anybody in the world knows what it is. But if anybody does, give me a call, please.”

Howe is currently recuperating from “an essential operation” that scuttled Yes’s plans to promote its latest album, Aurora, which came out in April. The group will be returning to the road next May for dates in the U.K. and also plans to tour in Japan and North America.

item.title: How a simple guitar hook inspired Tears for Fears’ biggest hit: “I tuned the E string down to D and came up with this riff”
item.dc:content:
Tears for Fears guitarist Roland Orzabal says he wasn't convinced about the hit potential of "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" when the group recorded it 40 years ago. And neither, he adds, was his bandmate, Curt Smith.

But thanks to a chance riff he came up with on his Fender Stratocaster, the song generated enough interest to keep its creator from throwing it away.

Released on the group’s 1984 album, Songs From the Big Chair, "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" was in fact Tears for Fears' second number-one single, following on the success of its predecessor, "Shout," which had ascended to the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100.

Now three-times Platinum, “Everybody Wants to Rule the World” is the band's top-selling track of all-time, winning the Brit Award for Best Single in 1986 and helping drive Songs From the Big Chair to five-times Platinum sales. Tears For Fears recast it as "Everybody Wants to Run the World" to raise money for the African famine relief organization Sport Aid in 1986.

Amid its prominent synthesizers and drum machines, "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" is awash in electric and acoustic guitars played by Orzabal, who handled the song’s first break — the “rhythm solo,” as he calls it — and a second burning guitar solo played by the band’s touring guitarist, Neil Taylor.

Orzabal says his indoctrination into the guitar universe began "around the age of 13, 14," while he was growing up in Bath, England.

"A guy on the same street as me introduced me to bands like Budgie, Uriah Heep and a band called Led Zeppelin or something like that,” he says with a laugh. “I didn't like it at first, 'cause I was into glam rock. It took a long time for that music to wash over me. And, of course, once you start trying to copy Jimmy Page it becomes a little bit off-putting. But I appreciate a lot of those artists now.”

Today, Orzabal’s guitar collection numbers about 50 specimens, including the walnut Fender model known as "The Strat" he played on “Everybody Wants to Rule the World.” Manufactured from 1980 to 1983, this deluxe version of the Fender Stratocaster offered nine pickup combinations and featured gold hardware, a colored headstock and a unique bridge.

But as Orzabal explains, guitar didn't figure much in Tears for Fear's music at that point. Roughly six months before writing and recording Songs From the Big Chair, the band released the single “Mother’s Talk,” a track they’d recorded with great difficulty, using primarily synthesizers.

“It had been a very painful process,” Orzabal says of that song’s creation. “It had been mainly synthesizer and marimbas and xylophones. There wasn't much rock about it. Chris Hughes [who produced the group's 1983 debut, The Hurting] was brought back in to produce us, and he changed it all around. It was a difficult process, but the record company seemed to like it.”

With a month off to write songs for the new album, Orzabal retired to his home in Bath, England, and got to work using his walnut Strat, a Prophet 5 synthesizer and a LinnDrum rhythm box. “The downstairs had no furniture in it, so there was a lot of echo,” he says. “I would copy the drum parts from certain records into the drum machine. It gave me confidence knowing that had produced a great song, and I would write to those beats.”

One of those rhythms was from "Waterfront" by Simple Minds. “Just that simple ba-bump, ba-bump, ba-bump,” Orzabal says. "So that was the bass drum and the snare. There was another track by Lynx called ‘Throw Away the Key,’ and that had a very strange high-hat part. And I had this other pattern to counteract the high-hat part and put that in.” Together, the three rhythm tracks inspired the compelling shuffle rhythm that is the hallmark of “Everybody Wants to Rule the World.”

“And then,” Orzabal continues, “I tuned my guitar's E string down to D, and I came up with this riff.” He sings the percolating arpeggiated guitar line that opens the song. “I didn't really think anything of it, to be honest with you. It didn't have the depth of the other material I'd been working on.

“But my wife at the time liked it. So I thought, Okay, maybe I'm wrong."

I tuned down the E string to a D, and I came up with this riff... which I didn't really think anything of, to be honest with you."

— Roland Orzabal

Once in the studio, Orzabal shared his songs, which were still in their early stages of creation. They included “Shout” and "Everybody Wants to Rule the World," which at the point was called "Everybody Wants to Go to War.” Although Orzabal wasn’t convinced of the latter’s value, Hughes and the duo's label rep, David Bates, were immediately interested.

“Chris and David were adamant about it,” he recalls. “They wanted some kind of drive-time American hit — whatever that was — and they thought this could be. But neither Curt nor I were convinced. So Chris said, ‘All right, we'll do a proper day's recording on the other songs, and at the end of the day we'll put up the beats and just jam and muck around with it.’ "

When they finally returned to the song, its appeal slowly became apparent to its creator. “At some point I realized that it shouldn't be ‘Everybody Wants to Go to War,’ which was an annoying title,” Orzabal says. “We recorded it with Curt singing it. I didn't want to sing it — I didn't want anything to do with it.”

Besides, Orzabal had enough to do playing his walnut-bodied Strat. “I'd just bought it for its looks alone,” he says of the instrument. “It had gold everywhere. Where you would have the bridge tone control, you had a [nine-position] pickup selector switch. I played the guitar through a Boss compressor — I remember it was blue [most likely the Compression Sustainer CS-2 pedal, released in 1982] — into a Roland JC-120 with the chorus on. That's all.”

I played my walnut-bodied Strat through a Boss compressor into a Roland JC120 with the chorus on. That's all."

—Roland Orzabal

When it came time to record a solo, Orzabal took a chordal approach to the job. “The rhythm solo is my kind of thing, but it was a lot of drop-ins — all kinds of things just to sort of get the shape of it.”

But when Hughes and Bates decided he song needed a blazing-hot solo for the song’s outro, Orzabal knew it wasn’t his thing. “At the end they decided to put on a real, proper lead guitar solo,” he recalls, “and the first thing we said, without thinking, was ‘Neil Taylor.’ Neil had been floating around Tears for Fears for awhile, but he wanted to do his own thing. But we always knew he had a very idiosyncratic way of playing —far better than us when it comes to playing lead.”

Orzabal recalls that as recording proceeded, they often felt the beat needed to be faster. “We thought it was too slow, so every time we would record on it, we would put it up at least two percent,” he says. As a result, he says, the pitch "ended up between D and E flat.”

Released on March 22, 1985, “Everybody Wants to Rule the World” began its chart ascent, reaching number one in the U.S., Canada and New Zealand, and number two in the U.K., Australia, Ireland and the Netherlands. The song’s music video went into regular rotation on MTV and became a staple of the channel through much of that year,

We always knew Neil had a very idiosyncratic way of playing — far better than us when it comes to playing lead.”

—Roland Orzabal

Forty years on, Tears for Fears now have seven studio albums to their credit, including last year's The Tipping Point, the group's first in 18 years. October 25 will see the release of Songs for a Nervous Planet, which includes a set from the band’s latest tour plus four new studio tracks. It will be accompanied by Tears for Fears Live (A Tipping Point Film), which screens in theaters on October 25 and 26 (tearsforfearsfilm.com). Orzabal and Smith are also about to start work on the next Tears for Fears album, with the former predicting that "there will be more guitar" this time around.

As for the popularity of “Everybody Wants to Rule the World,” Orzabal says he’s gotten used to it, as well as fans’ reactions when it’s performed in concert. “You’re never really surprised by the hits,” he says. “What’s shocked me was that people were so keen to listen to the new material, and so patient. When Curt decided to do [2022’s] ’The Tipping Point’ as the first song of the show, I was a bit nervous of opening with a new track. But moving from that into ‘Everybody Wants to Rule the World’ — it was just fantastic. It’s the old and the new, and it all works together.”

item.title: “It felt like there were insects in my legs.” Peter Frampton on the moment he knew something was wrong
item.dc:content:
Peter Frampton’s career has produced only one Grammy for the classic-rock guitarist. It’s not for Frampton Comes Alive !, the 1976 smash hit that made him a global superstar, but for Fingerprints, his 2007 instrumental album.

But at the age of 76, the guitarist measures success on his own scale.

“In my mind, I’m more successful than I’ve ever been — because I like myself, I like what I do,” Frampton told The New York Times. “I’ve always been someone who didn’t think I was good enough, but I’ve reached the point where I don’t care what anybody else thinks. I should have felt that way a long time ago.”

That perspective has come through both the highs and lows of his career, as well as the physical challenges he has faced in recent years. Frampton recalls the first sign that something might be wrong. It was 2009, when he was 59. He and his son, Julian, were on a rare road trip to Big Sur to reconnect and write songs together.

In my mind, I’m more successful than I’ve ever been — because I like myself, I like what I do,”

— Peter Frampton

“Julian said, ‘Let’s run up this hill.’ Normally I would beat him, and I didn’t,” Frampton says from his home studio in Nashville. “It felt like there were insects in my legs, like they were vibrating.”

Frampton later learned that he had Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM), a progressive muscle-wasting disease that weakens the arms and legs. He was diagnosed around 2014 after suffering several falls at home and onstage, but he didn’t publicly reveal the diagnosis until 2019.

His career had already taken him through extraordinary highs and lows. In recent interviews he’s said the success of Frampton Comes Alive! overwhelmed him — and that its hastily recorded follow-up, I’m in You (1977), was a mistake. Suddenly he was everywhere — on the radio, TV and posters on fans’ walls, with his famed Fenix Les Paul electric guitar.

“The pressure was so great,” he said. “There was absolutely no need to do I’m in You then and there. The biggest mistake was just not shutting down at that point.”

His career slowed afterward as musical tastes shifted. Years later, speaking at The Art of Music event at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City last year, Frampton said it was then that he began planning for the next phase of his career.

“That’s when I sort of stopped working and basically just started writing on my own and getting ready for something that was to come.”

Julian said, ‘Let’s run up this hill.’ Normally I would beat him, and I didn’t.”

— Peter Frampton

His evolution since then resulted in what may be his most personal — and political — record. Carry the Light, released earlier this year, found the guitarist reflecting on life, family and the current political climate, with assistance from friends that include Graham Nash, Sheryl Crow and Tom Morello.

The album developed over three years, as he and his son, Julian, reconnected following the COVID-19 pandemic. Just before then, Frampton became a grandfather for the first time.

But the joy of that milestone was tempered by the effects of IBM. Since revealing his diagnosis, Frampton has made fewer appearances. He surprised attendees at the 2025 NAMM music show with an appearance at the Martin Guitar booth, where he first hinted he was recording Carry the Light. But standing — and even playing guitar — has become more difficult, forcing him to adjust how he frets chords and notes.

While he’s unsure whether he’ll tour again — his last tour, Let's Do It Again!, concluded in November 2025 — he remains hopeful and is keeping positive.

“People say, ‘Oh, you must be so upset,’ and, yeah, I am. But you can fix the little things,” Frampton says.

“But big things never worried me, because they’re the things you can’t do anything about. If I don’t accept what I have, I’m going to be mad for the rest of my life.”

item.title: Brian May says Eric Clapton changed his guitar playing — then Jimi Hendrix came along. “He just made me feel like I couldn’t play”
item.dc:content:
Before he became one of rock’s most distinctive guitarists, Brian May was a teenager in southwest London trying to find his musical voice. Like many aspiring British players of the era, he was captivated by the guitar heroes emerging from the local club scene. But two musicians in particular would fundamentally alter the way he thought about the instrument: Eric Clapton and Jimi Hendrix.

Speaking about his formative years in a school band called 1984, May recalled regularly performing soul covers by Sam & Dave and Otis Redding before Britain’s psychedelic explosion changed everything.

“We played a mixture of adapted soul stuff,” he said. “It was just pre-psychedelia. We used to try and do a couple of songs of our own. Luckily, as time went on, Pink Floyd, Cream, and Jimi Hendrix came along, and we started doing that.”

The first major revelation came from Eric Clapton during the guitarist’s tenure with the Yardbirds.

“Clapton was unbelievable, just so sparkling and fluid,” May said. “He was what turned me away from the Shadows style and sent me back to listening to B.B. King, Bo Diddley, and all those people I’d heard before.”

At the time, May admitted he had underestimated the blues, viewing it largely as a repetitive form.

“I thought it was all the same: 12-bar blues, and that was it,” he explained. “I didn’t realize the depth or emotion there was in it until I saw Eric Clapton doing it. That somehow made it accessible for me.”

Inspired by Clapton’s playing, May began tracing the guitarist’s influences and immersing himself in the records that had shaped the British blues boom.

“I went back and listened to his influences,” he said. “I listened to Clapton very closely, and to people like Mike Bloomfield on the first album by the Paul Butterfield Blues Band.”

May was equally enthralled by Jeff Beck, who replaced Clapton in the Yardbirds and pushed the electric guitar into increasingly adventurous territory.

“I couldn't believe what he could do,” May recalled. “I remember seeing him put the guitar down, make it feedback, and play a whole tune without even touching the fingerboard. That was the first time I saw a Les Paul guitar. I saw a gig at the Marquee soon after Beck had joined, and Eric Clapton came on and jammed at the end. That was pretty amazing; I'll never forget that.“

But even the combined impact of those two British guitar giants could not prepare him for what came next.

After years of developing his own expressive approach to the instrument, May believed he was beginning to achieve the sounds he heard in his head.

“I was beginning to make the guitar sort of talk,” he recalled. “I always wanted the guitar to play for people, to talk the same way a vocal did and have feeling in it.”

Then he encountered Hendrix.

“When I saw Hendrix, I thought, Oh my God. This guy is doing everything that I was trying to do.”

The experience was humbling.

“He just made me feel like I couldn’t play,” May said. “It makes you feel very uncomfortable when you thought you knew everything that was going on, and then suddenly somebody comes along who seems to be doing all sorts of things you hadn’t even thought of.”

Initially, May suspected that some of Hendrix’s seemingly impossible sounds might have been studio trickery. Hearing the guitarist’s conversation-like soloing on “Stone Free,” he wondered whether recording techniques were responsible.

That skepticism vanished when he saw Hendrix perform live at London’s Savoy Theatre while supporting the Who.

“He completely blew me away,” May said. “I thought, ‘He’s it.’”

From Clapton, he learned that blues guitar could communicate emotion and nuance — even if he did once earn Slowhand’s wrath when he and Eddie Van Halen dedicated a blues jam to the guitarist that Clapton called “so horrible.” From Hendrix, he discovered that the instrument’s expressive possibilities were far broader than he had imagined.

Those influences would eventually help shape the singular voice May developed with Queen — a style capable of singing, soaring, and, just as he had always wanted, making a guitar talk.

item.content:encoded:
Before he became one of rock’s most distinctive guitarists, Brian May was a teenager in southwest London trying to find his musical voice. Like many aspiring British players of the era, he was captivated by the guitar heroes emerging from the local club scene. But two musicians in particular would fundamentally alter the way he thought about the instrument: Eric Clapton and Jimi Hendrix.

Speaking about his formative years in a school band called 1984, May recalled regularly performing soul covers by Sam & Dave and Otis Redding before Britain’s psychedelic explosion changed everything.

“We played a mixture of adapted soul stuff,” he said. “It was just pre-psychedelia. We used to try and do a couple of songs of our own. Luckily, as time went on, Pink Floyd, Cream, and Jimi Hendrix came along, and we started doing that.”

The first major revelation came from Eric Clapton during the guitarist’s tenure with the Yardbirds.

“Clapton was unbelievable, just so sparkling and fluid,” May said. “He was what turned me away from the Shadows style and sent me back to listening to B.B. King, Bo Diddley, and all those people I’d heard before.”

At the time, May admitted he had underestimated the blues, viewing it largely as a repetitive form.

“I thought it was all the same: 12-bar blues, and that was it,” he explained. “I didn’t realize the depth or emotion there was in it until I saw Eric Clapton doing it. That somehow made it accessible for me.”

Inspired by Clapton’s playing, May began tracing the guitarist’s influences and immersing himself in the records that had shaped the British blues boom.

“I went back and listened to his influences,” he said. “I listened to Clapton very closely, and to people like Mike Bloomfield on the first album by the Paul Butterfield Blues Band.”

May was equally enthralled by Jeff Beck, who replaced Clapton in the Yardbirds and pushed the electric guitar into increasingly adventurous territory.

“I couldn't believe what he could do,” May recalled. “I remember seeing him put the guitar down, make it feedback, and play a whole tune without even touching the fingerboard. That was the first time I saw a Les Paul guitar. I saw a gig at the Marquee soon after Beck had joined, and Eric Clapton came on and jammed at the end. That was pretty amazing; I'll never forget that.“

But even the combined impact of those two British guitar giants could not prepare him for what came next.

After years of developing his own expressive approach to the instrument, May believed he was beginning to achieve the sounds he heard in his head.

“I was beginning to make the guitar sort of talk,” he recalled. “I always wanted the guitar to play for people, to talk the same way a vocal did and have feeling in it.”

Then he encountered Hendrix.

“When I saw Hendrix, I thought, Oh my God. This guy is doing everything that I was trying to do.”

The experience was humbling.

“He just made me feel like I couldn’t play,” May said. “It makes you feel very uncomfortable when you thought you knew everything that was going on, and then suddenly somebody comes along who seems to be doing all sorts of things you hadn’t even thought of.”

Initially, May suspected that some of Hendrix’s seemingly impossible sounds might have been studio trickery. Hearing the guitarist’s conversation-like soloing on “Stone Free,” he wondered whether recording techniques were responsible.

That skepticism vanished when he saw Hendrix perform live at London’s Savoy Theatre while supporting the Who.

“He completely blew me away,” May said. “I thought, ‘He’s it.’”

The impact was so overwhelming that May believed even one of Britain’s biggest bands couldn’t compete.

“The Who couldn’t follow him in those days,” he said. “Anybody in the world would find it hard to follow Hendrix.”

The lessons May absorbed from both players would remain central to his own style. From Clapton, he learned that blues guitar could communicate emotion and nuance — even if he did once earn Slowhand’s wrath when he and Eddie Van Halen dedicated a blues jam to the guitarist that Clapton called “so horrible.” From Hendrix, he discovered that the instrument’s expressive possibilities were far broader than he had imagined.

Those influences would eventually help shape the singular voice May developed with Queen — a style capable of singing, soaring, and, just as he had always wanted, making a guitar talk.

item.title: Olivia Rodrigo’s “The Cure” started with a guitar mistake: “I messed up”
item.dc:content:
Olivia Rodrigo’s “The Cure” started with a guitar mistake — and ended with Dan Nigro having to Melodyne a piano to match an acoustic guitar that was 15 to 20 cents sharp.

Speaking to the Song Exploder podcast, Rodrigo and her co-writer and producer Nigro broke down the making of the song, which Rodrigo has called her favorite track on her latest album, You Seem Pretty Sad For a Girl So in Love.

The song began with a conversation Rodrigo had with a friend while sitting next to him in his Jeep. She told him that she was in love, but also miserable much of the time, and that she wanted to write love songs.

“He’s like, ‘You have to write about how you’re actually feeling. You can’t pretend to write a certain way. You can’t write in the way that you think you’re supposed to feel.’”

A few days later, Rodrigo started writing “The Cure” on her couch with an acoustic guitar. And although she admits, “I’m not great at guitar,” that turned out to be an advantage.

“I was trying to play a chord and I played it wrong. I messed up where my fingers were, but it actually just sounded cool. And I was like, ‘Oh, that’s great!’ A wonderful thing about being a novice is sometimes you make a happy accident.”

When she brought the song to Nigro, they worked out the guitar part and added a bridge. But when it came time to record it, Nigro didn’t exactly follow standard acoustic-guitar recording procedure.

Rather than set up microphones specifically for the guitar, he used two microphones that were already positioned above his piano.

“These two microphones that are up on my piano were there,” he says. “And instead of micing the guitar properly, I literally just stood on the piano bench and played the guitar into the two piano mics. It was a really rough take, and then [Olivia] recorded her vocals to my guitar.”

That rough guitar recording became the foundation for the vocals — and created a second, rather unusual recording problem. Nigro says he deliberately avoided pitch correction on Rodrigo’s vocals, leaving the two vocal tracks to rub against each other slightly and preserve the song’s uneasy character.

“There’s no Auto-Tune, and there’s no Melodyning or anything,” he says. “They’re just her vocal tracks; they kind of rub a little bit in spaces [and] that makes it feel unsettling. And I feel like as much as we have all the modern tools that we can, like, make a vocal feel perfect, it felt imperfectly perfect.”

But the guitar itself wasn’t quite in tune. Nigro had recorded the part so quickly that he hadn’t checked the tuning, leaving the instrument 15 to 20 cents sharp.

“My guitar is actually about 15 to 20 cents sharp, and so I ended up having to tune every other instrument to the guitar and the vocal because I didn’t want to mess with it,” he says. “When I played the piano, because the piano was actually in tune, I had to Melodyne the piano to be in tune with the guitar.”

So while Melodyne wasn’t used to clean up Rodrigo’s vocals, it was used to make the properly tuned piano conform to the accidentally sharp guitar.

That imperfection became part of the character of “The Cure,” a song Rodrigo describes as “very tense.” Nigro deliberately kept building that tension into the second verse, withholding the drums when listeners might expect them to arrive.

“I think everyone thinks when they hear it for the first time that the drums are about to come in, but they don’t,” he says.

When the drums and strings finally arrive, Rodrigo says the payoff feels earned — the same philosophy that shaped the song’s guitar recording in the first place: rather than polish away every imperfection, they kept the elements that made the track feel human and unsettled.
item.description: Dan Nigro explains how an accidental chord, a hastily recorded acoustic guitar and an out-of-tune guitar shaped the song’s tense, deliberately imperfect sound
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Swann

item.title: Jeff “Skunk” Baxter says guitarists need to master these two tricks: “I only give two lessons”
item.dc:content:
Jeff “Skunk” Baxter has played on hundreds of recordings as a member of Steely Dan and the Doobie Brothers, as well as in his long career as a session musician. He has two essential pieces of advice for guitarists, which he shared during a conversation about performance with co-hosts Jason Alexander and Peter Tilden.

The men were appearing on an episode of the podcast Really? no, Really?. Titled “Guitars & Guided Missiles: Jeff ‘Skunk’ Baxter’s Extraordinary Career,” the episode offers an examination of both Baxter’s history and his unique approach to the guitar and problem solving.

“I only give two lessons,” Baxter tells Alexander. “One is use a metronome. ’Cause if you can't groove, you're not gonna get any work.”

But it’s lesson number two that takes the conversation in a different direction. Baxter — who has riffed on the hidden charms of modern electric guitars — introduces the concept by pointing to Canadian jazz pianist Oscar Peterson.

“If you ever watch Oscar Peterson play, he's playing, but you can hear him going [scats]. Basically, he's singing. And I always tell anybody who wants to learn to play the guitar to sit down and sing while you play, because eventually you'll be able to connect singing the melodies in your head to your fingers.

“And that's how you get what the psychologists call 'flow,' where you remove the conscious piece. That's what most people do when they're improvising — they’re actually translating the voice in their heads to their fingers.”

Alexander agrees, offering a powerful illustration of Baxter’s point from his own viewing history.

“I remember watching a great documentary years ago about Isaac Stern, the violinist, in China. There was a section where he was teaching protégés — I mean, really gifted young violinists — and he was doing a master class.

“And this young woman got up and she played, you know, 16 bars of a piece, and it sounded great. And he went, ‘Yeah, put the instrument down. Sing it. Sing what you just played.’ And she sang it. And he said, ‘Now, pick up the instrument and sing it as you play it.’ And it transformed her playing. And I thought that was remarkable.”

Baxter explains that singing while playing is transformational because it forces a musician to shape their phrasing, adding nuance, interest, and expression to the performance.

“The melodies usually are pretty close, but the phrasing is, I would say, 60 percent of why people enjoy what you play,” Baxter says. “It’s how you play it, not necessarily what you're playing.”
item.description: The Steely Dan and Doobie Brothers veteran explains why one of his two essential tips can change the way you play

item.title: Dolly Parton wrote “9 to 5” with her fingernails: “I have a credit on the back of the album that says, ‘Nails by Dolly!’”
item.dc:content:
September 25 is Dolly Parton Day, a fitting date for celebrating the life and music of the late country icon because it can be written as 9/25 — a numerical nod to her signature song, “9 to 5.”

Guitarists marveled for years at Parton’s ability to fret a guitar while wearing her famously long acrylic nails. But those glamorous extensions — part of her signature look — did more than make her guitar playing a little more challenging. They also helped her write one of her biggest hits.

Parton died August 25 at age 80, leaving behind a seven-decade career as a singer, songwriter, actress and philanthropist. Among her many achievements, she wrote thousands of songs and earned 11 Grammy Awards, while her Imagination Library distributed more than 300 million books to children around the world.

But “9 to 5” remains one of Parton’s most instantly recognizable songs. Written for the 1980 comedy of the same name, it became her first number one hit on the Billboard Hot 100, earned her two Grammys in 1982 and was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Original Song.

And the story of how she wrote it is wonderfully Dolly Parton.

The movie starred Parton alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin as three office workers who plot to get even with their sexist, egotistical boss. Fonda had championed Parton for the role, and Parton agreed to appear on the condition that she would have a chance to write the theme song.

The song came to her while she was on the set, with her guitar back in her trailer. And, fittingly for a movie about office workers, Parton found an unlikely substitute for a typewriter: her fingernails.

“I was bored always in between takes because they have so much time between setups with lighting,” she explained on The Graham Norton Show. “And you just sit around, and what are you going to do?”

Part of her deal with Fonda was that she would get to write the theme song. But without her guitar at hand, she began experimenting with the sound of her acrylic nails.

“I would take my nails, and because it was acrylic nails it makes like a percussive sound,” Parton explained. “It sounds like a typewriter, too.”

She began clacking her nails together to create a rhythm while jotting down words and ideas inspired by what she was seeing around the set.

“So I just started to write little words and things that I would see, and things I would think that would fit with that day-to-day nine-to-five job. Then I’d go back at night to my hotel room and put those things down,” she said.

The idea stuck. And the sound of those nails eventually became part of the finished recording.

Parton even gave her manicure an official credit on 9 to 5 and Odd Jobs, the album on which the song appeared.

“I have a credit on the back of the album that says, ‘Nails by Dolly!’”

That little detail is one of those perfect Dolly Parton stories: her trademark look wasn’t simply decoration. She found a way to make it part of the music.

And those nails had long presented another musical challenge for Parton. How, exactly, did she manage to fret an acoustic guitar while wearing them?

Her solution was to work around them. Parton explained that she often used open tunings and barre chords, allowing her to play without having to curl her fretting fingers as much. She also favored the three-quarter-sized acoustic guitars she had played since her youth.

There were limits, though.

“If I’m really serious about it, I just have to saw ’em down!” she said.

Much of Parton’s distinctive guitar style comes from her rhythmic right hand. Her playing combines the Maybelle Carter-style “thumb and flick” approach with the alternating bass technique associated with players such as Hank Williams and Johnny Cash. Her thumb picks out bass notes while her first finger flicks down across the strings to sound the corresponding chord.

You can hear and see that approach in action when Parton performs the title track from her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, all while sporting her trademark nails. Her picking-hand nails even tap against the guitar’s body, adding another percussive element to the performance.

It’s a fitting reminder of something that came through in so much of Parton’s music: she could turn just about anything into an instrument — even her fingernails.

item.title: Dolly Parton got out of bed to record her final song with U2. Says Bono, “I can’t even listen to it now”
item.dc:content:
Country music legend Dolly Parton was never a stranger to collaboration. While songwriting sessions with Linda Ronstadt and Kenny Rogers are classic examples of more predictable team-ups, she was always happy to go a little off-piste, too, as her 2025 collaboration with Mötley Crüe attests.

However, it was Irish rockers U2 who got the honor of recording Parton’s last-ever song with her, and Bono says her passing has now made it too painful to listen to.

The Irish band have sold an estimated 175 million records during their career. They’ll be looking to give that figure a shot in the arm when they release Carnaval de Luz, their first album in over a decade, this November. But following Parton’s passing at 80 last month, one song from the new batch is getting more attention than most.

“When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song,” Bono tells Rolling Stone of “Torn,” a song that Snow Patrol’s Johnny McDaid also helped write.

“And you can hear that,” he adds. “I can’t even listen to it now.”

The track will close the band’s first full-length record of new music since Songs of Experience in 2014. Mind you, the band has already released two EPs — Days of Ash and Easter Lily — this year. They’re dead center in a purple patch right now.

Like many U2 songs before it, the original idea for their duet drew influence from Irish folk music. Parton wasn’t overly fond of the suggested sketch, with Bono saying she quipped, “That’s a little too Irish for me,” when it was first presented to her. In classic Parton fashion, the tireless songstress had a backup plan in her back pocket.

“She said, ‘I got this song. It’s called ‘Torn’; do you wanna see where you can take it somewhere else, maybe?’” he recalls.

A post shared by U2 (@u2)

A photo posted by

Details about the song are still closely guarded at this point, but it has been revealed that Daniel Lanois, who has worked with U2 before as well as the likes of Neil Young, Peter Gabriel and Willie Nelson, plays pedal steel on the track. It’s a hire that ensures the signature Parton flavor comes from more than just her belted vocals.

An official press release from the band, meanwhile, describes “Torn” as “a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances.”

Not only is it another unlikely collaboration from an artist who remained unpredictable and vivacious until the very end, it feels like a dream for Bono that it even happened.

“It’s very moving to have had these intimacies with such a figure,” he says. “The fact that they’re not there now, in any way you can call back, other than through her songs, is very sobering.”

The news comes as Parton’s estate deals with an increasingly complicated aftermath of her death. On September 23, a Tennessee judge granted a temporary restraining order against her nephew Bryan Seaver and his security company, following allegations from Parton’s estate that he had made threatening statements toward employees, attorneys and business partners. Seaver, who served as Parton’s head of security and announced her death last month, has denied making threats and called the restraining order a “publicity stunt.”

Parton was laid to rest at a private Nashville ceremony at the end of August, and was the subject of a teary tribute at the Emmys just two weeks later.

Her career would begin with just one little guitar, and would go on to span a staggering eight decades. During that time, she released 49 studio albums, with her last, Rockstar, showing another side to the singer once more.

It was an album that Steve Albini had wanted to produce before his passing, but it was U2 who got the honor of one last studio trip with the Queen of Country.

item.content:encoded:
Country music legend Dolly Parton was never a stranger to collaboration. While songwriting sessions with Linda Ronstadt and Kenny Rogers are classic examples of more predictable team-ups, she was always happy to go a little off-piste, too, as her 2025 collaboration with Mötley Crüe attests.

However, it was Irish rockers U2 who got the honor of recording Parton’s last-ever song with her, and Bono says her passing has now made it too painful to listen to.

The Irish band have sold an estimated 175 million records during their career. They’ll be looking to give that figure a shot in the arm when they release Carnaval de Luz, their first album in over a decade, this November. But following Parton’s passing at 80 last month, one song from the new batch is getting more attention than most.

“When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song,” Bono tells Rolling Stone of “Torn,” a song that Snow Patrol’s Johnny McDaid also helped write.

“And you can hear that,” he adds. “I can’t even listen to it now.”

The track will close the band’s first full-length record of new music since Songs of Experience in 2014. Mind you, the band has already released two EPs — Days of Ash and Easter Lily — this year. They’re dead center in a purple patch right now.

Like many U2 songs before it, the original idea for their duet drew influence from Irish folk music. Parton wasn’t overly fond of the suggested sketch, with Bono saying she quipped, “That’s a little too Irish for me,” when it was first presented to her. In classic Parton fashion, the tireless songstress had a backup plan in her back pocket.

“She said, ‘I got this song. It’s called ‘Torn’; do you wanna see where you can take it somewhere else, maybe?’” he recalls.

A post shared by U2 (@u2)

A photo posted by

Details about the song are still closely guarded at this point, but it has been revealed that Daniel Lanois, who has worked with U2 before as well as the likes of Neil Young, Peter Gabriel and Willie Nelson, plays pedal steel on the track. It’s a hire that ensures the signature Parton flavor comes from more than just her belted vocals.

An official press release from the band, meanwhile, describes “Torn” as “a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances.”

Not only is it another unlikely collaboration from an artist who remained unpredictable and vivacious until the very end, it feels like a dream for Bono that it even happened.

“It’s very moving to have had these intimacies with such a figure,” he says. “The fact that they’re not there now, in any way you can call back, other than through her songs, is very sobering.”

The news comes as Parton’s estate deals with an increasingly complicated aftermath of her death. On September 23, a Tennessee judge granted a temporary restraining order against her nephew Bryan Seaver and his security company, following allegations from Parton’s estate that he had made threatening statements toward employees, attorneys and business partners. Seaver, who served as Parton’s head of security and announced her death last month, has denied making threats and called the restraining order a “publicity stunt.”

Parton was laid to rest at a private Nashville ceremony at the end of August, and was the subject of a teary tribute at the Emmys just two weeks later.

Her career would begin with just one little guitar, and would go on to span a staggering eight decades. During that time, she released 49 studio albums, with her last, Rockstar, showing another side to the singer once more.

It was an album that Steve Albini had wanted to produce before his passing, but it was U2 who got the honor of one last studio trip with the Queen of Country.

item.title: Lonnie Mack's Flying V — played through Stevie Ray Vaughan’s rig — heads to auction
item.dc:content:
Lonnie Mack’s beloved 1958 Gibson Flying V is heading to auction, along with the 1962 Magnatone Custom 440 combo and strap he used throughout his career. The Flying V — number 7 off Gibson’s production line — has a starting bid of $300,000 and is expected to rise when it goes under the hammer at Heritage Auctions.

For guitar players, though, the significance of the instrument goes well beyond its rarity. Mack never quite became a household name, but serious players knew his power and influence. Through his mix of blues, country and soul, he left an indelible impression on a young Stevie Ray Vaughan — who would eventually help bring his hero’s career back from the brink.

When Vaughan discovered Jimi Hendrix’s music via a lucky dumpster find, his life was irrevocably changed. He never had the chance to meet Hendrix, but when another pillar of his musical inspiration needed a helping hand, Vaughan was able to be his hero.

“Lonnie was a big influence on me,” the bluesman said in Guitar Player’s April 1985 issue, speaking during a break in a recording session at Austin’s Cedar Creek Studio. Mack’s career, playing and comeback via Strike Like Lightning, which he co-produced with Vaughan, were key topics of conversation.

“A lot of people don’t realize how big an influence he is on today’s guitar players in general, especially when it comes to phrasing,” Vaughan said. “That first album of his, The Wham! Of That Memphis Man, is the first record I ever bought. Actually, my brother Jimmie first turned me on to Lonnie, but I beat him to the punch getting the album to the house.”

After the success of his debut album, Mack struggled to properly follow it up, with subsequent records suffering from poor promotion. Compounding matters, as the British Invasion took hold in the States — the Beatles’ Ed Sullivan debut came the year after Wham! was released — his opportunities and prominence began to wane.

During his bleakest spell on the fringes of the music business, Mack was reportedly selling Bibles out of the back of his car. He was later hired to play bass on the Doors’ 1970 album Morrison Hotel, where he can be heard on “Roadhouse Blues” and “Maggie M’Gill.”

It was the better part of a decade later that Mack and SRV crossed paths. The meeting proved fortuitous for both men.

“Stevie impressed the hell out of me,” Mack said in that same interview. “He wasn’t right for the South band [Mack’s group], which was country-rock, but he was definitely a great player.”

“I was playin’ the Rome Inn in Austin, and we had just hit the opening chords of ‘Wham!’ when this big guy walked in,” Vaughan recalled. Little did he know he was playing Mack’s biggest hit in front of the man himself.

“He looked just like a great big bear,” Vaughan added. “As soon as I looked close at his face, I realized who he was, and naturally he was blown away to hear us doing his song. We talked for a long time that night, and he wanted to produce us. So it’s kind of ironic the way things turned out.”

Indeed, plans were made, and in 1985, Vaughan and Mack wound up working together on Strike Like Lightning, Mack’s comeback record. Vaughan co-produced the album, helping bring the guitarist back into the spotlight.

Mack had essentially one guitar throughout his career, and he didn’t need anything else. It was a red 1958 Gibson Flying V, number 7 off Gibson’s production line. A quick look at it reveals that he was more than happy to modify the guitar, with a metal bar running across the split in the V to accommodate a Bigsby vibrato. The guitar was also sent to Gibson for its distinctive refinish in 1963, the same year his debut LP was released.

Notably, the guitar has more than Mack’s own history attached to it. On Strike Like Lightning, it was plugged into some of SRV’s most distinctive tonal weapons.

First, it ran through the guitarist’s fabled Ibanez Tube Screamer, with the signal then feeding into a mic’d Fender Vibroverb, another piece of Vaughan’s arsenal.

Their album together had plenty of poetry to it. The Wham of That Memphis Man was the first record SRV ever bought, and together, they reworked its instrumental title track, renaming it “Double Whammy” for obvious reasons.

A year after its release, Mack was asked by Guitar World how he arranged the song with his biggest fan. His response typified the informal chemistry between the two.

“I’d just say, ‘go!’” he laughed. “I’d say, ‘Okay, you play rhythm, take the second solo,’ like that; we never worked anything out in detail.”

For more SRV, check out our recently republished 1984 Guitar Player interview, taking in everything from Dumbles to strippers and crazy gigs.

item.title: New Found Glory will play Disney World shows in memory of Chad Gilbert
item.dc:content:
American pop-punk band New Found Glory has found a fitting way to pay tribute to their late guitarist, Chad Gilbert — they’re headed to Disney World.

Gilbert was part of the Coral Springs, Florida, band’s founding lineup in 1997 and went on to build a cult following across 11 albums. In recent years, he battled multiple forms of cancer and earlier this month tragically passed away at age 45.

There’s been an outpouring of love for the guitarist from across the music scene, and now his surviving bandmates have found a fitting way to honor his memory by going ahead with a series of shows at Epcot at the Disney World resort in their home state.

The shows were arranged before Gilbert’s passing, but they’ve now taken on a different meaning.

“We want to thank everyone for the overwhelming amount of love and tribute posts for Chad these past few days,” the band says in an official statement via Instagram. “Seeing how deeply he touched so many lives means everything to us, and we know he would be so proud to see it.”

The band also announced that it was pulling out of its upcoming appearance at Aftershock Festival to give its members time to grieve. Though taking place before the festival, the Epcot shows will be the band’s first since Gilbert’s death, and they will go ahead as planned. In doing so, the band will unite two of Gilbert’s biggest passions.

“Anyone who knew Chad knew that he was a massive Disney fan,” the post continues. “Our shows at Epcot were dates he was so excited for and he was actively planning to be on stage with us there. He had already worked on the setlists with us and was practicing as much as possible to be ready.

A post shared by New Found Glory (@newfoundglory)

A photo posted by

“Because of how much he wanted to play these shows, taking the stage at Epcot feels like the right way to honor him, and what he would want us to do. Our plan from the beginning with him was to announce our Epcot sets ahead of time, so we feel it’s only appropriate to share them with you now as we prepare to play in his memory.”

Given his illness, Gilbert — whose main electric guitars were Les Pauls and Telecasters — had been unable to play many shows with the band in recent years. Real Friends guitarist David Knox has been filling in for him at recent shows, but Gilbert was able to return to the stage for a show in Nashville on June 8, performing two songs from a motorized scooter as his daughter watched on. He underwent brain surgery in March after struggling to control his left hand.

At Epcot, the band will play three shows each night at America Gardens Theatre in the American Adventure pavilion, at 5:30 p.m., 6:45 p.m. and 8 p.m. The shows will take place September 28 and 29 as part of the Epcot International Food & Wine Festival.

A post shared by Mark Hoppus (@markhoppus)

A photo posted by

“Every note we play and every word you sing at Epcot is for Chad,” the band concludes. “Thank you all for wrapping us in so much love, understanding, and support as we come together to honor his legacy.”

Meanwhile, Blink-182 bassist and Fender signature artist Mark Hoppus has paid an emotional tribute to the guitarist, who touched the lives of many.

“Chad was the best friend to every person he met,” he writes. “The most positive and creative force in any room he walked into. These past years he fought his sickness with the soul of a joyous, courageous warrior. With dignity, love, and gratitude. He never complained once, only kept saying how lucky he was. For everything. Today we lost a good one, and the world won’t be the same.”

Gilbert is survived by his wife and daughter, as well as his mother, Jackie, and brother, Brian.

item.title: As Ed Sheeran deals with tour fallout, Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour: “What happened to me is bigger than one artist”
item.dc:content:
Macklemore is turning the controversy surrounding his departure from Ed Sheeran’s U.S. tour into a new run of shows centered on his support for Palestinians.

The rapper announced the Free Palestine Tour Thursday, with initial dates set for Dublin, Paris and London. Additional artists and U.S. dates will be announced soon, he said, with all proceeds from the tour set to benefit organizations supporting Palestinians. The Dublin date is scheduled for October 26, with the Paris and London dates to follow.

The announcement comes less than two weeks after Macklemore was removed from Sheeran’s Loop Tour following comments he made during a September 4 performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Macklemore told the crowd that one reason he wanted to join the tour was to be able to say “Free Palestine” from stadium stages, and he performed his 2024 protest song “Hind’s Hall.”

A post shared by BEN (@macklemore)

A photo posted by

Macklemore was subsequently dropped from the remainder of the U.S. leg of the tour. Sheeran has said the decision was made by the tour’s promoter, Messina Touring Group, after venues indicated they would not host the shows if Macklemore remained on the bill.

Several of Sheeran’s other supporting acts — including Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga — subsequently withdrew from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Sheeran also incurred the ire of former Pink Floyd bass guitarist Roger Waters, a longtime supporter of Palestinian causes, who called him "a little prick" in a video about Macklemore’s removal from the Loop tour.

Sheeran has continued the Loop Tour, performing largely on his own after the supporting acts departed.

At his September 19 concert in Philadelphia, Sheeran addressed the controversy from the stage. He said he had made “mistakes” and apologized to fans, while also describing the situation in Gaza as “catastrophic and unjustifiable.” Sheeran said he wanted his shows to be about “unity and humanity, not politics,” but acknowledged that the controversy had placed him in the middle of a debate over freedom of speech and the conflict.

Macklemore, meanwhile, said the experience had convinced him that artists should use their platforms to speak out even when doing so carries consequences.

“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage,” he wrote in announcing the new tour. “When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”

He said he spent the past week reaching out to other artists who have publicly supported Palestinians and began discussing a new tour. Macklemore acknowledged that the project has come together quickly, with artists, schedules and other details still being finalized.

“But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done,” he wrote. “So we’re going on tour.”

The first announced dates are in Dublin, Paris and London, with artist announcements and U.S. dates to follow. Macklemore is directing fans to his website to sign up for updates and first access to tickets. The presale is scheduled to begin Monday, September 28, at 10 a.m. local time, with the general on-sale beginning Wednesday, September 30, at 10 a.m.
item.description: The announcement comes after Macklemore was removed from Sheeran’s Loop Tour, prompting the remaining supporting acts to withdraw in solidarity; Sheeran has since resumed the tour with a new lineup.

item.title: Why Krist Novoselic hated Kurt Cobain’s original “Heart-Shaped Box” solo: “Why are you sabotaging this beautiful song?”
item.dc:content:
The controversy surrounding Nirvana’s final album, 1993’s In Utero, has been well documented. The band had deliberately set out to make a rawer, less polished follow-up to Nevermind, enlisting Steve Albini to record the album in just 10 days. But reports that executives at their label, DGC, were unhappy with the finished record’s abrasive sound and commercial potential led to a contentious post-production process.

Nirvana ultimately stood by most of Albini’s work, but they did bring in Scott Litt to remix “Heart-Shaped Box” and “All Apologies,” both of which would become singles. While Kurt Cobain said he felt the vocals weren’t prominent enough in Albini’s original mixes, bass guitarist Krist Novoselic has now revealed that he had a rather different objection to “Heart-Shaped Box” — one he had raised with Cobain and Albini while the album was being recorded.

The trio — Kurt Cobain on guitar and vocals, Krist Novoselic on bass and Dave Grohl on drums — had decided to go back to basics ahead of their session with Albini. They wanted the album released warts and all, despite concerns that its roughness would make it an unsuccessful follow-up to Nevermind.

But by the time they decided to remix All Apologies and Heart-Shaped Box, as Novoselic told Mojo, the latter song had been nagging at the bassist for a while.

“That was the thing with Steve. It felt like once the record was done it was completely done,” he said. “That’s when the record label kinda stepped in and said, ‘Hey!’ We had a confrontation about the situation.”

He continued: “But you know why we had to remix Heart-Shaped Box? You should hear the original version of that song — the guitar solo has this effect on it. It just sabotages the whole song. Steve and Kurt were colluding!

“I would go to Kurt, ‘Why are you sabotaging this beautiful song by putting this hideous abortion in the centre of it?’ He’d be like, ‘Well, I think it sounds cool.’”

He added that he couldn’t clearly remember the reasons Cobain and Albini offered for having tracked it that way. “Some statement against commercial radio or something — the popular mainstream aesthetic… I dunno!”

When Litt was hired to remix the two tracks, Novoselic reflected: “Maybe I should have spoke up at the time [of recording].”

But he countered his own position: “I think it’s a great-sounding record. It’s a highly artistic record. I don’t know who else could have produced it except Albini.

“It’s my favorite Nirvana record, and I’ll tell you why. There was a lot of stuff going on with the band; externally and internally, there was a lot of pressures. But when we walked through that door we left all that stuff outside the door. We just played music, we worked together really well, we were laughing, we were concentrating, we were open.

“And that really shows on the record. We didn’t mess around. Nobody got bombed, everybody was focused and clear-headed. I’m really proud of it, it’s a beautiful record.”

He went on: “Sometimes the lyrics on In Utero are really creepy. I listen to ’em now and it’s like, ‘Why didn’t I hear that back then?’”
item.description: While In Utero remains Novoselic’s favorite Nirvana album, he admits he clashed with Cobain over an intentional attempt to sabotage their biggest track.

item.content:encoded:
The controversy surrounding Nirvana’s final album, 1993’s In Utero, has been well documented. The band had deliberately set out to make a rawer, less polished follow-up to Nevermind, enlisting Steve Albini to record the album in just 10 days. But reports that executives at their label, DGC, were unhappy with the finished record’s abrasive sound and commercial potential led to a contentious post-production process.

Nirvana ultimately stood by most of Albini’s work, but they did bring in Scott Litt to remix “Heart-Shaped Box” and “All Apologies,” both of which would become singles. While Kurt Cobain said he felt the vocals weren’t prominent enough in Albini’s original mixes, bass guitarist Krist Novoselic has now revealed that he had a rather different objection to “Heart-Shaped Box” — one he had raised with Cobain and Albini while the album was being recorded.

The trio — Kurt Cobain on guitar and vocals, Krist Novoselic on bass and Dave Grohl on drums — had decided to go back to basics ahead of their session with Albini. They wanted the album released warts and all, despite concerns that its roughness would make it an unsuccessful follow-up to Nevermind.

But by the time they decided to remix All Apologies and Heart-Shaped Box, as Novoselic told Mojo, the latter song had been nagging at the bassist for a while.

“That was the thing with Steve. It felt like once the record was done it was completely done,” he said. “That’s when the record label kinda stepped in and said, ‘Hey!’ We had a confrontation about the situation.”

He continued: “But you know why we had to remix Heart-Shaped Box? You should hear the original version of that song — the guitar solo has this effect on it. It just sabotages the whole song. Steve and Kurt were colluding!

“I would go to Kurt, ‘Why are you sabotaging this beautiful song by putting this hideous abortion in the centre of it?’ He’d be like, ‘Well, I think it sounds cool.’”

He added that he couldn’t clearly remember the reasons Cobain and Albini offered for having tracked it that way. “Some statement against commercial radio or something — the popular mainstream aesthetic… I dunno!”

When Litt was hired to remix the two tracks, Novoselic reflected: “Maybe I should have spoke up at the time [of recording].”

But he countered his own position: “I think it’s a great-sounding record. It’s a highly artistic record. I don’t know who else could have produced it except Albini.

“It’s my favorite Nirvana record, and I’ll tell you why. There was a lot of stuff going on with the band; externally and internally, there was a lot of pressures. But when we walked through that door we left all that stuff outside the door. We just played music, we worked together really well, we were laughing, we were concentrating, we were open.

“And that really shows on the record. We didn’t mess around. Nobody got bombed, everybody was focused and clear-headed. I’m really proud of it, it’s a beautiful record.”

He went on: “Sometimes the lyrics on In Utero are really creepy. I listen to ’em now and it’s like, ‘Why didn’t I hear that back then?’”

item.title: Black Sabbath’s first manager says these lost 1969 recordings show Tony Iommi’s evolution: “Any real Black Sabbath fans will really want to hear this”
item.dc:content:
Black Sabbath’s first manager said it was important that their 1969 demo tapes be released so fans could hear the development of Tony Iommi as a world-changing guitarist.

The tracks were laid down in Birmingham during the brief period when the band called themselves Earth, with a sound that was still rooted in blues and jazz. They’d started out as the Polka Tulk Blues Band in 1968 before shortening the name to Polka Tulk, then becoming Earth. They took on their best-known name in August 1969.

Jim Simpson looked after their affairs in those early days and was instrumental in making the recordings, which he wanted to release in 2025 as Earth: The Legendary Lost Tapes. Those plans were stalled after Sharon Osbourne stepped in, and the masters have since been handed over to the band.

In an interview earlier this year (via Blabbermouth), Simpson explained what he thought had gone wrong.

“The sleeve notes, which I wrote, talked about those great days when Birmingham established itself as the U.K. home of rock and roll. And it exalted some of the names that were coming through and the people who made us famous musically.

“It ended up by saying, ‘At the end of the decade came along one band who would not only change the face of music in the U.K., but create their own style and go on to world domination.’ I didn’t mention Black Sabbath, electric guitarist Tony Iommi, bass guitarist Geezer Butler, singer Ozzy Osbourne and drummer Bill Ward. It irked somebody.”

No release plans have been revealed, although Iommi said in July 2026 that they’d appear “at some point.” Simpson said: “Right at the beginning I was told that the band didn't want it to happen.” He went on to argue that, regardless of the musicians’ concerns, it was important for the music to be heard.

“They were a blues band when I met them,” he emphasised. “And the album’s nine tracks. It starts off with four blues tracks [and] a couple of jazz tracks, because of Tony Iommi's love of gypsy jazz. The two jazz tracks are both called Song For Jim. One featured Tony on guitar, the other featured Tony on flute. We’d already recorded one with guitar, so we recorded it again with flute. And he did a good job.

“They all did a good job. But after the first few tracks, the remaining four tracks get towards, but never quite reach, what you know of as Black Sabbath. It slowly got heavier and heavier. It’s a historical document. Any real Black Sabbath fans will really want to hear this.”

Earlier this year, Iommi — who joined fellow flautist Ian Anderson in Jethro Tull for a few weeks in 1969 before returning to Sabbath to apply what he’d learned — said he’d enjoyed listening to the Earth recordings. “It’s weird when you hear stuff from so long ago; all these things crop up that you forgot about,” he told Rolling Stone. “I sat listening to them all, and it was good because there’s some jazzy stuff and bluesy stuff we done on them where we just used to jam. On a lot of the jams, it was all guitar, and I forgot about half of that. I can’t play that now.”
item.description: The nine tracks capture Earth moving from blues and jazz toward the heavier sound that would soon make Iommi and his bandmates world famous.

item.title: Joe Satriani reveals how Frank Sinatra helped shape his favorite guitar solo: “That’s my model”
item.dc:content:
Joe Satriani recalled two twists of fate that turned the title track of his 1989 album Flying in a Blue Dream into one of his favorite pieces of all time. In a recent interview with Guitar.com he said he’d been working on another track, titled “Big Bad Moon,’ but realized it wasn’t working at that point. That’s when another thought occurred to him.

“I had a memory of when I was a kid, having these flying dreams as I was trying to go to sleep,” he said. “It just filled me with a kind of musical inspiration… I suddenly picked up this acoustic guitar and I heard these chords. I tuned the guitar to an open F for some reason — maybe because I kept thinking a low C was the note I was hearing in my head — and I started playing these chords that sounded right to me.”

Once he’d mapped out the piece, he told himself: “That’s really interesting. You’ve never done that before.” He added: “This was all happening minute by minute. I got so excited that I completely forgot about ‘Big Bad Moon’ and just focused on this. I had my Tascam four-track cassette recorder — a great, fun little deck — and I was busy recording bits of it as I was writing.”

He was still wondering about the music’s direction as he listened back.

“The funniest thing came to my mind: Frank Sinatra,” he said. “Very often, Frank would start a song and tell you a story in a colloquial, American spoken way of singing. By the end of his melody, not only would the register move up and up, but he’d finally say the word that is the chorus at the very end.

“I thought, ‘That’s my model. That’s what I have to do here, because I’m telling a story, but it’s about flying.’ As I get to the height of the story, I need to be high up in the sky flying around. I started to think, ‘Just pace it the way that Frank Sinatra would have paced it. Go slowly, go way behind the beat, just go late, late, late, and then move your way up.’”

When it came to recording the full track, fate intervened once again, this time in the form of a radio broadcast that introduces the music. Satriani said he’d been encountering constant interference issues at the Coast Recorders studio in San Francisco because the room wasn’t set up for high-gain guitars at high volume.

“We were sitting there laughing, like, ‘How are we going to record this part if it’s so noisy?’ Every time I turned the volume knob from two to three, I’d get a different radio station. At one point, we heard this kid’s voice coming through, talking about something… it sounded like an old 1950s Art Linkletter radio show or TV show from when we were kids.”

Producer John Cuniberti decided to try recording the voice onto the leader tape ahead of Blue Dream. Satch — who recently listed the “small realities” that every player needs to know — remembered:

“As soon as the kid says, ‘And sometimes afterwards they like each other, and sometimes they don’t,’ the leader ended, the magnetic tape hit the heads, and the guitar chords came pounding in. We were like, ‘Damn!’ The timing was just too good to be true for a song written about being a kid having flying dreams.”
item.description: Satriani says he drew on Sinatra’s way of building a melody to create the soaring title track to Flying in a Blue Dream — then a stray radio broadcast added another twist to the recording
