item.title: How Elliott Randall nailed Steely Dan’s “Reelin’ in the Years” solo without writing a note: “I never plan a solo in advance”
item.dc:content:
Elliott Randall’s electric-guitar solo on Steely Dan’s “Reelin’ in the Years” is one of those performances that sounds almost impossible to have happened spontaneously. But that’s essentially how it came together: Randall had no solo written, no elaborate rig and no particular plan beyond responding to the track in front of him.

The result became one of the most celebrated guitar solos in rock. Jimmy Page has reportedly called it his favorite solo of all time, while readers of our sister publication, Guitar World, selected it as the 40th greatest guitar solo ever in a poll several years ago.

Written by Donald Fagen and Walter Becker, “Reelin’ in the Years” appeared on Steely Dan’s 1972 debut album, Can’t Buy a Thrill. Fagen and Becker knew they had a great song, but they were struggling to find the right guitar solo to complete it. So they called on Randall, whom they knew from their days playing in the backing band for Jay and the Americans and who had also played on several of the duo’s pre–Steely Dan demos.

“They were having trouble finding the right ‘flavor’ solo for ‘Reelin,’ and asked me to give it a go,” Randall told Guitar World several years ago. Presumably, Dan’s guitarists Jeff “Skunk” Baxter, Denny Dias and Becker himself had given the solo a try without success.

“Most of the song was already complete,” Randall adds, “so I had the good fortune of having a very clear picture of what the solo was laying on top of. They played it for me without much dialog about what I should play.

“It just wasn’t necessary because we did it in one take and nothing was written.”

As Randall explained in a 2007 interview with Guitar Player, the performance heard on the record was, more precisely, his first recorded take. He had done an earlier run-through that several people in the studio felt was even better, but the tape machine hadn’t been armed.

“I never plan a solo in advance,” Randall said. “If I did, it wouldn’t be improvisation, which to me is one of the most exciting things about being a soloist. What you hear on the Steely Dan record is the first recorded take of my response to the track.”

The experience had a lasting effect on Steely Dan’s recording process. “From then on, Katz [Steely Dan’s producer] never let a run-through go by without ensuring that it was being recorded,” Randall recalled.

Randall’s approach was remarkably straightforward. He recorded the solo on his ’63 Fender Stratocaster, which featured a PAF humbucker in the neck position, plugged directly into an Ampeg SVT amp and miked with a single AKG 414.

“The SVT wouldn’t have been my first choice for an amp, or even my fifth choice,” Randall said. “But it was the only amp in the studio that night. My Strat has been my number one axe since 1965.”

Jeff “Skunk” Baxter played the harmony parts, while Randall handled the entire lead performance — intro, answers, main solo and ending — as one continuous take.

The whole solo just came to me, and I feel very fortunate to have been given the opportunity to play it.”

— Elliott Randall

“The whole solo just came to me, and I feel very fortunate to have been given the opportunity to play it,” Randall said.

That spontaneous quality is central to Randall’s view of studio playing. As a longtime producer and session musician, he says his job is to help make the best possible recording while responding to what the artist and producer want from him.

“My job as a studio musician is to facilitate the making of the best possible recording,” he said. “As I’ve also been a producer since the ’60s, I have specific ideas about how to do that, but if I’m not the producer of a session, it behooves me to make my clients happy.

“And if they are asking for ‘classic Randall,’ I have to determine what their concept of that is. Of course, I do love when someone wants me to be ‘collaboratively creative.’”

There is even more Randall on the four-channel quadraphonic mix of “Reelin’ in the Years,” which contains additional lead fills that aren’t heard in the more familiar two-channel stereo version.

Beyond his legendary work with Steely Dan, Randall has performed and recorded with artists ranging from the Doobie Brothers to Asia and James Galway. He has also worked as a producer, teacher, clinician and technological consultant to major musical-instrument manufacturers.

But for many guitarists, it’s those few minutes on “Reelin’ in the Years” — improvised in the studio and captured on tape before anyone had quite decided what the solo should be — that remain his signature.

item.title: Freddie Mercury sounded like “a strangled sheep” at Queen’s first show, says Roger Taylor
item.dc:content:
Queen’s first-ever live performance was organized by drummer Roger Taylor’s mother to raise money for charity. The young musician, however, felt the band still had a long way to go as they stepped offstage together for the first time. Surprisingly, he says Freddie Mercury was the weak link.

Winifred Taylor had arranged for the band to play a concert for the British Red Cross. It was a group that Mercury, then known as Freddie Bulsara, had assembled from the ashes of Smile. The show took place in Truro, Cornwall, in June 1970, and was originally intended to be a Smile performance. Queen would take the mantle instead. Bass player John Deacon wouldn’t join until the following year, so the bass spot was filled by Taylor’s friend Mike Grose. Brian May rounded out the trio with his homemade Red Special electric guitar.

May and Mercury, as history remembers, became a formidable songwriting partnership. There were occasional arguments over guitar solos, songs written in the bath, and songs that possess a strange kind of magic. Yet for Taylor, who has just released his latest solo album, Violence Insane In a Beautiful World, there were few signs of the majestic history that lay ahead of them that day.

“I think we were paid £50, which was an enormous amount in those days,” he tells the BBC. “We had just started Queen then, and Freddie hadn’t really developed his voice, his vocal capacities, to the full.

“He sounded quite alarming some of the time,” he recalls. “He sounded a little bit like a strangled sheep at times, with a very fast falsetto. But of course he kind of invented himself out of it all.”

We didn’t know what a gem we had at first.”

— Roger Taylor

Mercury’s strongest assets were slow to reveal themselves.

“We didn’t realize at the time what a great musician he was,” Taylor admits. “A great piano player. A fantastic songwriter. We didn’t know what a gem we had at first.”

That gem, of course, was still rough around the edges at that first show in Truro City Hall.

Another key aspect of the band’s trademark sound took shape in the local area. Roughly 10 miles northwest of Truro, the band found remarkable natural reverb in the caves at Chapel Porth beach, St. Agnes. There, they would refine their vocal harmonies.

“I think we must have been in caves because it sounds bigger,” Taylor says. “The sound rattles everywhere.”

Despite the bumpy first show, the band’s potential soon became much clearer, with their self-titled album arriving three years later. It peaked at number 24 in the U.K. charts, despite May’s dissatisfaction with its production.

Speaking to Guitar Player about the album’s troubled and involuntarily rushed recording in 2021, May said they didn’t have the chance to flex their muscles until its follow-up. The record was still an important first step, though — the moment when Queen began putting paint on the proverbial canvas.

Queen’s success wasn’t forged after one humble charity gig. Mercury would go on to blossom into one of rock’s most distinguished and cherished talents, though May says there was at least one occasion when he left the group speechless. Not all of Mercury’s ideas were solid gold.

It’s been 35 years since Mercury’s all-too-soon passing in 1991, at just 45. His legacy shows no signs of waning. Now, one of the band’s most infamous and controversial concerts is set for a 40th-anniversary theatrical release, bringing a monumental moment in rock history to the big screen in 4K.

“There will never be an event quite like that again,” May said of that show. The same could be said of Mercury — even if Taylor thought his first gig was less than perfect.

“He sounded quite alarming some of the time,” he recalls. “He sounded a little bit like a strangled sheep at times, with a very fast falsetto. But of course he kind of invented himself out of it all.”

We didn’t know what a gem we had at first.”

— Roger Taylor

Mercury’s strongest assets were slow to reveal themselves.

“We didn’t realize at the time what a great musician he was,” Taylor admits. “A great piano player. A fantastic songwriter. We didn’t know what a gem we had at first.”

That gem, of course, was still rough around the edges at that first show in Truro City Hall.

Another key aspect of the band’s trademark sound took shape in the local area. Roughly 10 miles northwest of Truro, the band found remarkable natural reverb in the caves at Chapel Porth beach, St. Agnes. There, they would refine their vocal harmonies.

“I think we must have been in caves because it sounds bigger,” Taylor says. “The sound rattles everywhere.”

Despite the bumpy first show, the band’s potential soon became much clearer, with their self-titled album arriving three years later. It peaked at number 24 in the U.K. charts, despite May’s dissatisfaction with its production.

Speaking to Guitar Player about the album’s troubled and involuntarily rushed recording in 2021, May said they didn’t have the chance to flex their muscles until its follow-up. The record was still an important first step, though — the moment when Queen began putting paint on the proverbial canvas.

Queen’s success wasn’t forged after one humble charity gig. Mercury would go on to blossom into one of rock’s most distinguished and cherished talents, though May says there was at least one occasion when he left the group speechless. Not all of Mercury’s ideas were solid gold.

It’s been 35 years since Mercury’s all-too-soon passing in 1991, at just 45. His legacy shows no signs of waning. Now, one of the band’s most infamous and controversial concerts is set for a 40th-anniversary theatrical release, bringing a monumental moment in rock history to the big screen in 4K.

“There will never be an event quite like that again,” May said of that show. The same could be said of Mercury — even if Taylor thought his first gig was less than perfect.

item.title: Dolly Parton’s longtime manager accuses her nephew of threats and extortion: “An obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign”
item.dc:content:
A fight over Dolly Parton’s entertainment empire has spilled into public view, with her longtime manager accusing her nephew and former security chief of intimidation, threats and an escalating effort to extract money from the late singer’s estate.

Danny Nozell, Parton’s longtime manager and head of She’s Alive, the corporation that oversees her businesses, has filed for a restraining order against Brian Seaver, Parton’s nephew, who was dismissed as head of security for Parton’s properties last week. Seaver was the person who publicly announced Parton’s death on August 25 in a video.

According to The New York Times, Nozell’s filing accuses Seaver of launching “an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” in an effort to obtain money from Parton’s estate.

The filing includes a series of text messages that appear to show Seaver making increasingly aggressive threats. In one message sent to at least one partner of Dollywood, someone identified as Seaver wrote that he would become “the hand of retribution for my entire family.”

In another message, dated September 3, Seaver referred to himself as a “killer” and claimed he had sold $27 million worth of arms and ammunition to Haitian police on the day the “9 to 5” singer/songwriter and guitar player died.

Other messages allegedly threatened to “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us.” The message also included a demand for payment.

Parton’s businesses include Dollywood, her SongTeller hotel and Life of Many Colors museum that is set to open this month.

Seaver and his security company had protected Parton and her properties for many years. But according to Nozell’s complaint, the operation was far from a conventional security detail. He describes it as “a heavily armed, paramilitary-style force” with access to military-grade weapons.

Nozell and other Parton business associates reportedly became increasingly alarmed as Seaver made demands in the period surrounding Parton’s death. Some have left, while others have hired their own security teams, according to the filing.

Seaver has defended his conduct and his work protecting Parton and her family in comments to TMZ.

“We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much,” he said.
item.description: A restraining-order request alleges Brian Seaver, who ran security for Parton’s properties, threatened to damage her business relationships and demanded money from her estate.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Scapelliti

item.title: Steve Howe reveals his hidden skill: “I’m the best in London”
item.dc:content:
Steve Howe is known for being one of rock’s great virtuosos on both electric and acoustic guitar, but he has another, much more unexpected skill — he plays the washboard.

It goes back to Howe’s childhood in London, when he was growing up during the skiffle boom of the late 1950s that influenced musicians ranging from the Beatles to Pink Floyd. The British skiffle craze drew heavily from American folk, blues and country music, and washboards were a common part of the sound.

Howe was also listening to plenty of American roots music at home. His parents’ record collection included artists such as Tennessee Ernie Ford and Chet Atkins, and Atkins in particular showed Howe how much rhythmic and percussive detail could be pulled from an acoustic instrument.

So while Howe would eventually become famous for his guitar playing, he also picked up a few other instruments along the way. The washboard was one of them — and it eventually landed him an unlikely studio gig with producer Trevor Horn.

Horn was working with former Sex Pistols Svengali Malcolm McLaren on the 1983 album Duck Rock when he needed someone who could play washboard. As Howe tells it, there weren’t exactly a lot of candidates.

One of my hidden skills is definitely the washboard. I think it’s terrific. I think it’s a brilliant instrument, totally underrated.“

— Steve Howe

"One of my hidden skills is definitely the washboard,“ he tells Guitar Player. “On my own albums I’ve done quite a lot of washboard. I think it’s terrific. I think it’s a brilliant instrument, totally underrated.

"I have a story; one day the phone rang and it was Trevor Horn, and he said to me, 'I’ve got something going on with a recording here. It’s Malcolm McLaren, and he wants a washboard. Don’t you play washboard?'

“I said, 'Yes, I’m the best in London,' and he says, 'Well, you’re the only one in London. I can’t find anybody who plays it. Come in.' So I went a few days later and played on some track Trevor was producing.

“I quite like that story."

It wasn’t just a one-off for Howe, either. He continued to use the washboard on his own recordings, including his 1993 solo album The Grand Scheme of Things.

These days, Howe is focused on getting back to full strength after undergoing surgery earlier this year. Yes is now scheduled to hit the road in early May next year, with plans to perform its 1971 album Fragile and more in the U.K. before heading to Japan. North American dates are also being planned, with details still to come.
item.description: The Yes guitarist has an unusual talent that dates back to the skiffle boom — and it once made him the only player Horn could find for a session with Malcolm McLaren.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Swann

item.title: Suzi Quatro on why she deserves a Rock Hall induction — and her worst onstage moments
item.dc:content:
Suzi Quatro believes she deserves a place in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame — and after more than half a century of breaking ground for women in rock, she has certainly paid her dues.

When the 22-year-old Quatro released her first single, “Rolling Stone,” in 1972, she was a rock and roll outlier. Propelled by Peter Frampton’s guitar playing, the song may only have been a commercial success in Portugal, but Quatro was doing something far more significant: beating down a door that had long been locked for women rockers.

The bass player and vocalist, full of rock’s trademark attitude, has been recognized as the world’s first “Rock Chick”, inspiring a generation of female-powered acts to follow in her wake. The Runaways and Heart are two vital examples, while Joan Jett has recalled being inspired by Quatro because “she had the guts to get on stage and play” at a time when women were grossly underrepresented in rock.

Nearly 55 years after “Rolling Stone” introduced her to the world, Quatro is still going strong, as defiantly punk and Detroiter as ever. She has enjoyed — and sometimes endured — a chaotic career, one she was happy to regale in a new interview with the Guardian.

And some of her stories demonstrate exactly the kind of professional resolve that has kept her onstage for more than half a century. For Quatro, the golden rule has always been simple: whatever happens, the show must go on.

“We were doing a show once, going down a storm, and I had a section with the drummer,” Quatro, a trained percussionist, remembers. “Then the P.A. blew, and all the audience could hear were drums. We looked at each other and went, ‘Right, let’s go!’

“So, we did a 15-minute drum solo together, because whatever happens onstage, the golden rule is you have to make it work. Everybody thought it was part of the show.”

She has had to improvise through considerably more embarrassing situations, too. Quatro says most of her fan interactions are great, but there are always exceptions.

“A couple of years ago I was coming out to do my final song, and everybody had their hands up for a high-five,” she recalls. “So did a little bit of that, and one girl grabbed my hand, held on to it with a death-grip, and tried to pull me off the stage. I tried to pull back, and my entire jumpsuit ripped, right across my ass.”

Eventually, she broke free and shuffled back toward her onstage monitor, where she — “very professionally!” — finished the song sitting down.

“As soon as the song was over, the monitor guy came and put a towel around my waist, and I walked off,” Quatro adds. “I wish I could find that girl because I would love to give her a piece of my mind. I was really upset.”

The incidents are funny in retrospect, but they also speak to the attitude that has defined Quatro’s career. She has spent decades proving that she belongs onstage, and she has no intention of stopping until she feels she can no longer deliver at her own standard.

Freedom is her latest studio album. It’s her 18th solo album overall, and her first since Face to Face, a collaborative record with KT Tunstall in 2023. As the title suggests, she isn’t ready to have her wings clipped yet.

“When I was 35, a journalist stupidly asked me, ‘When are you going to retire?’” she remembers. “I said, ‘I will retire when I go on stage, turn my back on the audience, shake my ass, and there’s silence.’”

The sentiment hasn’t truly changed some 40 years later, although Quatro has updated the punchline.

“When I got to 65, I said, ‘I will retire when I go onstage, turn my back on the audience, and my ass shakes by itself’,” she laughs. “I’m 76 now, but at 75 I gave my final quote on this subject, and it was serious — I will retire when I go on stage and do not deliver to my standard. When I feel that, I’m done.”

That distinguished, generation-inspiring career has led many fans to call for Quatro’s induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and Quatro herself says it would be a “no-brainer.” Yet she has never even received a nomination, while Oasis and Iron Maiden were among those getting the nod in the British-heavy class of 2026.

Debbie Harry and Chrissie Hynde are also notable members of Quatro’s fan club, having followed the path she blazed in the 1970s. With more than 55 million albums sold, the case for recognition is one Quatro clearly feels is worth making.

Still, after everything she has endured onstage and off, she isn’t letting the omission stop her.

“It used to bother me, but now I’ve read up on lots of people who aren’t in it, and I’m in good company,” she says. “I just hope they’re not waiting for me to die so they can do it posthumously.”
item.description: The self-proclaimed “rock chick” has spent more than five decades breaking ground for women in rock — and insisting the show must go on no matter what
item.dc:creator: Phil Weller

item.title: Johnny Marr says every guitarist needs these three guitars: “They do a thing no other guitar can do”
item.dc:content:
Johnny Marr has just made headlines after selling nearly 100 guitars from his collection for just shy of $5 million at auction. That’s a lot of cherished instruments to let go of, but it turns out he only feels he — and every player, in fact — needs three specific guitars.

During last week’s Christie’s auction, the former Smiths guitarist saw several of his historic instruments fetch six-figure sums. A whopping £3,649,280, or around $4.87 million, was spent during the auction, with the money going to selected charities.

During a recent interview with one-time Top Gear host Chris Evans for Virgin Radio, Johnny Marr made it clear why he was happy to slim down his collection. He was asked a hypothetical question: If he could only have three guitars in his life, what would he choose? He answered it with ease.

First up is a bona fide classic electric guitar.

“So, you get a Gibson ES-335, ideally from between 1961 and 1963,” he says. “The reason is that they’re versatile, and they have a really rich, dark sound, made famous by Eric Clapton in Cream.”

As he says, one of Clapton’s main Cream workhorses was a 1964 Gibson ES-335 in its usual and iconic Cherry Red finish. As Guitar World reports, conflicting stories exist about how he got the guitar, but the most likely scenario is that he acquired it in 1968, which is why it became such an important instrument for Cream during the London dates of Cream’s farewell tour just weeks later.

It stayed in his collection until 2004, when it was auctioned off for his Crossroads charity. It sold for $847,500. That lineage, in turn, inspired Marr to get his own mid-’60s Cherry Red 335, with a ’63 model heard across his latest solo album, The Age of Everything.

“They just do a thing that other guitars can’t do,” he says.

Next up, Marr picks a guitar even closer to home.

The way my signature Jag sounds, you don’t have to get a Rickenbacker, a Gretsch, a Jazzmaster or a Strat.”

Johnny Marr

“The other guitar, in all honesty, you get my signature Jag,” he explains. “The reason is because of the way my signature Jag sounds; you don’t have to get a Rickenbacker, and you don’t have to get a Gretsch, a Jazzmaster or a Strat, because, inadvertently, I ended up designing a guitar that does all the things [those three guitars do].”

Marr’s signature Fender Jaguar first arrived in 2012, with key features including a four-position Tele-style pickup selector that replaced the Jag’s high-pass filter and individual pickup on/off switches, allowing players to flit between the bridge position, both pickups in parallel or both in series.

Its bridge saddle is also inspired by Fender Mustang guitars, which have better tuning stability when abusing the whammy bar. It became one of Fender’s best-selling signature guitars.

An updated version arrived last year, and Marr reinvented the Jag all over again. New lipstick pickups and a whole new pickup system were noteworthy changes.

“I would have said you need a Rickenbacker for that jangle, and you need a Strat for that slinky sort of thing, and maybe a Gretsch for that ringing thing,” Marr extends. “Well, because all of those are encompassing sort of my sound, I realized after I designed my Jag, it did all three.”

Last but not least, he unplugs to complete the trio.

“Then I’d get a Martin acoustic guitar, a D-28, because if you’ve got to be able to play the acoustic,” he quips. “It’s a little bit of a clumsy comparison, but if you can’t, it’s like learning to drive an automatic car, then getting into a manual.

“Being able to play acoustic makes you infinitely better on the electric, and vice versa,” he reasons.

For Marr — a player with a hatred for satin necks and Yngwie Malmsteen — those guitars are the holy trinity. Other players may disagree, but it’s a versatile trio whichever way you look at it.

Elsewhere, he’s talked about his strange method to avoid impulse buying guitars, explained how Paul McCartney came to his aid when the Smiths broke up, and what made his songwriting tandem with Morrissey magic.
item.description: The former Smiths man has just sold nearly 100 of his most prized instruments. He says this trio is all he needs
item.dc:creator: Phil Weller

item.title: How Alice Cooper spun a 1960s ballad into his own glam-rock anthem
item.dc:content:
In 1973, Alice Cooper was no longer just a rock star; he was the ringmaster of a high-decibel circus that thrived on shock and spectacle. But as he and his band prepared to record the masterpiece that would become Billion Dollar Babies, they lacked the perfect “curtain raiser” — a song that could encapsulate the thrill of a performance in a sold-out arena.

The solution arrived from the most unlikely of places: a folk-pop tune originally made famous by Judy Collins. What followed was a radical sonic transformation of the song, turning it into a menacing but triumphant call to arms that united fans for Alice’s grand entrance.

Billion Dollar Babies marked the start of a new era in Cooper‘s career, and he was adapting his persona to fit. The success of his 1972 hit “School’s Out” brought Cooper fame among teens and infamy among their outraged parents who feared the song would encourage rebellion and school absenteeism.

In response, he began his metamorphosis from underground shock rocker to headline-grabbing provocateur. His Billion Dollar Babies song “Elected” was part of the new image, a satire that cast Alice as a presidential candidate for the rock and roll generation.

Bob Ezrin, Cooper’s producer, had the talents for helping Alice through this evolution. His keen sense for novelty, combined with his theatrical approach to music, elevated his productions, whether by having kids sing along on the chorus of “School’s Out” or by adding a brass section on "Elected."

For Cooper’s new emergence on the world stage, Ezrin discovered a song he thought made the perfect opening track: “Hello, Hooray.”

Written by Canadian singer-songwriter Rolf Kempf, the tune had been famously covered by Collins on her 1968 album, Who Knows Where the Time Goes. At its core, the lyrics are about a performer preparing to step into the spotlight, a theme that seemed well suited to Cooper’s new persona.

But the singer needed convincing.

“I heard it and I said, ‘Bob, this is a folk song,’” he recalled on The Alice Cooper Show Radio Special. “He said, ‘No, listen to the lyrics. It’s about a guy who is about to go onstage. And he’s terrified — but he’s ready.’

“It was the perfect opening for Billion Dollar Babies.”

“I said, ‘Bob, this is a folk song.’ He said, ‘No, listen to the lyrics. It’s about a guy who is about to go onstage. And he’s terrified — but he’s ready.’”

— Alice Cooper

Together with Ezrin, Cooper reconstructed Kempf’s folk-pop tune into a bombastic declaration of Cooper’s newfound power. In addition to giving the tune new lyrics that addressed the audience, they pumped it up with an orchestral arrangement and a fusillade of cannon blasts that echo over the song’s extended outro.

But the song wouldn’t be complete without some heavy guitar licks. For that, Ezrin enlisted studio guitarist Steve Hunter, and suggested he apply some harmonized slide guitar work to the intro and solo.

Hunter’s big career moments were still largely ahead of him — handling electric guitar on Aerosmith’s “Train Kept A’ Rollin’,” tackling a tricky acoustic part on Peter Gabriel’s “Solsbury Hill” and helping Lou Reed capture his first Gold record with Rock ’N’ Roll Animal — but he had great instincts for what a song needed.

Even so, he was initially skeptical of Ezrin’s approach.

“It had a great arrangement, and it had terrific parts played very well by the Alice Cooper boys,” he tells Guitar Player. “But I was taken aback when producer Bob Ezrin suggested a slide part for the song’s solo section. I had tried my hand at slide playing a few times, and I quickly discovered it was much harder than it appeared. I decided to leave the slide stuff to Johnny Winter or George Harrison.

“Luckily for me, however, I had spent five years of my youth learning how to play lap-steel — thanks to my father — and I experimented with making my lap-steel technique sound like slide guitar.”

For the session, however, Hunter showed up toting not a lap steel but a beat-up, mid-to-late-1950s Gibson electric six-string pedal steel. It was a basic model with just four pedals, but one of those was badly damaged, leaving just three pedals to work with.

“Whatever Bob had in mind when he envisioned a ‘slide part,’ it was a pedal-steel performance.”

— Steve Hunter

“I tuned the guitar to an open E, the first pedal to an open A, and the third pedal to an A minor chord, so I would have at least one minor,” he says. “Plus, I could use the relative major/minor chord relationship to get another minor. That was just about the extent of my music theory in those days.”

“With all of its problems, when you plugged the pedal steel into a Marshall half-stack, it sounded amazing,” Hunter continues, “likely due to the fact that its pickup was probably a PAF. Whatever Bob had in mind when he envisioned a ‘slide part,’ it was a pedal-steel performance.”

Although Hunter usually approached soloing through improvisation, he and Ezrin agreed a constructed solo was what the song required.

“I worked out the solo,” he says, “then doubled the first half and played harmony to the second half. Over the chords immediately following the solo, I pushed a couple of the Gibson’s ‘chord pedals’ — which is what I called them — to follow the progression.

“The tone was pretty organic. No effect pedals. We did use outboard studio gear, such as compressors and EQ, but my guitar tones were primarily from the volume and tone controls on the amp, and the volume and tone controls on the guitar. I still love the tone of that old pedal steel on ‘Hello Hooray.’”

Unfortunately, he no longer owns the Gibson pedal steel.

“It died a sad death,” he says. “If I had known then what I know now, I would have at least kept that PAF pickup.”

As for Ezrin, his instincts were spot on. “Hello Hooray” (minus the original‘s comma) became a hit for Cooper — it reached number 35 on the Billboard Hot 100 — and made for a grand spectacle as the opening tune on the Billion Dollar Babies tour.

“That song was the quintessential Alice opening,” Cooper says. “It was the call to arms. It told the audience, ‘The show is starting, and you’re part of it now.’”

item.title: Metallica’s James Hetfield on Tony Iommi and the Black Sabbath riff that shaped his playing: “He is the riff lord”
item.dc:content:
James Hetfield has named Tony Iommi as the single biggest influence on his rhythm guitar playing and songwriting — and pointed specifically to Black Sabbath’s “Children of the Grave” as a masterclass in riff construction.

“Tony Iommi is the riff lord, in my mind, and he is the one that has inspired me the most out of any guitar player for my rhythm guitar playing and songwriting,” Hetfield says in the latest episode of James Hetfield’s Riff Life on SiriusXM’s Maximum Metallica.

Discussing “Children of the Grave,” Hetfield breaks down what makes Iommi’s playing so effective, from the song’s central electric guitar riff to the way the guitarist uses chords, percussion and effects to expand its sound.

“Obviously, Tony is the riff lord and everyone starts the song together on the one riff,” he says. “Tony plays off that riff, goes in to hit the big giant chords, which opens the song up. I really love the drum overdub that they did to help with that percussion of the riff and the real cool ghostly guitar sounds at the very, very end.”

Hetfield’s admiration for Iommi is hardly surprising. Metallica took up the mantle of heavy metal’s original architects when they emerged in the 1980s, with Black Sabbath’s influence running throughout the band’s music. Iommi acknowledged that lineage in 2024, saying it was “brilliant to hear about other musicians liking what I’d done, taking the same kind of idea and improving on it, evolving it into their own sound.”

Metallica made that connection especially clear at Black Sabbath’s star-studded “Back to the Beginning” farewell show last year, performing “Johnny Blade” from Sabbath’s 1978 album Never Say Die! — a deeper cut rather than one of the band’s most obvious classics.

Metallica guitarist Kirk Hammett has been equally emphatic about what Black Sabbath’s four original members mean to heavy music. Reflecting on the band’s influence ahead of the farewell show, he said:

“If it wasn’t for those four guys, man, we might still be just kind of like wandering around in the dark. But the fact that they created a genre — not only created it, but then developed it and then turned it into like a few different things over the course of their career — is completely awe inspiring to me and my peers musically.”

item.title: How the search for Mick Ronson’s Ziggy Stardust Les Paul ended in $200,000 and heartache
item.dc:content:
For years after Mick Ronson’s death, the where-abouts of his stripped 1968 Gibson Les Paul Custom – the Ziggy Stardust guitar – were a mystery even to those who had been closest to him.

When Rick Tedesco asked Ronson’s friend and fellow performer Ian Hunter about it, the former Mott the Hoople frontman shrugged.

“God only knows where that went,” he replied. “Mick probably gave it to some guy walking across the street. He didn’t care about gear. It was just a tool to him.”

Mick probably gave it to some guy walking across the street. He didn’t care about gear. It was just a tool to him

Ian Hunter

For Tedesco, finding the guitar became a mission.

A guitarist, producer and engineer whose credits include work with Hunter, Alice Cooper and former Cooper band members Dennis Dunaway and Neal Smith, Tedesco had become a Bowie fanatic through the artist’s 1974 album, Diamond Dogs.

“I was a 13-year-old kid who was just obsessed with horror movies,” he recalls. “And then I saw that album cover. I just absolutely loved that album. I was like, ‘I’m done. That’s what I want to do.’”

Working his way backward through Bowie’s catalog, he soon discovered Ronson’s signature performances on the albums Hunky Dory, Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane and Pin Ups.

Eventually he caught D.A. Pennebaker’s 1973 Ziggy Stardust concert film on television. “There was Mick,” he recalls. “And that’s what I wanted to be – David Bowie’s guitarist.”

Tedesco was particularly drawn to Ronson’s Les Paul Custom. Originally a Black Beauty, the guitar was stripped in 1970 after Ronson heard that removing the finish could improve resonance and high-frequency tone.

He subsequently used it on his first record with Bowie, The Man Who Sold the World, right through Hunky Dory, Ziggy Stardust, Aladdin Sane and Pin Ups, making it the vehicle for each album’s searing power chords, singing leads and lyrical solos.

For Tedesco, a hardcore Bowie and Ronson fan, the guitar was an indelible part of his own identity as a guitarist.

By the 1990s, he was working at a music store in Danbury, Connecticut, when one day Hunter strolled in.

“Ian happened to live about 45 minutes away at the time,” he says. “I was like, Holy shit, it’s Ian Hunter! I even had posters of him and Mick on my wall.”

I was like, Holy shit, it’s Ian Hunter! I even had posters of him and Mick on my wall

Rick Tedesco

Hunter made repeat visits, and a friendship developed after Tedesco helped him refurbish his studio with an ADAT system.

“Mick had passed, and Ian didn’t really know what the hell to do,” Tedesco says. “He didn’t have his right-hand man anymore. So he started asking me, ‘Do you want to put some stuff down on this song?’”

Before he knew it, Tedesco was working with Hunter, who also introduced him to some members of Alice Cooper’s camp.

Hunter still had several of Ronson’s guitars, which he was holding onto for Suzi, Mick’s wife, but the stripped Les Paul Custom wasn’t among them.

“Nobody knew where it was,” Tedesco says. “I did some research and talked to one guy who thought he remembered an interview where Mick said he’d given it to the Hard Rock Cafe.”

Tedesco began calling Hard Rock locations, asking if they had the guitar, but a sweep of the company’s database came up empty.

“They had nothing of his at all,” he says.

I asked a guy there if they had Mick’s guitar, and he said, ‘Yeah, I’m standing right next to it’

Rick Tedesco

Afterward, Tedesco’s source confirmed that the guitar had gone to the Hard Rock, adding that the restaurant was located in Australia. Because that facility is licensed from, but not owned by, the Hard Rock, its holdings weren’t listed in the company’s records.

Tedesco felt a glimmer of hope.

One call to the restaurant was all it took. “I asked a guy there if they had Mick’s guitar, and he said, ‘Yeah, I’m standing right next to it,’” Tedesco says. “They had it hanging on the wall. I went through the roof.”

As it happened, the Hard Rock was open to a trade if Tedesco could give them a guitar to replace it.

“A lot of people like myself are huge fans of Mick’s, but he wasn’t a giant marquee name, so they didn’t really care about the guitar,” he explains.

He offered them a small collection that included some guitars signed by Hunter as well as some bearing Gene Simmons’ signature, and the deal was done.

It wasn’t without complications, though. In his excitement, Tedesco accidentally addressed his package to Newcastle, rather than Castle Hill, Australia. His guitars spent six weeks lost in a UPS lockup until the error was discovered.

Soon after, Ronson’s electric guitar showed up at his house.

There was no case. The guitar came all the way from Australia covered in bubble wrap

Rick Tedesco

“I had been out running some errands and got home to find this box leaning against my garage door,” Tedesco recalls. “I was so excited. And then I opened it up and saw a headstock. There was no case. The guitar came all the way from Australia covered in bubble wrap.”

To his relief, it made the trip unscathed, and with a bit of cleaning of its electronics, it was back in action.

For Tedesco, who’d purchased his childhood home after his parents retired, the coolest part of the experience was playing Ronson’s Les Paul in the very room where he’d first discovered the guitarist in the Ziggy Stardust film.

“It was such a weird cosmic circle,” he says.

Over the years, he put the guitar to good use. In addition to the Les Paul Custom, he’s owned Ronson’s Marshall Major tube amp head, among other gear, and two-inch tapes from the guitarist’s studio.

He made a video of his collection, allowing fans to see and hear these instruments for the first time in years.

He also loaned the guitar to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and shared it with fans who stopped by the Guitar Hangar, the musical instrument shop he opened in 1999.

Eventually, he offered a limited-edition Mick Ronson Tribute Guitar based on the Les Paul Custom. “I did all this with no intention of doing anything but sharing what I had with the Mick-loving world,” he says.

But eventually, Tedesco began receiving offers to buy the guitar. In 2014, he rejected one for $50,000 from producer Bob Rock, funneled to him by Suzi Ronson.

Soon after, a fan from England – Simon Dolan, the multimillionaire entrepreneur and race car driver – asked about buying both the guitar and Ronson’s Marshall Major head.

“‘It would have to be for stupid money, and I’m not looking to sell,’” Tedesco recalls telling him. “I said it would take at least 200 thousand, just for the guitar alone. And he goes, ‘Done!’

"And I thought, Oh god. Did I just sell my Mick Ronson guitar?”

I said it would take at least 200 thousand, just for the guitar alone. And he goes, ‘Done!’

Rick Tedesco

Two days later, the wire transfer came through his bank.

“I cried,” Tedesco says. “I’d never been so sad and sick over selling something.

“I called Ian up, crying, and he started laughing at me,” he says, cracking up at the memory. “He said, ‘You silly bastard! Mick would tell you you’re a fucking wanker. That’s why you buy something like that. It’s an investment. And it paid off!’

“But I felt like I had sold my soul. It took me several months to get over that.”

In the end, the money went to good use. At the time, Tedesco was getting ready for the grand opening of a new and larger Guitar Hangar in Brookfield, Connecticut, the store’s current location.

Owning that guitar was never ever about money

Rick Tedesco

“It allowed me to open in style, with tons of gear and without going into massive debt,” he says.

“But owning that guitar was never ever about money. I knew it was worth a lot, but I never envisioned parting with it. It was where I was forged. It put all of my parts together and made me go, Ah, there’s a place for me on planet Earth!

“And then it was gone.”

This story originally ran in the June 2022 issue of Guitar Player.

To his relief, it made the trip unscathed, and with a bit of cleaning of its electronics, it was back in action.

For Tedesco, who’d purchased his childhood home after his parents retired, the coolest part of the experience was playing Ronson’s Les Paul in the very room where he’d first discovered the guitarist in the Ziggy Stardust film.

“It was such a weird cosmic circle,” he says.

Over the years, he put the guitar to good use. In addition to the Les Paul Custom, he’s owned Ronson’s Marshall Major tube amp head, among other gear, and two-inch tapes from the guitarist’s studio.

He made a video of his collection, allowing fans to see and hear these instruments for the first time in years.

He also loaned the guitar to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and shared it with fans who stopped by the Guitar Hangar, the musical instrument shop he opened in 1999.

Eventually, he offered a limited-edition Mick Ronson Tribute Guitar based on the Les Paul Custom. “I did all this with no intention of doing anything but sharing what I had with the Mick-loving world,” he says.

But eventually, Tedesco began receiving offers to buy the guitar. In 2014, he rejected one for $50,000 from producer Bob Rock, funneled to him by Suzi Ronson.

Soon after, a fan from England – Simon Dolan, the multimillionaire entrepreneur and race car driver – asked about buying both the guitar and Ronson’s Marshall Major head.

“‘It would have to be for stupid money, and I’m not looking to sell,’” Tedesco recalls telling him. “I said it would take at least 200 thousand, just for the guitar alone. And he goes, ‘Done!’

"And I thought, Oh god. Did I just sell my Mick Ronson guitar?”

I said it would take at least 200 thousand, just for the guitar alone. And he goes, ‘Done!’

Rick Tedesco

Two days later, the wire transfer came through his bank.

“I cried,” Tedesco says. “I’d never been so sad and sick over selling something.

“I called Ian up, crying, and he started laughing at me,” he says, cracking up at the memory. “He said, ‘You silly bastard! Mick would tell you you’re a fucking wanker. That’s why you buy something like that. It’s an investment. And it paid off!’

“But I felt like I had sold my soul. It took me several months to get over that.”

In the end, the money went to good use. At the time, Tedesco was getting ready for the grand opening of a new and larger Guitar Hangar in Brookfield, Connecticut, the store’s current location.

Owning that guitar was never ever about money

Rick Tedesco

“It allowed me to open in style, with tons of gear and without going into massive debt,” he says.

“But owning that guitar was never ever about money. I knew it was worth a lot, but I never envisioned parting with it. It was where I was forged. It put all of my parts together and made me go, Ah, there’s a place for me on planet Earth!

“And then it was gone.”

Order Lisa S. Johnson's 108 Rock Star Guitars here and Immortal Axes: Guitars That Rock here.

This story originally ran in the June 2022 issue of Guitar Player.

item.title: Albert Lee on Ritchie Blackmore, Eddie Van Halen and his five years with Eric Clapton
item.dc:content:
“I've always played what I wanted to play and fortunately for me, I've always played with artists whose music I liked, so I really fitted in at the time,” Albert Lee tells Guitar Player. The country guitar legend has performed and recorded with artists such as Jerry Lee Lewis, Eric Clapton and Bill Wyman, to name but a few. He even participated in the supergroup Biff Baby’s All-Stars, featuring Eddie Van Halen, Steve Lukather and Steve Morse.

But one legendary act he played with remains a career highlight: the Everly Brothers.

“I did a long stint with them,” explains Lee. “During the ’70s they'd broken up and weren’t speaking to each other, so I got to know Don really well. He was playing at a local bar once a week with some old friends, and that turned into a regular thing and it was great fun.

“By that time, I was doing the occasional session in Los Angeles too, and because I didn't have an acoustic guitar with me, I used to borrow one or two of his guitars to take to the sessions. He was fine with it and would say, ‘Take this one, it's amazing.’ He then gave me one of his own Gibson J-200s and it's one of my treasured possessions now.”

Guitar Player asked Lee to look back on five of his memorable moments playing with rock’s finest artists.

Eric Clapton

“I was working on a session for a week with an artist called Marc Benno and at the end of the week, Eric's manager said that Eric had just done a tour without a second guitarist and so, how did I fancy going out with him? I thought, ‘Well, that's great, yes.’

“At the time I was just about to get my first real album released, so I don't know if I did a good thing or a bad thing, but I dropped the promotion of my new record and went out with Eric and it was great fun because we were all friends from the ’60s. I think he liked having me around and it worked really well because our styles are so different. I've heard most of the guys who played with him tried to sound like him, but I didn’t, I just did what I do. And likewise, he did the same thing, too.

“I was with him for five years, and during that period he fired his whole band twice, but I managed to survive. He was very happy for me to do a song or two during the show, he’d say, ‘Go on, Albert,’ and he’d go and sit behind the amp and have his brandy and lemonade and a cigarette. He was really enthused to have me around at that time. Then after five years he decided that I wasn't wanted anymore. I have to say that we're still good friends and since then, I've done most of the Crossroads concerts.”

Ritchie Blackmore

“I did an album with Jon Lord called Gemini Suite [in 1971] and Ritchie, because of his moods, decided he didn't want to do it, so Jon thought, Well, I'll get somebody else to do it. And it was good fun. Ritchie and I knew each other as he used to be with the Outlaws, an English country band that wore Western shirts and played instrumentals and also backed [English rock and roll singer] Mike Berry for a while in the ’60s.

“Ritchie and I played in this studio band called Green Bullfrog with producer Derek Lawrence who was friends with all the guys in that band. Derek had a lot of free studio time and told me, ‘Come tomorrow and we'll put down some tracks, with any songs you want to do,’ and that's how that all came about. He did have some kind of record deal, but rather than having to deal with the contracts for all those different record companies, he decided to give us nicknames. You can tell who's who, though.

“Ritchie did a few sessions with different people in the early years and he did a lot of sessions with [English record producer] Joe Meek, who was getting some very commercial sounds that people weren't getting at that time. Ritchie has always been really friendly with me and has always said nice things about me in articles.”

Jerry Lee Lewis

“I've always been a big fan of Jerry Lee Lewis. There was a period in the early ’70s when American record companies were getting records done in London with well-known British names, so we did a record [The Session, 1973] for Mercury Records and there were lots of artists on it. It was a lot of fun. Jerry always lived up to his reputation as ‘the Killer’ back then. He liked what I was doing and compared with some of the guitar players who were on it, I guess my sound was more to his liking, because of his country background.

“There was this one time at Wembley Arena in London and I was playing with Duane Eddy and I just happened to be walking down the hallway when Jerry's roadies called out to me: ‘Come down and say hello to Jerry.’ I was a bit nervous but I went in and said hello. His manager then pulled me aside and said, ‘Jerry’s guitar players have been drinking all day. Do you want to get up and play with Jerry?’ Of course, I said yes. Little Richard was on the show as well and he'd already done his set. They had agreed that Jerry would close the show so I was up there playing with Jerry and it was discussed that for the encore Little Richard would come on, and it all got pretty wild.”

The Crickets

“I'd always been a huge Buddy Holly fan. I was at a record launch party for my band Heads Hands & Feet and Ric Grech was there and we got to talking over a drink. I had missed Buddy when he and the Crickets came over to England for the first time. Ric said that the Crickets were coming over that weekend and that I better come along. Glen Hardin, the piano player, wasn't going to be able to make it in time because he was finishing up a tour with Elvis Presley, so they asked me to fill in.

“We had a little rehearsal a few days later and it was a lot of fun. We did the first gig at the Speakeasy in London, the late-night drinking establishment. It went really well, and at the end of the night Jerry Allison said, ‘Do you want to do the whole tour?’ So, I did.

“They shared lots of stories with me about touring America back then. It was quite difficult, driving overnight and hardly getting any sleep. Some of them were bus tours and other times they were in a van or a big car with a lot of instruments. And the buses weren’t like nowadays, with bunks and whatever; these were old-school buses, so you’d travel overnight sitting up.

“Then that February day, the heating had broken down on the bus and it was miserable. Buddy decided he couldn’t face it one more night, so he decided to rent a plane, a four-seater for him and his band. But Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper were really putting pressure on the guys, saying, ‘Oh God, I'd really like to get off that bus for a day,’ and we all know the rest of what happened. The weather was bad and the pilot was only about 21 and not really familiar with using flight instruments for night flying.”

Eddie Van Halen

“[The supergroup] Biff Baby’s All-Stars was actually started by Sterling Ball, Ernie Ball’s son. When I was with Heads Hands & Feet, Ernie and his son came along to our gig because they'd heard ‘Country Boy’ on the radio and they wanted to see this English band playing country music.

“I got really friendly with the family and I started to play local gigs with Sterling, who then put a band together and it developed from there. We did a lot of gigs.

“There was this one gig we did on a weekend during the NAMM show. By that time the Balls had gotten really friendly with Eddie Van Halen, Steve Lukather and Steve Morse, and we all played this show together. Eddie didn't want to play ‘Country Boy.’ He told me, ‘No, I don’t want to play on that’ because his style was so different from country, but I said, ‘You just do what you do with the tapping bit,’ and he did and he loved it.”

item.title: Mark Knopfler on his difficult collaboration with his childhood hero, Bob Dylan
item.dc:content:
The saying “Don’t meet your heroes” is one worth heeding, particularly if you’re in the creative arts. The pure feelings we harbor for artists when they’re afar often become tarnished by exposure to the all-too human qualities they exhibit in person, often to extremes.

Producer Rick Rubin writes in his book The Creative Act: A Way of Being, “Many great artists first develop sensitive antennae not to create art but to protect themselves. They have to protect themselves because everything hurts more. They feel everything more deeply.”

Mark Knopfler found out as much when he had a chance to produce his boyhood idol Bob Dylan in 1983. The album he was selected for was Infidels, a record that found Dylan returning to secular music following three albums of songs inspired by his experience as a born-again Christian.

Knopfler had helped out on one of those releases, playing guitar on 1979’s Slow Train Coming, the first disc in Dylan’s “Christian trilogy.” The album arrived shortly after Knopfler’s own ascendency to guitar hero status courtesy of Dire Straits’ 1978 self-titled debut and its hit song, “Sultans of Swing.”

“I was hugely influenced by him about the age of 14 or 15,” Knopfler told Dan Forte in an interview published in Guitar Player’s September 1984 issue. “I heard Bob Dylan from the very beginning, the ‘Hard Rain’ days, and went with him all the way up, and I'm still with him. I still think he's great. Blood on the Tracks is one of my favorite records.”

It’s a remarkable sentiment given that Dylan had put the guitarist through the ringer just one year before, while making Infidels. The former folk icon selected Knopfler to produce him after considering and rejecting David Bowie, Elvis Costello and Frank Zappa. Dylan felt inexperienced in the modern recording studio environment and needed someone who was up to speed with technology. His trio of rather bizarre choices suggests he was also looking to make a sea change in his musical approach and sound.

As it turns out, the songwriter had pretty much sewn things up on his own before Knopfler arrived and recording began at the Power Station in New York City, in April 1983. It was the first inkling Knopfler had that he would not be driving the sessions as much as navigating them, guiding the players through Dylan's temperamental fluctuations.

Dylan's choices for band members dictated Infidel’s strong rhythmic vibe and highly polished style. For the rhythm section he hired bass guitarist Robbie Shakespeare and drummer Sly Dunbar, a tandem better known as Sly & Robbie who found fame both as producers and as Island Records recording artists, where they also produced acts like Black Uhuru, Wailing Souls and Grace Jones.

Dylan had likewise selected former Rolling Stones lead guitarist Mick Taylor, possibly before choosing Sly & Robbie. The two had met the previous summer, and Dylan had begun showing him his new songs months before recording began.

Knopfler, for his part, brought in keyboardist Alan Clark and engineer Neil Dorfsman, who had worked on Dire Straits’ 1982 album, Love Over Gold, and Knopfler’s soundtrack for the movie Local Hero. As one of the album’s musicians, as well as its producer, Knopfler was paired with Taylor, who played slide guitar for much of the record.

The result was the sound of two virtuosos lending their fluid electric guitar chops to what many consider to be one of Dylan’s best albums from his later catalog. Combined with the strongly syncopated rhythms of Sly & Robbie, they helped Infidels achieve a remarkable, and successful, shift in style for Dylan, as exemplified by standout tracks like “License to Kill,” “Neighborhood Bully,” “Sweetheart Like You” and the stunning lead track, “Jokerman.”

“I suggested Billy Gibbons, but I don't think Bob had heard of ZZ Top,” Knopfler told Guitar Player. “It would have been great to have done that with Billy.”

As Knopfler would soon find out, working with his hero was anything but smooth. Dorfsman’s recollections of the sessions are vivid and excruciating.

“I don’t want to use the wrong word, here, but Bob was also a little bit of an agent provocateur, or he even had a little saboteur in him,” Dorfsman told Uncut. “If things were going maybe too well, in somebody else’s definition, he would consciously make an effort to make that stop.”

On one session, Dylan took the tinfoil wrapper from the sandwich he’d had for lunch and began flexing it, accordion style, into the microphone. ”It was just his way of saying, ‘I’m bored with this, I don’t want to do this particular song anymore,’” the engineer recalled.

I don’t want to use the wrong word, here, but Bob was also a little bit of an agent provocateur, or he even had a little saboteur in him."

— Neil Dorfsman

Dylan also announced one night that he wanted to start recording a Christmas album immediately. “We all laughed, thinking, He’s just messing with us,” Dorfsman said. “But, of course, years later, he subsequently came out with a Christmas record. It was kind of intimidating, challenging, but also hilarious in its own crazy way.”

Tasked with keeping the sessions running smoothly, Knopfler found himself frustrated at how differently it was going from what he had initially imagined.

“I know that it really, really bothered Mark, that song choices were dictated a little bit, and were turning out to be different from the song choices he thought we were going in to do,” Dorfsman said. “I could feel the air just sort of going out of Mark a little bit, when he realized that the traditional role of the producer was not going to be in play on this record... I’m sure it was very frustrating to Mark.”

Knopfler admitted as much — albeit with admirable diplomacy — when speaking with Forte for Guitar Player.

“Was it difficult producing Dylan?”

“Yeah. You see people working in different ways, and it's good for you. You have to learn to adapt to the way different people work.

“Yes, it was strange at times with Bob. One of the great parts about production is that it demonstrates to you that you have to be flexible. Each song has its own secret that's different from another song, and each has its own life. Sometimes it has to be teased out, whereas other times it might come fast. There are no laws about songwriting or producing. It depends on what you're doing, not just who you're doing. You have to be sensitive and flexible, and it's fun.

“I’d say I was more disciplined. But I think Bob is much more disciplined as a writer of lyrics, as a poet. He's an absolute genius. As a singer — absolute genius. But musically, I think it’s a lot more basic. The music just tends to be a vehicle for that poetry.”

I’d say I was more disciplined. But I think Bob is much more disciplined as a writer of lyrics, as a poet.”

— Mark Knopfler

Regardless of the trials he endured, Knopfler maintained his love for Dylan’s work on the album, particularly the song “I and I.” He was particularly moved by the song’s first lines: “Been so long since a strange woman has slept in my bed / Look how sweet she sleeps, how free must be her dreams / In another lifetime she must have owned the world or been faithfully wed / To some righteous king who wrote psalms beside moonlit streams.”

“To hear the first lines of ‘I And I,’ that's enough to make anybody who writes songs want to retire,” Knopfler told GP. “It's stunning.

“Bob's musical ability is limited, in terms of being able to play a guitar or a piano,” he explained. “It's rudimentary, but it doesn't affect his variety, his sense of melody, his singing. It's all there. In fact, some of the things he plays on piano while he's singing are lovely, even though they're rudimentary. That all demonstrates the fact that you don't have to be a great technician.

“It's the same old story: If something is played with soul, that's what's important. My favorite records, by and large, aren't wonderful technical achievements, with the exception perhaps of people like Chet Atkins. But generally speaking, all you've got to do is listen to a Howlin' Wolf album. That's just soul.”

On one session, Dylan took the tinfoil wrapper from the sandwich he’d had for lunch and began flexing it, accordion style, into the microphone. ”It was just his way of saying, ‘I’m bored with this, I don’t want to do this particular song anymore,’” the engineer recalled.

I don’t want to use the wrong word, here, but Bob was also a little bit of an agent provocateur, or he even had a little saboteur in him."

— Neil Dorfsman

Dylan also announced one night that he wanted to start recording a Christmas album immediately. “We all laughed, thinking, He’s just messing with us,” Dorfsman said. “But, of course, years later, he subsequently came out with a Christmas record. It was kind of intimidating, challenging, but also hilarious in its own crazy way.”

Tasked with keeping the sessions running smoothly, Knopfler found himself frustrated at how differently it was going from what he had initially imagined.

“I know that it really, really bothered Mark, that song choices were dictated a little bit, and were turning out to be different from the song choices he thought we were going in to do,” Dorfsman said. “I could feel the air just sort of going out of Mark a little bit, when he realized that the traditional role of the producer was not going to be in play on this record... I’m sure it was very frustrating to Mark.”

Knopfler admitted as much — albeit with admirable diplomacy — when speaking with Forte for Guitar Player.

“Was it difficult producing Dylan?”

“Yeah. You see people working in different ways, and it's good for you. You have to learn to adapt to the way different people work.

“Yes, it was strange at times with Bob. One of the great parts about production is that it demonstrates to you that you have to be flexible. Each song has its own secret that's different from another song, and each has its own life. Sometimes it has to be teased out, whereas other times it might come fast. There are no laws about songwriting or producing. It depends on what you're doing, not just who you're doing. You have to be sensitive and flexible, and it's fun.

“I’d say I was more disciplined. But I think Bob is much more disciplined as a writer of lyrics, as a poet. He's an absolute genius. As a singer — absolute genius. But musically, I think it’s a lot more basic. The music just tends to be a vehicle for that poetry.”

I’d say I was more disciplined. But I think Bob is much more disciplined as a writer of lyrics, as a poet.”

— Mark Knopfler

Regardless of the trials he endured, Knopfler maintained his love for Dylan’s work on the album, particularly the song “I and I.” He was particularly moved by the song’s first lines: “Been so long since a strange woman has slept in my bed / Look how sweet she sleeps, how free must be her dreams / In another lifetime she must have owned the world or been faithfully wed / To some righteous king who wrote psalms beside moonlit streams.”

“To hear the first lines of ‘I And I,’ that's enough to make anybody who writes songs want to retire,” Knopfler told GP. “It's stunning.

“Bob's musical ability is limited, in terms of being able to play a guitar or a piano,” he explained. “It's rudimentary, but it doesn't affect his variety, his sense of melody, his singing. It's all there. In fact, some of the things he plays on piano while he's singing are lovely, even though they're rudimentary. That all demonstrates the fact that you don't have to be a great technician.

“It's the same old story: If something is played with soul, that's what's important. My favorite records, by and large, aren't wonderful technical achievements, with the exception perhaps of people like Chet Atkins. But generally speaking, all you've got to do is listen to a Howlin' Wolf album. That's just soul.”

item.title: We review the Silvertone 1446 semihollow and find a mid-priced steal that’s more than a handsome rocker
item.dc:content:
Although the original Silvertone 1446 hollowbody electric was born in the early 1960s, these days you’ll often hear the instrument referred to as “the Chris Isaak guitar.” That’s on account of the fact that the retro crooner cradled one in publicity photos around the same time his moody “Wicked Game” became a huge radio hit in 1990. (Incidentally, the tune’s lilting guitar lines were played by lead guitarist James Calvin Wilsey on a Fender Stratocaster.)

Regardless of your familiarity with (or affinity for) Isaak, old Harmony and Silvertone guitars have long been a more accessible entry point to the vintage guitar market than more prominent names, partially because they feature construction details some players, rightly or not, consider cost-cutting compromises. For example, Silvertones typically had three-bolt neck joints rather than the set-neck construction found on more expensive Gibson and Gretsch instruments of the era.

The latter was true of the original Silvertone 1446, which was built by the Chicago-based Harmony Guitar Company and sold in Sears catalogs and department stores, yet it was still considered a top-of-the-line instrument. Beyond its swanky looks — including distinctive hexagonal pickup surrounds and diamond-shaped selector plate — the vintage 1446 also boasted characterful mini humbuckers designed by Gibson pickup pioneer Seth Lover, creator of the legendary PAF (Patent Applied For) humbuckers in highly sought-after Les Pauls and SGs.

The Silvertone brand has changed hands a few times, most recently in 2020, when Texas-based RBI Music bought rights from Korean manufacturer Samick. With the launch of the 1446 seen here, RBI offers a modernized instrument that mates iconic visuals of yore with set-neck construction and a semi-hollow rather than a hollow body.

In place of the 24-inch-scale original’s wood bridge mounted to a “floating” wood foot, the 24 3/4-inch-scale reissue has a center-block-anchored, Tune-o-matic-type bridge with roller saddles meant to offer more stable tuning and smoother action with the Bigsby B70 vibrato. (Trapeze-tailpiece versions are also available in Gloss Black and Tobacco Sunburst.)

The pickups feature sharp-looking brushed-steel covers and surrounds that look pretty much identical to the originals. At the other end of the 12-inch-radius rosewood fretboard, Waverly-style open-gear tuners look equally elegant. The instrument streets for $999 sans case and is made in China.

RBI says the Alnico 5 magnet mini-humbuckers were designed by Trev Wilkinson and are “exacting era-specific recreations inspired by the rare original P19 pickups.” To my ear, they sound hotter than one would expect from a vintage guitar from the early ’60s. Particularly the bridge pickup.

Plugged in to an edge-of-breakup vintage Supro-style combo amp, in addition to silver-panel Fender combos, our test 1446 proved surprisingly toothsome and plenty bright with the treble pickup soloed and full-up. Pushed to varying degrees with a J. Rockett Archer and a Catalinbread Skewer treble booster, it can get downright vicious. Not metal vicious by any means, but certainly more ripping than some might anticipate from the guitar’s sophisticated old-school looks.

Even so, notes remained clear and well defined. What’s more, backing off the bridge pickup’s volume knob a quarter of the way and dialing the tone back perhaps two-thirds availed a balance of bite and responsiveness that felt more in keeping with the model’s sonic roots.

The neck pickup sounds a bit more polished, but still clear and assertive. Capable of both muscular corpulence and chimey detail, the neck ’bucker had me working knobs less, too. Either soloed or in tandem with the bridge pickup, it yielded a range of vibes from jazzy to soulful/rootsy and chukka-chukka reggae-ready. In fact, brighter bridge-pickup settings were quite useful in expanding the range of dual-pickup tones, even into quasi-Strat-like territories.

For funsies, I compared the 1446 to both my recent-make Gretsch Broadkaster (a semi-hollowbody with Filter’Tron-style pickups) and a Guild X-175 Manhattan hollowbody with authentic old Franz-style “soapbar” pickups. The R pickups out-muscled both. And, of course, the 1446 handled high volumes much better than the Guild — even with a bunch of Auralex foam stuffed inside it.

Conclusion

I’ve long been interested in original Silvertone 1446s, but have never had the opportunity to play one. However, with the plethora of construction departures on this new iteration, it’s safe to say an A/B test with a vintage specimen would be an apples-to-oranges aural affair. Watching videos of original 1446s, one immediately discerns a sense of hollow earthiness that is no doubt inextricably linked to its bolt-on neck design, among other things.

The new 1446, with its set neck and center block — which spans the entire length of the body, splitting it into two smaller sound chambers rather than a large one — was clearly intended to be a handsome rocker. And that it is.

But it’s also much, much more than that. Vintage nitpickery aside, it constitutes a fantastic alternative to the usual semi-hollowbody options — especially at this price point. At $999 street, it is a mid-priced steal, on par in every way and then some with competing options from Gretsch, Guild, Ibanez, Epiphone and others.

SPECIFICATIONS

CONTACT silvertoneguitars.com

PRICE $999 street

BODY Arched maple-laminate semi-hollowbody with center block,

PICKUPS Wilkinson R-Series mini humbuckers

SCALE 24 3/4"

NECK Soft C-shaped mahogany with 12"-radius rosewood fretboard and pearloid block inlays and 20 Silvertone “Easy Feel” ball-end frets

CONTROLS Two Volume and two tone knobs with vintage-style “cupcake” knobs, 3-way pickup selector

HARDWARE Bigsby B70 vibrato, Tune-o-matic-style bridge with roller saddles, single-ply cream pickguard, chrome hardware

FINISH Gloss Black

ASSEMBLED China

PRO Nice setup with smooth, comfortable frets. Versatile, quality pickups by Trev Wilkinson. Modernized center-block and set-neck construction facilitate high-volume friendliness and more sustain than a vintage 1446

CON Departures from original hollowbody and bolt-on construction make this more of a visual tribute than a bona fide reissue. Vibrato bar slightly loose
item.description: With a set neck, center block and Wilkinson-designed mini-humbuckers, RBI Music’s $999 reissue puts a decidedly muscular spin on the vintage Silvertone design

item.title: George Harrison wanted the Beatles to record this song in 1963. It became one of the biggest hits of his solo career
item.dc:content:
Today is Global Beatles Day.

During a 1963 visit to St. Louis, George Harrison found a record he couldn't stop thinking about.

He even imagined the Beatles recording it. But despite his enthusiasm, the song never made its way into the band's repertoire. Harrison would eventually get another chance with it — 24 years later.

It all stemmed from an early 1960s vacation.

“In 1963, the year before the Beatles first came to America, I took a trip to St. Louis to visit my sister, who was living there at the time,” Harrison wrote in The Beatles Anthology. “The whole Beatlemania thing had really begun in the U.K., and we’d had three or four hit singles.

“So while visiting my sister, I went around to all the music shops looking for new singles and especially albums that were really hard to find in Liverpool. And that’s where I finally found the James Ray album, If You’re Gonna Make a Fool of Somebody.”

In particular, the song that grabbed his attention most was “Got My Mind Set on You,” and Harrison thought it had the makings of a Beatles recording — despite one significant drawback.

“It would have been great for the Beatles to cover, except it wasn’t really rock and roll,” he admitted. “It was trying to rock, but it sounded like it was produced by a jazz musician — it had all these squawky horns and stuff.”

As Harrison later recalled, the song “stuck in my mind.” More than two decades passed before he finally revisited it while working on Cloud Nine, his 1987 comeback album after a lengthy break from recording.

Produced by Jeff Lynne, Cloud Nine found Harrison returning to a more electric guitar–driven sound. Revisiting Rudy Clark’s song, he stripped away the brass-heavy arrangement that had bothered him in the first place and gave it a contemporary rock treatment.

“I finally decided to try and put more of a rock edge on the song,” he wrote.

The changes made all the difference. Driven by punchy drums and a leaner arrangement, Harrison’s version of “Got My Mind Set on You” became a massive hit, reaching number one in the United States and giving him one of the biggest singles of his solo career.

In a fitting twist, the song Harrison once hoped the Beatles might record ultimately found its audience through him instead. After carrying it around in his head for nearly a quarter-century, he finally discovered what he'd sensed back in that St. Louis record store: the song had staying power.

Notably, the success of “Got My Mind Set on You” paved the way for Harrison’s next success, the Traveling Wilburys. When his record company asked for a B side to accompany a 12-inch remix of the hit, Harrison enlisted Lynne, Roy Orbison, Bob Dylan and Tom Petty to help him write "Handle With Care." The song was ultimately deemed too good to waste as a flip side and became the debut single by the newly christened Wilburys, one of the biggest supergroups of all time.
item.description: After discovering the track during a visit to America, Harrison carried it with him for nearly a quarter-century before revisiting it on ‘Cloud Nine’

item.title: New Found Glory guitarist Chad Gilbert dies at 45 after cancer battle
item.dc:content:
New Found Glory guitarist and co-founder Chad Gilbert died Sunday, September 20, at age 45 following a yearslong battle with cancer.

Gilbert’s wife, Lisa Cimorelli, and his New Found Glory bandmates announced his death on social media, saying he died peacefully in his sleep surrounded by family and friends.

“On the morning of September 20th, Chad Everett Gilbert passed away peacefully in his sleep,” they wrote. “He left this world surrounded by friends and family and took his final breaths with his wife and mother by his side, just as he wished.”

“We are devastated and shocked by how quickly he left us, yet so grateful for how peacefully and smoothly he went. The amount of visitors that crowded the hospital lobby at a moment’s notice is a testament to how beloved and cherished Chad was, and always will be,” the statement continued. “He was a legendary musician, but his favorite accomplishment was being a husband and father. His biggest dreams came true.”

Gilbert had been undergoing treatment for metastatic pheochromocytoma, a rare adrenal cancer, since 2021. In February, he underwent emergency brain surgery after experiencing weakness in his left hand and leg and doctors discovered three tumors in his brain. The surgery was successful, but revealed that his cancer had progressed to adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), a different and more aggressive form of adrenal cancer.

Just four months later, Gilbert returned to the stage in his hometown of Nashville. On June 8, he played guitar with New Found Glory during “Hit or Miss” and “My Friends Over You” from a motorized scooter.

“I got to play a show in front of my daughter, something I truly never thought I’d get to do again,” he wrote on Instagram after the performance. He also thanked “all the nurses and doctors, my amazing team that have kept me alive through my battle.”

Gilbert remained open about his determination to keep making music and spending time with his family throughout his treatment. Speaking to People in April, he said, “I got my dream in my family, and to have done so many things creatively.

“I always wanted to play music, and I got that, but my biggest dream was to be married to a beautiful wife that would love me and have a daughter,” he said of his daughter, Lily, who was 5 at the time. “That was my dream, so I accomplished my dream.”

Gilbert co-founded New Found Glory in Florida in 1997 and served as the band’s lead guitarist and songwriter for nearly three decades. The group went on to release more than a dozen albums and become one of the defining bands of the pop-punk era.

He favored Gibson Les Paul electrics for much of his time with the group before switching to Telecasters, whose light weight was easier on his spine.

“Chad’s guitar playing, songwriting, humor, and relentless drive helped shape New Found Glory for nearly three decades,” his bandmates wrote. “Through more than a dozen albums, endless tours around the world, and more accolades than we ever could have imagined, Chad challenged all of us to grow as musicians, performers, and human beings.”

“While we are devastated to lose him, we are so grateful for the incredible life he lived, the memories we shared, and the brotherhood we had. His influence will always be part of New Found Glory and his spirit will be felt on every stage we stand on, with every note we play,” they continued. “Rest in peace, Chad. We love you forever ❤️.”

Gilbert is survived by his wife and daughter, as well as his mother, Jackie, and brother, Brian.
item.description: The pop-punk pioneer returned to the stage just four months after emergency brain surgery, playing guitar from a motorized scooter in his hometown of Nashville.
