item.title: Lita Ford on the Runaways, rock and roll — and what happens to hecklers who get in her face
item.dc:content:
“Back in the early 1980s, there were no other girls out there that could play like I could play,” Lita Ford says. “And I had to prove it was me playing those songs, because nobody could accept it.”

These days, it’s a well-established fact that Ford knows her way around an electric guitar. From her groundbreaking work in the 1970s with all-female hard rockers the Runaways to her string of shredding, glam-tinged melodic metal efforts in the ’80s and early 1990s, Ford has remained a highly visible figure in the rock-guitar world for more than 40 years.

And in recent years she has also been celebrated as a major influence on a new generation of guitar-playing front women, in particular Halestorm’s Lzzy Hale, who credits Ford with “kicking the door down” for waves of female six-string slingers.

To make that happen, however, Ford occasionally had to do some actual kicking. As she explains, you may underestimate her skills as a guitarist, but you’ll do so at your own peril.

“I remember one time around ’81, there was a guy in the front row at a show,” Ford recounts. “He was right up against the stage, and he had an unopened can of beer. While I was playing, he shook that beer. I was watching him do it, but he didn’t know I could see him. I was acting like I didn’t see him.

“I knew he was gonna spray me down with his beer, so I waited for him to get the can up, and as he was about to pop the little tab, I walked over and kicked him in the wrist as hard as I could. I know I broke his wrist, because I used to wear these great big clodhopper platform shoes onstage!”

Ford lets out a laugh. “But it was like, Dude, you’re gonna spray me with that? I don’t think so. If someone spits at me, I spit back.”

As Ford tells it, her indoctrination into rock and roll came very early in life. Born in England, she moved with her family to Long Beach, California, at age four. Before she was even a teenager, she says, she was already taken with the heaviest sounds of the era.

“I asked my mother for a guitar,” she recalls. “And she bought me this Sears acoustic model. I ended up giving it away to my girlfriend, and I got another guitar that was a step up from Sears — it was, I don’t know, maybe a Bloomingdale’s model or something. I was playing heavy metal on this acoustic guitar. It was all Black Sabbath and Deep Purple riffs, but it just didn’t sound right to me. It didn’t have the balls I was looking for.”

After a cousin chaperoned Ford to a 1971 Black Sabbath concert at the nearby Long Beach Arena, she knew exactly what she needed. “I saw Tony Iommi, and I had to have a Gibson SG,” she says. “I just loved the darkness and the low end of the sound. I went to this hospital where my mom worked, and I bullshitted my way in and got a job. I saved up $375 from that job and bought myself a chocolate-colored SG.”

Ford was still playing that SG when, a few years later, she joined the Runaways at the tender age of 16; it’s the guitar that can be heard on the band’s classic, self-titled 1976 debut. At that time, however, she needed to update her amplifier.

I went to this hospital where my mom worked, and I bullshitted my way in and got a job. I saved up $375 from that job and bought myself a chocolate-colored SG.”

— Lita Ford

“I had been using my father’s reel-to-reel,” Ford says, laughing. “It was this huge thing, and it had an echo on it that sounded like a delay, which was great. It was like, Wow, I’ve got effects and everything! It was bizarre, but it worked. But once I was in the Runaways, I used a Marshall.”

Later in 1976, Ford augmented her Runaways gear with a pair of eye-catching Hamer Standards — one black, one white. These Gibson Explorer–inspired guitars became her main instruments throughout the rest of her tenure with the band and can be heard on the Runaways’ later albums.

Ford says she enjoyed her time in the Runaways, but the group’s explicit punk stance proved somewhat suffocating, considering that she’d grown up on a steady diet of Iommi, Ritchie Blackmore, and Jimmy Page.

“I would go home and learn stuff like ‘Stairway to Heaven’ — all the riffs, all the solos,” she says, “because that was the type of stuff I wanted to play in the band. But when I got into rehearsal, we would end up doing, you know, ‘Cherry Bomb.’ It was always that chunky, straight-ahead thing.”

It wasn’t until the Runaways dissolved in 1979 that Ford finally found the space to spread her guitar wings.

“I really took over my own self,” she continues. “I cut my hair and changed my clothes. I came up with my own style, my own look, my own way of playing.”

I would go home and learn stuff like ‘Stairway to Heaven’ — all the riffs, all the solos, because that was the type of stuff I wanted to play in the band.”

— Lita Ford

She also swapped out her guitars. “I got into B.C. Rich,” says Ford, who rediscovered her stolen B.C. Rich Mockingbird through an audition. “They became my home away from home. [B.C. Rich founder] Bernie Rico, Sr. was just fantastic, and I was always over there carving out new ideas and helping to make new stuff.

“They would make anything I asked them to make. By the end of the ’80s, I had a stack of different B.C. Rich guitars, and I would play them all in concert, because I wanted to show them off.”

By the latter part of the decade, Ford was also enjoying the success of a bona fide hit record: 1988’s Lita. Her third solo effort overall, the album spawned two hit singles — the hard-rocking “Kiss Me Deadly” and the ballad “Close My Eyes Forever,” sung as a duet with Ozzy Osbourne — and eventually became her first Platinum-seller.

Ford stuck to her guitar-playing guns, so much so that when she saw hard rock’s popularity declining in the early ’90s, she opted to bow out altogether rather than change her music to suit prevailing trends. “The music scene was changing,” she says. “Grunge was kickin’ in, and I was getting tired. So I said, ‘It’s a good time to disappear.’ What else was I gonna do? Go be a country star?”

Ford spent roughly 15 years away from the music scene before returning. It wasn’t easy to dive back in.

“Not at all,” Ford says. “It wasn’t like riding a bike. I had to relearn how to do it. I hadn’t been playing guitar all those years I was away. I even had to get used to wearing clothes again. Because I was living on a deserted island, all I wore was Billabongs. Then all of a sudden it was, ‘My God, I’ve got on high heels and leather pants!’”

Nevertheless, Ford has been fully back in the creative swing of things ever since. As for the music, it remains true to her heavy metal roots.

“Yeah, absolutely,” she says. “If it’s in your blood, it’s in your blood. It never really goes away.”

item.title: “We were gonna be the American Led Zeppelin — and he couldn’t take it.” Sammy Hagar on the torment of Ronnie Montrose
item.dc:content:
Sammy Hagar certainly gets his due as a singer, frontman, band leader, songwriter and, of course, liquor and restaurant entrepreneur. That he’s also a solid guitar player is often lost in the mix.

That, however, could have something to do with those who have stood beside him throughout his 54-year recording career.

The Red Rocker came to prominence in 1973 as the frontman for Montrose, collaborating with Ronnie Montrose over the course of two albums — Montrose and Paper Money — and favorites such as “Bad Motor Scooter” and “Rock the Nation.”

After Montrose changed the lineup in 1975, Hagar embarked on a solo career and scored his own batch of hits (“There’s Only One Way to Rock,” “I Can’t Drive 55” and more). He also teamed with Journey’s Neal Schon in 1983 for the short-lived supergroup HSAS, which released the live album Through the Fire in 1984.

The following year, Hagar performed with Eddie Van Halen at the first Farm Aid concert, then went on to spend 11 years with Van Halen, recording four number one albums with the band following the departure of David Lee Roth. (Hagar would return for one more tour in 2004 and record three new songs for The Best of Both Worlds compilation.)

He worked with Schon again and, later, Joe Satriani in the side project Planet Us. Satriani would also join Hagar in another supergroup, Chickenfoot, and later become part of Hagar’s Best of All Worlds Band in 2024. In between, Hagar brought Vic Johnson into his bands the Waboritas and the Circle.

That’s a lot of electric six-string firepower to be attached to in one career, and Hagar does not take those associations for granted. He loves to talk about his good fortune, too — which he did with us via Zoom from Maui as he prepares for a new run of Best of All Worlds dates beginning June 13 in St. Louis. Here he tells us about four guitar greats he’s played with who aren’t Eddie Van Halen (we’ll leave that discussion for another day).

Ronnie Montrose

“Ronnie was on fire. That’s the way he played — like it’s burning. He wasn’t that fast. He wasn’t a shredder. He played well, and he played really fiery.

“I learned how to play guitar from Ronnie. I learned more from Ronnie than Eddie as a guitarist. I still play more like Ronnie Montrose today. He really inspired my guitar playing.

“When he got into his Town Without Pity era, he started playing more like what Joe Satriani plays — with that sound and that vocal style. He probably would’ve gotten even better; he just had some real head problems. I’ve never seen a guy like that. He fired everybody. The second you had one smidgen of success with him, he broke up the band.

“Montrose — we were about to explode. We were gonna be the American Led Zeppelin, and he couldn’t take it. I don’t know what it was. He was afraid of success. He’d sit there in the studio holding his face like, ‘Oh God, what are we gonna do?’ I’m like, ‘Fuck, let’s jam! Let’s make some music.’

“He was so tormented, man. I don’t know why; I think it must’ve been some far-out childhood thing that happened to him. I mean, come on — the guy shot himself in the head. It’s horrible. [Montrose died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound on March 3, 2012.]

“That broke my heart when he did that. It made me think, Could somebody have helped him? What happened here? How do you let some guy do that? I wasn’t around, but if I’d been around and knew he was in that kind of condition, I would’ve put this guy in a hospital or taken him under my wing. I would’ve helped.”

Neal Schon

“Neal’s been my friend forever. Before Journey broke, we were buddies. We used to play shows together, and he would always come jam with me when I’d play Winterland [in San Francisco]. Neal just walks around with a fuckin’ guitar around his neck. He takes it off to shower, and that’s probably it. He probably fucks with a guitar around his neck. He’s just always playing.

“He’s a great, melodic player. He uses the whole neck and makes it look like a toy. I can tell a Neal Schon solo instantly because he plays a really cool, melodic lick, and then he goes [scats] — just spills out all these crazy, whacked-out notes. I don’t know if any of them are real notes, but if you’re not hitting bad notes, it doesn’t matter.

“I could say, ‘Let’s write a song, Neal,’ and he’ll write a song in five minutes. Him and Joe Satriani — they’re so frickin’ prolific, it’s scary. And it’s ’cause he’s got the guitar on all the time, so he’ll think, ‘Here’s what I was playing a couple minutes ago. This could be a song.’ That’s Neal.”

Vic Johnson

“I call him Vic ‘Right Hand’ Johnson all the time. He’s got a right hand like The Edge, like Pete Townshend. He can shred — his left hand’s great — but his right hand, man, he kicks off a groove and you don’t need to hear the drums. He puts it right in the pocket.

“He was never in a band till he got in my band, and he was kind of a sideman. Earlier on, if he’d had a superstar singer — a Sammy Hagar, a David Lee Roth or a Robert Plant or somebody — Vic would’ve been much more famous as a guitar player.

“Vic’s got the biggest, fattest sound. When I pick up his guitar, his strings are really fat — big ol’ fat strings. I can’t play ’em. I can’t bend ’em, but he’s got those big, ol’ strong hands, and he gets a lot of tone out of there.

“Joe [Satriani], Neal Schon — Eddie, when he heard Vic play — they all go, ‘Yeah, he’s got a cool tone.’ Vic’s pretty much a simple Ronnie Montrose-style guitar player like me, but he’s got the baddest tone of all of us.”

Joe Satriani

“Joe’s got the same thing Jeff Beck had, and that’s that he can make the guitar sing. He’s got the tone and the touch — his vibrato and the way he uses his whammy bar — like Jeff Beck. Songs like ‘Summer Song’ or ‘Surfing With the Alien’ sound like there’s a singer in the band.

“He’s one of the few instrumentalists who can carry it to where you can tolerate it. When I go see an instrumentalist, by about the third song I’m going, ‘Well, when’s the singer coming out?’ ’Cause I’m getting bored. But Joe will play the next tune and you’re like, ‘Wow, that’s a cool melody!’ In my head, it’s like he’s singing it.

“I think Joe could be one of the best guitar players on the planet right now. Look — he taught Steve Vai how to play, so Steve will never be better than him. He taught Kirk Hammett how to play, so Kirk will never be better than him. ’Cause you can’t outdo the teacher.

“Joe knows exactly what Eddie was playing; that’s why I love having him in this band. He studied it. He watched live tapes, he saw him live, he listens to the records and knows exactly what Eddie was doing. That’s the difference between him and some kid in a music store playing ‘Eruption’ exactly like Eddie. Joe knows what he’s doing, and he knows what Eddie was doing, and that’s different from simply emulating somebody.

“He’s a genius, honest to God. I’m not joking about his intelligence. He’s super smart. When you interview him, his answers are so thoughtful and so deep. I love the guy.

“Lemme say one bad thing about him so you don’t think I’m kissing his ass too much: He plays too fuckin’ loud. And he doesn’t need to play that loud ’cause he has in-ears. But he’s used to not having a singer, so he thinks, ‘I gotta be the loudest thing.’ [laughs] We’re still working that out.”

item.title: Johnny Marr on the “magic” of writing the Smiths’ songs with Morrissey
item.dc:content:
Nearly 40 years have passed since Johnny Marr walked away from the Smiths. It was 1987 when a communication breakdown between the guitarist and the group’s frontman, singer Morrissey, caused him to leave the group.

But as he tells Britain’s Channel 4 News in a new interview, he still has fond regard for the group and the years when he and Morrissey crafted the group’s catalog of cherished songs.

Marr explains that the Manchester scene in the 1980s was home to Factory Records, which was known for acts like Joy Division and New Order. The Smiths chose to go with a rival label, Rough Trade.

“I was working in a clothes shop when the band was formed, and other Mancunian musicians used to come into the shop, and most of them were on Factory Records,” Marr explains. “So because of the shop, I knew everyone on Factory, and it was the obvious thing to do to sign to Factory. And that became a narrative.”

Factory Records owner Tony Wilson never signed the Smiths, to his great regret. But Marr says that was unlikely to have happened.

“I was never going to sign Factory. Personally I would never let that happen because it was just too obvious, and it wasn’t that kind of music either.”

Factory acts “weren’t guitar bands per se,” Marr says. “They were doing other things with funk and keyboards... different, almost like non-guitar bands. So it was very deliberate that we were going to be a guitar band, and that was my role in it.”

Marr also reveals how he and Morrissey wrote together. Although sometimes their sessions took place separately — Marr writing the music and passing a tape off to Morrissey — he says of the early days of their writing, “We’d get together face to face, and I’d go, ‘I’ve got this.’ And then I’d record it on the tape machine and he’d take the cassette away.”

Later, “when I’d made a few hundred quid,” he purchased a Tascam Portastudio. “I would make these slightly more elaborate demos with a little drum machine and about three or four guitars on top, and then I’d get on my motorbike and ride round because he lived around the corner 10 minutes [away], and I’d drop it through his letterbox.”

But Marr’s fondest memories are of the making of the group’s 1986 third album, The Queen Is Dead. He recalls how he and Morrissey would sit just a few feet apart with a Walkman cassette player between them.

“It was amazing,” he says. “It was magic. I’d literally have the guitar and I’d have the cassette machine between my knees and I’d go, ‘I’ve got this one.’ And I’d press record.

“I think when I pressed ‘record’ the two of us breathed in, and then when I finished we then breathed out. That’s what it felt like.

“Any songwriter will tell you it’s the best feeling in the world.”

Marr also reveals that he wrote songs in threes, anticipating how Morrissey, bassist Andy Rourke and drummer Mike Joyce would embellish his chords with their contributions.

“It was the greatest,” Marr says. “We’ve got three new Smith songs. I can’t wait to hear what the words are. I can’t wait to hear what the vocals are, what the bass is, what Andy does, and what Mike does.

“Man, it was magic!”

Marr is celebrating the results of his guitar auction, held September 16 at Christie’s. Nearly 100 guitars — electrics and acoustics — from Marr’s collection went under the hammer, raising more than £3.6 million for the Guide Dogs for the Blind Association and the Autistic Society.

The guitarist spoke about a few of the instruments in his Channel 4 interview, highlighting the 1959/1960 Gibson ES-355 he got when the Smiths signed to Sire Records in the U.S. (and which sold at the auction for £204,800).

“We were about to do our record deal with Sire Records in America and the head of Sire Records was a really famous guy called Seymour Stein, and he’d been around since the ’60s. I was getting these stories out of him about the Rolling Stones, and he happened to say that he got Brian Jones a couple of guitars in the ’60s. So I saw my opportunity there, and I said to him, ‘Well, look, Seymour, if you get me a guitar, we’ll sign.’

“True to his word. We trudged across in the snow to 48th Street, New York.”

Marr found what he wanted at We Buy Guitars.

“I looked through the window and I saw that hanging up on the wall. And then I darted back to the hotel that we stayed in, and I started playing it. And the very first thing I played was ‘Heaven Knows I’m Miserable Now.’ And I always say that guitar definitely had that song in it. I mean, I know it was. It might seem a little cosmic, but I know that certain instruments have music in them.”

item.content:encoded:
Nearly 40 years have passed since Johnny Marr walked away from the Smiths. It was 1987 when a communication breakdown between the guitarist and the group’s frontman, singer Morrissey, caused him to leave the group.

But as he tells Britain’s Channel 4 News in a new interview, he still has fond regard for the group and the years when he and Morrissey crafted the group’s catalog of cherished songs.

Marr explains that the Manchester scene in the 1980s was home to Factory Records, which was known for acts like Joy Division and New Order. The Smiths chose to go with a rival label, Rough Trade.

“I was working in a clothes shop when the band was formed, and other Mancunian musicians used to come into the shop, and most of them were on Factory Records,” Marr explains. “So because of the shop, I knew everyone on Factory, and it was the obvious thing to do to sign to Factory. And that became a narrative.”

Factory Records owner Tony Wilson never signed the Smiths, to his great regret. But Marr says that was unlikely to have happened.

“I was never going to sign Factory. Personally I would never let that happen because it was just too obvious, and it wasn’t that kind of music either.”

Factory acts “weren’t guitar bands per se,” Marr says. “They were doing other things with funk and keyboards... different, almost like non-guitar bands. So it was very deliberate that we were going to be a guitar band, and that was my role in it.”

item.title: Ed Sheeran breaks his silence on Gaza after the Macklemore tour controversy: “I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore”
item.dc:content:
Ed Sheeran apologized to fans at his Philadelphia concert Saturday night, acknowledging that he had made “mistakes” in his response to the controversy that has engulfed his tour and speaking publicly for the first time about his views on the war in Gaza.

“I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I am so, so sorry,” the acoustic guitarist told the crowd at Lincoln Financial Field, according to multiple reports.

The singer, who has traditionally avoided political commentary, said he could no longer remain silent about the humanitarian crisis.

“I’ve tried in my career to not be a political commentator of any kind because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division, about humanity, not politics,” he said. “But this is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore.”

Sheeran condemned the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack while expressing strong criticism of the devastation in Gaza.

“What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain,” he said. “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, children’s lives. And the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank, it cannot be overlooked.”

He also addressed the broader free-speech dispute that has left him performing without any supporting acts.

“This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views, and everyone here can stand beside people that they don’t agree with on everything, but they can all agree on singing these songs,” Sheeran said.

I’ve tried in my career to not be a political commentator of any kind... But this is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore.”

— Ed Sheeran

The Philadelphia show was Sheeran’s first since his U.S. tour erupted into controversy over the removal of Macklemore, who had said “Free Palestine” from the stage during a September performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Sheeran subsequently said the decision to remove Macklemore was made by the tour’s promoter after venues indicated they would not allow the rapper to perform.

Messina Touring Group said venues on the remaining U.S. dates had told the promoter they would not allow concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup, potentially forcing the cancellation of the tour.

The decision prompted the other supporting acts to withdraw in solidarity. Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham and Sheeran’s touring band Beoga all announced that they would no longer participate. Finneas wrote that “artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed” and said, “I stand with Palestine and its people.”

The controversy also prompted Sheeran to speak out about the role of venues in determining what performers can say onstage. Before Saturday’s concert, he said he was “deeply worried” about venues requiring artists to have their content approved in advance.

“This happens in so many places that I perform around the world,” he said, “but it should never happen in the free world.”

Sheeran had faced criticism for initially declining to take a public position on the conflict, including from former Pink Floyd bass guitarist Roger Waters, who criticized him on social media and called him “a little prick.” The controversy also created an unintentionally awkward twist for Guitar Center, which had launched a contest in August offering undiscovered musicians the chance to open for Sheeran on the December 11 date of his Loop Tour in Mexico City.

In Philadelphia, Sheeran said he still wanted his concerts to provide a place where people with opposing views could come together.

“My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me,” he said.
item.description: As his tour resumed on Saturday night, the guitarist opened his show by apologizing to fans and called the devastation in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable”

item.title: Samantha Fish on the guitarists and music of her life
item.dc:content:
More often than not, Samantha Fish is the only guitar player in her band. But she has a good history of playing nice with others.

The Kansas City, Missouri, native has been at it since she was a teenager, and recording since 2009’s Live Bait with her Samantha Fish Blues Band. Over the years she’s teamed with Cassie Taylor and Dani Wild as Girls With Guitars and teamed with Texas titan Jesse Dayton on 2023’s Grammy Award-nominated Death Wish Blues. She’s also had albums produced by fellow guitarists such as Mike Zito, Luther Dickinson, Jon Spencer, Bobby Harlow of the Go and Martin Kierszenbaum.

“The music community is so special,” Fish tells us from her current residence in New Orleans. “I’m not talking about any specific region; it’s just a great community of musicians and people playing real instruments as we kind of tiptoe into this digital and, daresay, AI age. I’ve always been encouraged by people older than me and by my peers to grow and explore and not take any shortcuts or anything like that.”

Fish’s collaborative acumen, meanwhile, has been best demonstrated on stage, where she’s been shown an open door from a wealth of colleagues — opportunities she certainly does not take for granted.

“Every time I’m onstage with a guitar player I feel like I learn something,” Fish acknowledges. “You watch their technique and approach and think about how that applies to how I do it. I feel like you can only do what you can do; I’ve gone toe to toe with people before and tried to turn it into a competition, like a lot of people do … and try to see who can out-gun each other.

“But I feel like the best musical things happen when it’s more of a conversation. So for me it’s, ‘What can I say that’s going to add to and elevate this?’ That’s how I approach jamming with people. That’s the most honest way to do it, not come with my stuff and outgun somebody.”

Fish, who released her latest studio album, Paper Doll, last year and Paper Doll Live earlier this year, recently announced this year’s edition of her Shake ’Em Down Tour, joined by Cedric Burnside and Daddy Long Legs for 14 dates starting December 2 in Pensacola, Florida, and wrapping up 18 days later in Louisville. She’s also writing songs for her next album, which Fish says “is still pretty vague to me. It’s taking a shape, but I’m not ready to say what that is — ’cause it will probably change.”

In the meantime, Fish took a few minutes to sit down and reminisce about some of her favorite onstage playing encounters.

Eric Gales

Among Fish’s career highlights is performing at Eric Clapton’s 2023 Crossroads Guitar Festival in Los Angeles, collaborating with Eric Gales on her “Black Wind Hollow” during her set and then joining him for Screamin’ Jay Hawkins’ “I Put a Spell on You” and the Alabama State Troupers’ “Going Down,” the latter with Christone “Kingfish” Ingram.

“That was one of those incredible invitations. I’ve always wanted to perform at Crossroads since, I think, 2010 when I stumbled on a DVD recording of the concert. That was just one of those things I put on the bucket list in my brain, in the back of my head, that if it ever happens again it would mean so much to be included.

“So when they invited me and wanted me to play with him — done! I’d played with Eric before, and he’s really one of the best, such an incredible performer and player. The way he puts together melodies, his note selection, he’s otherworldly. He takes you to space and back.

“To get the opportunity with him, and Kingfish as well, was really special. I felt like these are my friends. We’re in the blues community, so it’s special. Crossroads is a super-curated thing; I let them tell me what they wanted to do. I can’t remember if we chose ‘I Put a Spell on You’ or if they did; it might have been a request. It’s a big production and they’ve got this rotating stage; on one side somebody’s performing and on the other side it’s frantically trying to get our stuff set up so that when it rotates we’re ready to go. To put on that kind of a show it requires so much planning, to the minute. To the second, actually.

“There wasn’t any rehearsal; I sent Eric the song, ‘Black Wind Hollow,’ and we knew the others. We kind of talked out the changes and everything. But Eric’s band is so good, and they’re standards. There’s so many versions of them, I knew it would be something we could do really well together.”

Buddy Guy

“Buddy Guy somebody I’ve gotten the opportunity to perform with a few times, on the road opening shows and stuff. We played in Central Park together; Bobby Rush was there, too, so that was a cool show. He is one of the best conversationalists on guitar there is, hands down. He’s such an expert when it comes to that.

“I’ve learned a lot from Buddy over the years. He’s the truth; he tells the truth when he’s up there, and it’s nice to be able to bounce something back to him. Recently he was in New Orleans and I went to see the show and went backstage just to say hello. And he’s like, ‘You’re getting up, right?’ I had not planned on that, but of course I’m not gonna say no to an opportunity to learn something.”

Walter Trout

“Walter Trout is one of the first musicians I remember going to see as a young player, when he’d come to Kansas City and perform. I used to frequent this club called Knuckleheads a lot, and he was somebody the owner of the club was like, ‘You need to come see this guy. He’s gonna teach you something.’

“And he did. The guy is a very powerful guitar player, incredible story, incredible songs. It’s been awhile since we’ve played together, but it’s always great when we get the chance.”

Joe Bonamassa

“I’ve gotten to do the super jams on some of his cruises, and he’s a fun one to play off of, to go toe-to-toe with, as you say. He’s really super expressive and melodic, and he has way different ideas than I do, so it’s kind of fun to hear the way he puts notes together. That’s the fun part.

“I know he has a lot of amps up there — he’s definitely more into gear than I am — but it’s not as loud as you think. It’s workable. He’s got a lot of taste, and his band just sounds exceptional. They’re pristine.”

Slash

“I did a Slash tour, and that just made my little kid heart so happy, ’cause I was such a Guns N’ Roses fan. Do you know how many speeding tickets I got on Appetite for Destruction? So many that they almost took my license away. I told him that and he laughed — or gave me a pity chuckle. I’m not sure.

“He came out and played ‘I Put a Spell on You’ with us, and it was fun just to get to play with an icon like Slash, ’cause he’s such a great player and you can just tell it’s him in the way he plays. We did some back and forth; I wait a lot when I’m playing with somebody, ’cause I don’t want to step on anybody’s toes.

“I was more or less sitting back, waiting to hear what he was gonna say and take my time to respond. That’s always a good way to approach playing with anybody, I think.”

Luther Dickinson

The lead singer and guitarist for the North Mississippi Allstars, Luther Dickinson produced two of Fish’s albums — 2015’s Wild Heart and 2017’s Belle of the West — and she calls him “one of my favorite guitar players to play with. He’s really melodic and fun. Every time I’ve had the pleasure of sitting in with him or whatever, he’s just got a way of building melodies and a dynamic, and his tone is some of my favorite guitar tone out there. And every time you play with him, it’s different. We never do the same thing twice.”

Jesse Dayton

“We did that Death Wish Blues album [2023] and a whole collaborative tour and got nominated for a Grammy together. I’ve always been the only guitar player in my band for the longest time, so when Jesse and I started working together it introduced this opportunity for me to approach things differently, and I learned so much from that time period.

“We were on the road together for 18 months, and it was fun for me to approach the guitar from this other level — ‘What can I do to complement the lead right now? What can I play in front? Behind?’ It made me a stronger guitarist. Just to have that back-and-forth dynamic was really, really cool.

“And he’s such an explosive player! That [King double-cut hollowbody] guitar he’s got is so big. The sound of it is just monstrous. For me it was, ‘All right, I’ve got to figure out how to complement this — not compete sonically but take up a different space.’ It was really fun and really interesting.”
item.description: The blues-rock guitarist looks back at the players who shaped her approach, and explains why she prefers musical conversation to competition.
item.dc:creator: Gary Graff

“He came out and played ‘I Put a Spell on You’ with us, and it was fun just to get to play with an icon like Slash, ’cause he’s such a great player and you can just tell it’s him in the way he plays. We did some back and forth; I wait a lot when I’m playing with somebody, ’cause I don’t want to step on anybody’s toes.

“I was more or less sitting back, waiting to hear what he was gonna say and take my time to respond. That’s always a good way to approach playing with anybody, I think.”

Luther Dickinson

The lead singer and guitarist for the North Mississippi Allstars, Luther Dickinson produced two of Fish’s albums — 2015’s Wild Heart and 2017’s Belle of the West — and she calls him “one of my favorite guitar players to play with. He’s really melodic and fun. Every time I’ve had the pleasure of sitting in with him or whatever, he’s just got a way of building melodies and a dynamic, and his tone is some of my favorite guitar tone out there. And every time you play with him, it’s different. We never do the same thing twice.”

Jesse Dayton

“We did that Death Wish Blues album [2023] and a whole collaborative tour and got nominated for a Grammy together. I’ve always been the only guitar player in my band for the longest time, so when Jesse and I started working together it introduced this opportunity for me to approach things differently, and I learned so much from that time period.

“We were on the road together for 18 months, and it was fun for me to approach the guitar from this other level — ‘What can I do to complement the lead right now? What can I play in front? Behind?’ It made me a stronger guitarist. Just to have that back-and-forth dynamic was really, really cool.

“And he’s such an explosive player! That [King double-cut hollowbody] guitar he’s got is so big. The sound of it is just monstrous. For me it was, ‘All right, I’ve got to figure out how to complement this — not compete sonically but take up a different space.’ It was really fun and really interesting.”

item.title: Johnny Marr on shredders, guitar heroes — and why just sold nearly 100 of his guitars dating back to the Smiths
item.dc:content:
Johnny Marr’s guitars have just fetched more than £3.6 million at auction — but the Smiths guitarist has never been particularly interested in treating the electric guitar as a vehicle for theatrics.

The auction, held at Christie’s on September 16, saw nearly 100 guitars from Marr’s collection go under the hammer, raising more than three times their estimated value for the Guide Dogs for the Blind Association and the Autistic Society.

Among the highlights were the 1960 Cherry Red Gibson ES-355 Marr played on “Heaven Knows I’m Miserable Now,” which sold for £204,800, and the 1982 Rickenbacker 330 Jetglo he used on the Smiths’ self-titled debut before loaning it to Noel Gallagher for Definitely Maybe. The Rickenbacker fetched £358,400 and later appeared on the cover of Oasis’ “Supersonic” single.

“The auction has been a great experience and has exceeded all my expectations,” Marr said afterward. “I’d like to thank everyone who made bids and special thanks to Christie’s for making it so memorable.”

For Marr, though, the value of a guitar has never been measured simply by how much noise — or how many notes — a player can get out of it. As guitarist with the Smiths and throughout his solo career, he largely shunned guitar solos, prioritized songs over showmanship and frequently criticized the cult of virtuosity that dominated rock guitar culture in the 1980s.

That philosophy helped make Marr one of the most influential players of his generation. While the Smiths scored 17 hit singles in the 1980s, Marr built the band’s sound around intricate layers of overdubbed guitars, unusual chord voicings and a vast palette of tones. His style drew from the rock ’n’ roll primitivism of the ’60s, the grooves of the ’70s and the bright, chiming textures of the ’80s, creating a sound that inspired countless guitarists.

“I’ve always believed that any instrumentalist is basically just an accompanist to the singer and the words,” Marr told Guitar Player in 1990. “That’s born out of being a fan of records before I was a fan of guitar players. I’m interested in melody, lyrics, and the overall song. I don’t like to waste notes, not even one.”

That same year, Marr was particularly blunt about the guitarists who seemed to represent the opposite philosophy.

“Who was it that said, ‘The reason why all those guitar players play so many notes is because they can’t find the right one?’” he asked Guitar Player in a cover interview. “I like to put the right note in the right place, and my influences have always been those kinds of players. Keith Richards comes to mind, and I really like Nils Lofgren’s soloing, because he’s so melodic. I love John Lennon’s rhythm playing, and George Harrison was an incredible guitarist.”

Marr’s admiration for melody and economy put him at odds with much of the era’s guitar culture.

“There’s a lot of guitar culture that I don’t like at all,” he said. “I find the traditional idea of the guitar hero to be really irrelevant to the 1990s. I don’t think that young people are that impressed with some guy brandishing spandex trousers and a hideously shaped guitar, playing that kind of masturbatory, egotistical noise.

“Being a soloist who wants to just display virtuosity is a dated philosophy, and I don’t think there’s any room for it in pop music. It’s the last stand of late-’60s/early-’70s rockism, and it should have gone a long time ago.”

Despite his criticism of shred culture, Marr made clear he respected players with genuine technical ability.

“I have a healthy respect for guitarists like Joe Satriani and Eddie Van Halen, disciplined players who really know what they’re doing — if you’re going to be a virtuoso, you can’t be hit-and-miss. But I think people like Yngwie Malmsteen should be forgotten as soon as possible, I really do.”

Marr then offered one of the interview’s most provocative observations.

“It’s got very little to do with music, and the ‘I’m the fastest gun in town’ idea is almost like homosexual panic. Nothing against gays, but when players perpetrate this incredibly sexist image of being so macho, I find it suspicious.

“Plus, I can’t do all that stuff, so that’s why I say it’s stupid,” he added with a laugh.
item.description: The Smiths icon’s gear just sold for millions — proving that intricate melodies and anti-virtuoso discipline outlasted the spandex-clad soloists of his era.

item.title: Yes guitarist Steve Howe on the operation that postponed the Fragile tour
item.dc:content:
Yes guitarist Steve Howe is happy to entertain inquiries about his health — especially after postponing the group’s tour plans during the spring to undergo “an essential operation that requires recovery time.”

But he also doesn’t have a lot to say about it.

“I don’t want to dwell on it too much; if I start talking I’ll go somewhere I don’t want to go,” he tells us via Zoom from his home in the English countryside. “I had this major thing and it was pretty difficult, and it’s gonna take some time to get me back to normal.

“But I’m keeping up my playing and my momentum. It’s been three months now since I had the operation, so I’m making progress, slowly.

“So we rescheduled everything we had this year for next year and hopefully everything will be hunky dory and we’ll be back around and try and do all the things we were going to do this year.”

Yes will, in fact, hit the road early next May to play its 1971 album Fragile and more, first in the U.K. and then in Japan, with dates to be announced. North America is also in the band’s sights, with details still being determined, too.

Howe has had plenty to consider during his downtime, meanwhile. Yes did release Aurora — its 24th studio album and third in less than five years, and third consecutive album produced by Howe — during June. Weighing in at nearly an hour, including bonus tracks, it leans even further into the hallmarks of Yes’ progressive sound, with one epic in the four-part, 13:44 suite “Countermovement.”

And while, like its immediate predecessors — 2021’s The Quest and 2023’s Mirror to the Sky — Yes made use of file sharing and other technology, there were also more opportunities for band members to get together now that frontman Jon Davison and bassist Billy Sherwood are spending more time in the U.K., where Howe and keyboardist Geoff Downes reside. (Drummer Jay Schellen remains a full-time U.S. resident.)

On top of that, Yes has just come out with a 25th anniversary edition of Magnification, an album that found the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame troupe working with an orchestra again for the first time since its second album, Time and a Word, in 1970. It was also the only Yes album recorded as a quartet (no full-time keyboardist, though late drummer Alan White played some piano) and the last Yes album to feature co-founder Jon Anderson before his acrimonious departure in 2004.

So Howe, robust and in good humor, is eager to make up for lost time now, with plenty to review and look forward to in the not too distant future.

It must have been frustrating to have a new album and tours on the runway and have to put the brakes on everything earlier this year.

It’s immensely disappointing; I feel it probably more than anybody else because I’m the subject matter of it. I had ambitious goals that we just had to postpone ’til next year. But we still put Aurora out; it was in the process, so we couldn’t really stop it. Sometimes the world doesn’t wait for you and other times it does, so you have to make judgment calls.

This has been the most productive period for Yes since, really, the ’70s. Are these last three albums of a piece, do you think?

It’s immensely disappointing; I feel it probably more than anybody else because I’m the subject matter of it.”

— Steve Howe

Yeah, yeah. To my mind these are a sort of trilogy, obviously, a set towards continuing that Yes doesn’t exclusively rely on its old material, and there is a creative pulse in the band. The Quest was like a golden opportunity, and then we did Mirror to the Sky and stepped up a bit and got more compelling. And Aurora is the pinnacle of our achievement, to us. But primarily I’m happy we’ve been able to make new music. That’s a beautiful thing. We want it to be in respect of the past music but we don’t want to cheapen it by pastiching some features of our music together. We got it completely with a blank piece of paper and start saying, “What do we got?”

With you producing, of course, this really is your representation of Yes and what it is at this point in time.

It’s been joyful to produce Yes for three albums. I’ve helped to do that all through my career, but never have I had credit — and also the authority to do something I wanted to do. I’ve tried to make it as fun and as pleasant, as nice as possible. This wasn’t a moment for me to become dominant and sort of call all the shots. But like an orchestra, a conductor does have a job to do; although I don’t primarily do conducting I do have a responsibility — I do have a possibility, that’s a better word, of being able to steer this where it has the history kind of wrapped up in it but takes it somewhere new.

Everybody loves a big Yes epic. What’s the story of “Countermovement” on Aurora?

I surprised them with that one. We had two songs floating around, and neither of them had been developed a great deal. One day I thought, This is sort of untidy; maybe I can do a ‘Luminosity’ on it, or a ‘Mirror to the Sky.’ I think this album needs this.

They weren’t in the same keys and they weren’t at the same tempos, but that didn’t put me off them. And then I had two instrumentals that were viable, and I was happy to offer them to Yes. So what I did was kind of transplant those two instrumentals into the two songs and sort of jiggle around with it, a bit like a jigsaw trying to find out how they fitted together.

I don’t mind if somebody says ‘It’s too long’ or ‘Can you make it longer?’ Most probably the answer to both is ‘no.’”

— Steve Howe

To be honest it was longer once, and we got some advice that maybe that idea’s gone a bit far, so we brought them back in, trimmed them back so it was back into a conceivable shell.

So that’s what happened, and everybody grew to like it, and I think it does the album a pile of good.

How many times during Yes’s history have you heard the words, “It needs to be shorter?”

[laughs] Well, I suppose, straightaway, “Roundabout” was a bit too long for Atlantic. There’s been easier times and there’s been harder times. And you do have to consider length. I mean, Tales (of Topographic Oceans) was a colossal undertaking.

I don’t mind if somebody says “It’s too long” or “Can you make it longer?” Most probably the answer to both is “no.” But one must never be flippant about advice. It comes to you for a reason. That’s how I used to bounce back from criticism in the ’70s, when people would say, “What do you think about the press not liking your music anymore?” You learn to flow easily within criticism and not be undermined, which is an important ingredient.

There’s an acoustic segment in “Countermovement,” during the “Anytime Soon” section, that seems to make direct reference to “Your Move.” Deliberate?

No. It’s fortunate that whenever I pull that Portuguese guitar out, something happens. The first time everybody heard it was “Your Move,” so it has a constant link to that. But after that came things like “Wonderous Stories” and “Nine Voices” and now part of “Anytime Soon.” I don’t think it’s a total reference, but there are only so many things I can play on that guitar because of the tuning. “Wonderous Stories” was a test; in fact, “Nine Voices” was a test, in a way. But I like bringing that out and having that familiar sound. I also like the newer sounds.

But one of the sounds I like best, of course, the oldest sound I’ve got is my [Gibson ES-]175. That is again all over the soloing of this album, as it’s been throughout the years of me playing other guitars. It’s generally appeared again because it’s my best guitar.

On the other side of the spectrum on Aurora is “All Hands on Deck,” a three-minute jolt of total energy. Were you just in that mood on that day?

I don’t like Yes becoming a pomp sort of band, without any rock and roll. Without rock and roll we’re asleep at the wheel. We’ve got to be a rock band; I guess that’s partly why that song is there, the reason it’s brazen and bravado-ish. I like the rock ’n’ roll element being in Yes, and that’s what that song is.

When it started out, I just had a chorus — [sings] “all hands on deck” — and I thought people might like that, just for a change, instead of a page of endless lyrics. And they didn’t; they said, “Is there just a little bit more?” So I wrote some more and it’s still quite sparse. It’s not a big story, but it is about a sinking ship, which could be a metaphor for just about anything — a sinking band, a sinking planet, a sinking environment, whatever you like.

You bust out the washboard again for “Jambustin’,” one of the bonus tracks.

One of my hidden skills is definitely the washboard. I think it’s a brilliant instrument, totally underrated.”

— Steve Howe

One of my hidden skills is definitely the washboard. On my own albums I’ve done quite a lot of washboard. I think it’s terrific. I think it’s a brilliant instrument, totally underrated.

I have a story; one day the phone rang and it was [producer] Trevor Horn, and he said to me, “I’ve got something going on with a recording here. It’s Malcolm McLaren, and he wants a washboard. Don’t you play washboard?” I said, “Yes, I’m the best in London,” and he says, “Well, you’re the only one in London. I can’t find anybody who plays it. Come in.” So I went a few days later and played on some track Trevor was producing. I quite like that story.

Is this current burst of creativity continuing? Are you starting on the next one yet?

No, we haven’t, for one big reason: due to my operation we put everything on hold. But there are some ideas that have been floated around a little bit, and as this period of a year goes through, in a few months we might choose to do something, but we don’t tell anybody when we’re doing it. So the answer is [leans into screen and whispers] “no.”

The Magnification reissue is the other major Yes release this year. What kind of perspective do you have on that album 25 years on?

I don’t know whether you remember the old TV series with Phil Silvers in it [The Phil Silvers Show, a.k.a. Sergeant Bilko]? He used to say, “Oh, it’s hell, Sarge.” So that would be my first answer; “Steve, what do you think of Magnification?” “It was hell, Sarge.”

It was really difficult, and it shouldn’t have been because there were only four of us in the band. The only reason it’s passably good is because I put my foot down and said, “Those mixers are just awful.” I couldn’t believe it; the bass, drums and the guitar became a sort of backstory to the orchestra. So I insisted that even though it was against all odds for the schedule to allow us to do it, I was going to listen to the album and make notes.

I insisted that even though it was against all odds for the schedule to allow us to do it, I was going to listen to the album and make notes.”

— Steve Howe

These are the days of faxes, as well, so you can imagine they’re sitting in the studio and they get the first fax, “at .02 do this, at 10 seconds the guitar needs to be focused. Can you turn it up there?” I went through the album thoroughly and gave them faxes, every song, and said, “It’s got to be like this. You can’t put this out without me liking it.” So, yeah, I went through that, and the only reason I can listen to it is because that sort of detail went into it.

How do you feel about the songs, in hindsight?

Oh, any of its pitfalls are overshadowed, I think, by the adventurousness of what we did there. Some of the songs were pretty adventurous. They did take arrangements to a good level. So I’m fairly happy about that. A couple of the songs shouldn’t have been there, ’cause they weren’t really good. But I think Yes sometimes compensates with a bit of charm in a song; “It’s not a great song, but it’s quite charming,” I might say to myself.

Yes toured with Deep Purple a couple of years ago, and we recently saw them reunite, for a song with one of your contemporaries, Ritchie Blackmore. What did you make of that?

I thought it was great. They’re such a lovely bunch of guys, and their lead guitarist [Simon McBride] is fantastic. To have the balls or, let’s say, the gall on both sides of that endorsement, that Ritchie was prepared to come back and play the song and also they were prepared to open it up so that he could… There you are.

Music tells all sorts of stories in one second. It’s a bit like when Art went back with Paul and you had Simon & Garfunkel again, and what a moment. What a joy. But it doesn’t mean all unions are good, because they’re not; the Union Tour of Yes [1991–’92] was unbelievably difficult, for instance.

You’ll be doing the postponed Fragile tour dates in the U.K. and Japan next year. What else is on the docket?

Something will be happening pretty big for next year with touring in the U.S. but we cannot specify anything about that at the moment. After Japan we won’t be playing the Fragile tour anymore; we’ve got a brilliant idea — I can’t tell you what it is, but I can tell you it’s absolutely brilliant. [laughs] I’m kidding, but we’ve got an idea and it seems to hang together and it’s a little different. That’s what I think keeps Yes alive, is difference. The same isn’t enjoyable. You don’t want to just add a little thing to it, a twist in the tale. You want it to be different.

After all these years, has your view of what progressive rock is changed?

It starts with the word “freedom” — to do any musical molding, any musical style-referencing. It has to have structure; Chris [Squire] was a big advocate of that. He’d say, “Steve, yeah, that’s a really nice guitar solo, but I hope you appreciate the structure.” So we weren’t the kind of band where everybody improvised. “Five Per Cent for Nothing” might sound like that, but it wasn’t. That meant you worked together to make something that did have improvisation but it also had structure.

And I think there’s the beauty of being able to put in any musical reference, whether it’s washboard [chuckles] or folk or jazz or… Blues was the thing we avoided the most, but there’s still a little bit of it in there. Really what it is is the most marvelous hodgepodge. It has to combine things, ’cause if it doesn’t it’s just a song and it doesn’t resonate. It might be a nice song, but you can’t call it prog ’cause nothing happens to it.
item.description: Plus, Howe reveals the secret skill he’s brought to Yes for decades: “I’m the best in London”

They weren’t in the same keys and they weren’t at the same tempos, but that didn’t put me off them. And then I had two instrumentals that were viable, and I was happy to offer them to Yes. So what I did was kind of transplant those two instrumentals into the two songs and sort of jiggle around with it, a bit like a jigsaw trying to find out how they fitted together.

I don’t mind if somebody says ‘It’s too long’ or ‘Can you make it longer?’ Most probably the answer to both is ‘no.’”

— Steve Howe

To be honest it was longer once, and we got some advice that maybe that idea’s gone a bit far, so we brought them back in, trimmed them back so it was back into a conceivable shell.

So that’s what happened, and everybody grew to like it, and I think it does the album a pile of good.

How many times during Yes’s history have you heard the words, “It needs to be shorter?”

[laughs] Well, I suppose, straightaway, “Roundabout” was a bit too long for Atlantic. There’s been easier times and there’s been harder times. And you do have to consider length. I mean, Tales (of Topographic Oceans) was a colossal undertaking.

I don’t mind if somebody says “It’s too long” or “Can you make it longer?” Most probably the answer to both is “no.” But one must never be flippant about advice. It comes to you for a reason. That’s how I used to bounce back from criticism in the ’70s, when people would say, “What do you think about the press not liking your music anymore?” You learn to flow easily within criticism and not be undermined, which is an important ingredient.

There’s an acoustic segment in “Countermovement,” during the “Anytime Soon” section, that seems to make direct reference to “Your Move.” Deliberate?

No. It’s fortunate that whenever I pull that Portuguese guitar out, something happens. The first time everybody heard it was “Your Move,” so it has a constant link to that. But after that came things like “Wonderous Stories” and “Nine Voices” and now part of “Anytime Soon.” I don’t think it’s a total reference, but there are only so many things I can play on that guitar because of the tuning. “Wonderous Stories” was a test; in fact, “Nine Voices” was a test, in a way. But I like bringing that out and having that familiar sound. I also like the newer sounds.

But one of the sounds I like best, of course, the oldest sound I’ve got is my [Gibson ES-]175. That is again all over the soloing of this album, as it’s been throughout the years of me playing other guitars. It’s generally appeared again because it’s my best guitar.

On the other side of the spectrum on Aurora is “All Hands on Deck,” a three-minute jolt of total energy. Were you just in that mood on that day?

I don’t like Yes becoming a pomp sort of band, without any rock and roll. Without rock and roll we’re asleep at the wheel. We’ve got to be a rock band; I guess that’s partly why that song is there, the reason it’s brazen and bravado-ish. I like the rock ’n’ roll element being in Yes, and that’s what that song is.

When it started out, I just had a chorus — [sings] “all hands on deck” — and I thought people might like that, just for a change, instead of a page of endless lyrics. And they didn’t; they said, “Is there just a little bit more?” So I wrote some more and it’s still quite sparse. It’s not a big story, but it is about a sinking ship, which could be a metaphor for just about anything — a sinking band, a sinking planet, a sinking environment, whatever you like.

You bust out the washboard again for “Jambustin’,” one of the bonus tracks.

One of my hidden skills is definitely the washboard. I think it’s a brilliant instrument, totally underrated.”

— Steve Howe

One of my hidden skills is definitely the washboard. On my own albums I’ve done quite a lot of washboard. I think it’s terrific. I think it’s a brilliant instrument, totally underrated.

I have a story; one day the phone rang and it was [producer] Trevor Horn, and he said to me, “I’ve got something going on with a recording here. It’s Malcolm McLaren, and he wants a washboard. Don’t you play washboard?” I said, “Yes, I’m the best in London,” and he says, “Well, you’re the only one in London. I can’t find anybody who plays it. Come in.” So I went a few days later and played on some track Trevor was producing. I quite like that story.

Is this current burst of creativity continuing? Are you starting on the next one yet?

No, we haven’t, for one big reason: due to my operation we put everything on hold. But there are some ideas that have been floated around a little bit, and as this period of a year goes through, in a few months we might choose to do something, but we don’t tell anybody when we’re doing it. So the answer is [leans into screen and whispers] “no.”

The Magnification reissue is the other major Yes release this year. What kind of perspective do you have on that album 25 years on?

I don’t know whether you remember the old TV series with Phil Silvers in it [The Phil Silvers Show, a.k.a. Sergeant Bilko]? He used to say, “Oh, it’s hell, Sarge.” So that would be my first answer; “Steve, what do you think of Magnification?” “It was hell, Sarge.”

It was really difficult, and it shouldn’t have been because there were only four of us in the band. The only reason it’s passably good is because I put my foot down and said, “Those mixers are just awful.” I couldn’t believe it; the bass, drums and the guitar became a sort of backstory to the orchestra. So I insisted that even though it was against all odds for the schedule to allow us to do it, I was going to listen to the album and make notes.

I insisted that even though it was against all odds for the schedule to allow us to do it, I was going to listen to the album and make notes.”

— Steve Howe

These are the days of faxes, as well, so you can imagine they’re sitting in the studio and they get the first fax, “at .02 do this, at 10 seconds the guitar needs to be focused. Can you turn it up there?” I went through the album thoroughly and gave them faxes, every song, and said, “It’s got to be like this. You can’t put this out without me liking it.” So, yeah, I went through that, and the only reason I can listen to it is because that sort of detail went into it.

How do you feel about the songs, in hindsight?

Oh, any of its pitfalls are overshadowed, I think, by the adventurousness of what we did there. Some of the songs were pretty adventurous. They did take arrangements to a good level. So I’m fairly happy about that. A couple of the songs shouldn’t have been there, ’cause they weren’t really good. But I think Yes sometimes compensates with a bit of charm in a song; “It’s not a great song, but it’s quite charming,” I might say to myself.

Yes toured with Deep Purple a couple of years ago, and we recently saw them reunite, for a song with one of your contemporaries, Ritchie Blackmore. What did you make of that?

I thought it was great. They’re such a lovely bunch of guys, and their lead guitarist [Simon McBride] is fantastic. To have the balls or, let’s say, the gall on both sides of that endorsement, that Ritchie was prepared to come back and play the song and also they were prepared to open it up so that he could… There you are.

Music tells all sorts of stories in one second. It’s a bit like when Art went back with Paul and you had Simon & Garfunkel again, and what a moment. What a joy. But it doesn’t mean all unions are good, because they’re not; the Union Tour of Yes [1991–’92] was unbelievably difficult, for instance.

You’ll be doing the postponed Fragile tour dates in the U.K. and Japan next year. What else is on the docket?

Something will be happening pretty big for next year with touring in the U.S. but we cannot specify anything about that at the moment. After Japan we won’t be playing the Fragile tour anymore; we’ve got a brilliant idea — I can’t tell you what it is, but I can tell you it’s absolutely brilliant. [laughs] I’m kidding, but we’ve got an idea and it seems to hang together and it’s a little different. That’s what I think keeps Yes alive, is difference. The same isn’t enjoyable. You don’t want to just add a little thing to it, a twist in the tale. You want it to be different.

After all these years, has your view of what progressive rock is changed?

It starts with the word “freedom” — to do any musical molding, any musical style-referencing. It has to have structure; Chris [Squire] was a big advocate of that. He’d say, “Steve, yeah, that’s a really nice guitar solo, but I hope you appreciate the structure.” So we weren’t the kind of band where everybody improvised. “Five Per Cent for Nothing” might sound like that, but it wasn’t. That meant you worked together to make something that did have improvisation but it also had structure.

And I think there’s the beauty of being able to put in any musical reference, whether it’s washboard [chuckles] or folk or jazz or… Blues was the thing we avoided the most, but there’s still a little bit of it in there. Really what it is is the most marvelous hodgepodge. It has to combine things, ’cause if it doesn’t it’s just a song and it doesn’t resonate. It might be a nice song, but you can’t call it prog ’cause nothing happens to it.
